sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
This course introduces the fundamental principles governing aircraft flight, including basic
aerodynamics, atmospheric properties, aircraft performance, stability and control, propulsion systems,
and Hypersonic vehicles. Students explore the forces acting on an aircraft and the engineering concepts
that enable safe and efficient flight. The course provides a foundational understanding of flight
mechanics and aircraft systems, preparing students for advanced studies in aerospace engineering.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
Following are the scope and objective of this course:
a.  Understand the fundamentals of flight: Introduce the basic principles of aerodynamics, the four
forces of flight, and the physical concepts governing aircraft motion.
b.  Study aircraft systems and performance: Develop an understanding of aircraft structures,
propulsion systems, stability, control, and performance under various operating conditions.
c.  Apply engineering principles: Use fundamental concepts of mathematics, physics, and
engineering to analyse and solve introductory flight-related problems.
d.  Build a foundation for advanced aerospace studies: Prepare students for higher-level courses in
flight mechanics, aircraft design, aerospace propulsion, and aviation engineering.

sections.heading: Course Learning Outcomes
sections.text:
Upon successful completion of this course, the students will have the following learning outcomes:
a.  Explain the principles of flight by describing the four fundamental forces (lift, weight, thrust,
and drag) and their interactions during flight.
b.  Analyse atmospheric effects on flight by interpreting how atmospheric properties influence
aircraft performance and operations.
c.  Apply basic aerodynamic concepts to evaluate the performance of airfoil, wings, and aircraft
under various flight conditions.
Page 1 of 5
Birla Institute of Technology & Science, Pilani
Pilani Campus
ACADEMIC - UNDER GRADUATE STUDIES DIVISION
d.  Evaluate aircraft performance by estimating take-off, climb, cruise, descent, landing, range, and
endurance characteristics using fundamental engineering principles.
e.  Describe aircraft stability and control and explain how control surfaces affect aircraft motion
and manoeuvrability.
f.  Compare aircraft propulsion systems, including propeller- and jet-powered engines, and explain
their operating principles and performance characteristics.
g.  Learn Hypersonic flight, concepts of Newtonian theory and its application to Hypersonic
vehicles.
h.  Solve introductory flight-related engineering problems using mathematics, physics, and
computational tools where appropriate.
i.   Interpret the relationship between aircraft design and flight performance, recognizing how
design choices affect efficiency, safety, and operational capability.
j.  Communicate technical concepts related to flight through written reports, calculations, and
engineering discussions

sections.heading: Method of Conduct of the Course
sections.text:
The course will be conducted using a combination of instructor-centred and learner-centred methods.
The former would involve instructor-led class lectures and problem solving exercises while the latter
would involve student-led collaborative group projects using simulation for experiential learning,
technical report writing, and presentations.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Properties  of  living  systems,  Biological  macromolecules,  Basic  physiological  processes,
Genetics, Photosynthesis, Metabolism and Cellular systems. Experiments including but not limited
to Microscopy, Quantification of Biomolecules, Chlorophyll extraction, Water potential in plant
tissues and Cell cycle analysis.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The course  is aimed to provide a broad introduction to the major principles and topics in
biology. The relationship of the living organism with its environment at the molecular level is
highlighted in line with modern research in biological sciences. By the end of the course, the student
would have gained an overall understanding of the essential aspects of biology – both as a basic
science and as a branch with wide-ranging applications in industry, medicine and human health. It
is also expected that using the acquired knowledge, he/she would be able to devise/suggest strategies
to  solve some  of the imminent problems faced by mankind and the world at large through
technological solutions. Students shall also get hands-on experience on fundamental aspects of
practical biology.

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
This course is intended to offer an introduction to the world of Biological
Chemistry. The course deals with the structure, properties, and significance of the major groups of
biochemical compounds (amino acids, proteins, carbohydrates, nucleic acids, and lipids), the
bioenergetics, enzyme mechanisms and regulation of the central metabolic pathways. Efforts will
be made to include the recent advances and methodologies related to biochemistry. This would
help students going for higher level activities, appreciation of biochemical problems, evaluation
and problem solving.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Introduction  and  classification  of  microbes;  isolation,  cultivation,  physiological  and  biochemical
characterization of microbes; structure, physiology and genetics of microbial cell; synthetic microbiology;
host parasite relationship; physical chemical methods of controlling microbes; antimicrobial drugs; clinical
microbiology; microbiology of soil, water and food; and related lab components.

sections.heading: Scope & Objective
sections.text:
This course deals with the structure, physiology, genetics and growth of various microorganisms as well as
their control. Emphasis will be given on microbes and their role in human health, environment and industry.

sections.heading: Course Outline
sections.text:
Fundamental processes of life at cellular and sub-cellular levels; cell environments; membrane
transport; cell movements; division and control mechanisms.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
A fundamental branch in biological sciences, cell biology exposes the learner to the structural
and functional organization and working of the cell, the basic unit of life. The field is dynamic
and constantly evolving. This course will give an introduction to this branch of biology, by
providing experimental data wherever possible. Some of the major topics covered include the
working of the cell at microscopic and molecular levels, their physiological properties, structure,
intracellular organelles, interactions with microenvironments, division, regulatory mechanisms
and related experimental procedures. The topics learned in this course will also be foundational
for advanced courses in cell and molecular biology, as well as genetics and developmental
biology.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
The course deals with theoretical aspects and selected experiments of recombinant DNA manipulation.
Emphasis will be placed on procedures to create chimeric molecules using examples from actual experimental
work. Vector designing, PCR, DNA sequencing, in vitro mutagenesis, cloning in prokaryotic and eukaryotic
systems and whole genome approaches will be covered.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the course
sections.text:
Almost every field of modern experimental biology relies heavily on DNA manipulation techniques. This
course will expose the student to the foundations and principles underlying such molecular biology methods
and give a brief yet broad overview of the recent trends and applications of recombinant DNA technology.

edition). New York: Blackwell Science, 2006.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Basic functional processes in animals; like homeostasis, membrane physiology, digestive, respiratory,
excretory, circulatory, reproductive, nervous, sensory, muscular, endocrine systems will be studied at
structural, functional, cellular and molecular level.

sections.heading: Scope & Objective
sections.text:
This course attempts to bring the awareness among students for major features of animal physiology and co-
relate that to the human physiology. Emphasis will be on structure and function relationship and importanc
of every organ. In addition, the course will also discuss about some of the diseases that are associated with
complication in different organs.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
a. Integration of multiple organ systems to regulate and maintain homeostasis between the internal and external
environments.
b. Explore the process of enzymatic digestion and its physiological outcomes within the digestive tract.
c. Functional mechanisms of the human kidneys in regulating fluid homeostasis and urine formation.
d. Overview of the cardiac cycle, electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation, types of circulatory vessels,
regulation of systolic and diastolic blood pressure, and the various cellular components of blood.
e. Anatomical  and  functional  organization  of  nervous  system,  including  its  structural  and  spatial
characteristics.
f. The role of hormones in regulating homeostasis and supporting essential physiological functions.
g. Understanding gas  partial  pressures,  intrapleural pressure dynamics, lung volumes and  capacities,
respiratory disorders, and the oxygen-carrying capacity of hemoglobin.
h. Study of sarcomere structure, the molecular mechanism of muscle contraction, the physiological basis of
rigor mortis, and the phenomenon of muscle twitching.
i. Exploration of the regulatory mechanisms governing gametogenesis, fertilization, and progression of
pregnancy.

2nd edition, 2013, Brook/Cole Cengage Learning, Singapore

sections.heading: Method of Conduct of the Course
sections.text:
The Animal Physiology course will be delivered through a combination of interactive lectures, tutorials
(including lab based components during the tutorial hours), and group discussions to promote both conceptual
understanding and hands-on experience.
Lectures: Core physiological concepts will be taught through structured classroom lectures, supported by
visual aids such as diagrams, animations, and clinical case examples to enhance comprehension.
Tutorials and Group Discussions: These sessions will focus on clarifying doubts, exploring clinical
correlations, and encouraging critical thinking through problem-solving activities and peer interactions. In
addition, during some of the tutorial classes, practical sessions will be carried out to examine/ prepare cross-
sections of fixed tissues and performing tissue staining to facilitate a detailed understanding of the cross-
sectional anatomy of various organs, including the heart and kidney.
Assessments: The course will include periodic quizzes, written assignments, viva voce, and mid-term and
end-term examinations to evaluate student progress and understanding.
Self-directed Learning: Students will be encouraged to engage in independent study through guided reading,
online resources, and optional assignments to deepen their knowledge beyond the classroom.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Biomolecular Conformations, Structural genomics and proteomics, protein folding,
Forcefield, Simulation, Conformational analysis, ab initio structure prediction, comparative modeling, lattice
models, usage of modeling packages.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The course is designed to provide students the firsthand experience
of potential utility of biomolecular modeling especially in concurrent pharmaceutical research, and in cell and
structural biology.  It describes  the  functionality, advantages, and  limitations of standard computing
strategies for the simulation of biomolecules. Provide a working knowledge of freely available software to
carry out independent research projects in biomolecular modeling and explore the possibilities for modeling
to assist in the process of determination, analyzing, evaluating, displaying, and retrieving of 3D structure data
in a research or industry laboratory environment.

sections.text:
Enzyme nomenclature and classification; isolation and purification; structures; kinetics; regulation of
enzymatic reactions; evaluation of enzymes and other proteins.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
This course is designed to provide a broad introduction about enzymes, including their isolation,
purification, structure and kinetics. Efforts will be made to understand the molecular basis of how enzymes
catalyze the biological and non-natural reactions. Emphasis will be given to study the practical and
industrial application of enzymes. This course integrates basics as well as current advances in enzymology
and will create research interest among the students.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
The course will deal extensively with topics like molecular basis of T and B
cell antigen recognition and activation. Immunity to microbes and diseases caused by humoral
and cell mediated immune responses will be covered and emphasis placed on congenital and
acquired immuno-deficiencies. Advanced topics like antibody engineering will be discussed with
the help of review articles.

sections.heading: Scope and Objectives
sections.text:
The course intends to familiarize the students with modern concepts in
immunology. The endeavor will be to highlight concepts in immunology, which would have an
influence on understanding the fascinating entity which comprises the body’s immune system
and ancillary procedure of therapy.

sections.heading: Course of Description
sections.text:
Molecular taxonomy, Systematic Microbiology, Study of molecular
diversity of microorganisms, Molecular tools employed in the study of microbial ecology, clinical
microbiology,  human-microbe   interaction,  molecular   plant-microbe   interaction,   applied
microbiology, and synthetic microbiology.

sections.heading: Scope & Objective of the Course
sections.text:
This course deals with an in-depth study of microbial taxonomy and evolution, as well as the
molecular  aspects  of  microbe-host  interactions.  In  addition,  it  includes  applied  aspects  of
microorganisms being  utilized  in industry and human  health.  It  also emphasizes on recent
development in microbial genomics, nanotechnology and biotechnology.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Introduction  and  classification  of  microbes;  isolation,  cultivation,  physiological  and  biochemical
characterization of microbes; structure, physiology and genetics of microbial cell; synthetic microbiology;
host parasite relationship; physical chemical methods of controlling microbes; antimicrobial drugs; clinical
microbiology; microbiology of soil, water and food; and related lab components.

sections.heading: Scope & Objective
sections.text:
This course deals with the structure, physiology, genetics and growth of various microorganisms as well as
their control. Emphasis will be given on microbes and their role in human health, environment and industry.

Exp. 5: Staining of fungus- Lactophenol cotton blue staining

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Application of biotechnology to the management of environmental problems. Biotechnology for
enhanced plant and animal production through biological insecticides, herbicides resistance, mineral
cycling, conservation of genetic resources and biological nitrogen fixation. Use of biotechnological
processes for pollution control, bioremediation of toxicants and treatment of domestic and industrial
wastes. Ethical issues related with the release of genetically modified organism.

sections.heading: Scope and Objectives
sections.text:
The major objective of this course is to impart knowledge on application of biotechnological processes
for betterment of environment. This course is designed to make the student understand the various
biological phenomena, which can be exploited to save environment from eventual deterioration.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Biostatistics and Biomodeling course has two components. Biostatistics
part will provide an introduction to the basic concepts of statistical methods to equip students
with statistical reasoning in their fields of study. Topics include variables in biology, Standard
deviation; correlation and regression analysis; significance tests; chi square, t-test, ANOVA
etc. Emphasis is placed on the application of fundamental concepts to real world situations.
Biomodeling  is  designed  to  provide  students  the  first-hand  experience  of  modelling
biomolecules  to  elucidate  the  relationships between  sequence,  structure and  function.
Specifically,  different computing  strategies  for  the simulation of biomolecules  will be
discussed with regard to their utility, advantages, and limitations.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The student would learn how to collect data suitable for
statistical analyses, understand the general features of the data collected, making statistical
inferences and likelihood of occurrence of an event using probability calculations and tests of
significance.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Properties  of  living  systems,  Biological  macromolecules,  Basic  physiological  processes,
Genetics, Photosynthesis, Metabolism and Cellular systems. Experiments including but not limited
to Microscopy, Quantification of Biomolecules, Chlorophyll extraction, Water potential in plant
tissues and Cell cycle analysis.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The course  is aimed to provide a broad introduction to the major principles and topics in
biology. The relationship of the living organism with its environment at the molecular level is
highlighted in line with modern research in biological sciences. By the end of the course, the student
would have gained an overall understanding of the essential aspects of biology – both as a basic
science and as a branch with wide-ranging applications in industry, medicine and human health. It
is also expected that using the acquired knowledge, he/she would be able to devise/suggest strategies
to  solve some  of the imminent problems faced by mankind and the world at large through
technological solutions. Students shall also get hands-on experience on fundamental aspects of
practical biology.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Enzyme nomenclature and classification; isolation and purification; structures; kinetics; regulation of
enzymatic reactions; evaluation of enzymes and other proteins.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
This course is designed to provide a broad introduction about enzymes, including their isolation,
purification, structure and kinetics. Efforts will be made to understand the molecular basis of how enzymes
catalyze the biological and non-natural reactions. Emphasis will be given to study the practical and
industrial application of enzymes. This course integrates basics as well as current advances in enzymology
and will create research interest among the students.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
The food sector is very important from the economical point of view, and is
one of the industrial areas where Biotechnology has played and still plays a pivotal role. In this course,
a general view of the basic aspects (physical-chemical aspects, structure, spoilage), of foods and their
processing and preservation techniques will be taught. Further the most relevant aspects for a future
biotechnologist in the food industry will be studied: role of microorganisms and enzymes for the
production and transformation of foods and most recent advances in foods made of/with genetically
modified organisms. In addition, food safety and quality management along with food waste
management will be covered. Finally, case studies of successful entrepreneurship ventures in Food
Biotechnology will be discussed.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The aim of this course is providing the students with basic
knowledge about the applications of Biotechnology in the food industry and in food-related sectors.
These include the preservation tools used, production of recombinant proteins and additives to use in
food technology, transgenic foods, diagnostic system used in food industry including advanced
techniques like biosensors and artificial intelligence, and ethics and safety of food biotechnology.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
In this course students will be assigned study work in advanced areas of professional
interest. Each student will work under the overall supervision and guidance of a faculty member and will  in
the end submit a project report encompassing critical review of the material studied.
The organization and evaluation of the course would be achieved through seminars, group discussions, project
report etc. The course will be conducted by the team of teachers who provide guidance for study work.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The course aims at covering topics in advanced areas of professional
interest and will be conducted on self-study and seminar basis. The course is specially designed to provide an
opportunity to the students for development of their academic skills and logical thinking through open ended
advanced study oriented activities. As a part of education, this course follows a method of learning and,
therefore, the student's actual day-to-day task involvement would constitute the central thread of the learning
process. The evaluation will recognize this aspect by demanding day-to-day productivity, punctuality and final
achievement of the student.

sections.heading: Operation of the course
sections.text:
The plan of work for each student will be decided by the respective Instructors/supervisors. Each student
should adhere to the plan of work decided for and should regularly monitor the progress of the course
accordingly. The final report encompassing critical review of the material studied will be submitted to the
Instructor-in-charge through Departmental Committee on Academics (DCA) by the end of the class work.

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
Emotional & Social Intelligence, Relationships & Identity, Laws & Campus Policies and
Practice, Inappropriate Behavior & Consent, Substance Abuse, Emotional Maturity &
Communication, Recognizing Harm & Promoting Safety.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
This is the first of a two-part course that is a General Institute Requirement, for all
students in the first year of any program. It is intended to equip students with core
emotional,  social and  legal  literacy  for a healthy campus  life.  This  includes
conversations around gender, sexuality, mental health, understanding of boundaries
and consent, prevention of sexual misconduct, promoting responsible digital behavior
and building awareness against substance abuse.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
At the end of this part of the course, the student will be able to
CLO1.Recognize and apply core emotional and social skills for campus well-being,
including stress management, empathy, and self-awareness.
CLO2. Understand and navigate relationships with peers, faculty, and family, with
sensitivity to gender identity, sexuality, and high achievement pressures.
CLO3. Identify and challenge harmful social myths and stereotypes related to gender
roles, masculinity, and interpersonal dynamics.
CLO4. Establish and respect personal boundaries in social, academic, and digital
contexts.
CLO5. Demonstrate awareness of campus policies, legal protections (including
POSH), and the consequences of sexual misconduct.
CLO6. Understand reporting mechanisms and institutional responsibilities in
promoting a safe and inclusive campus environment.
CLO7. Engage with mental health literacy, recognize signs of emotional distress, and
promote openness around mental well-being.
CLO8. Reflect on individual responsibility in building a safe, respectful, and
accountable student community.

sections.heading: Course Format & Weekly Workflow
sections.text:
-  The course is fully online, with all content on a separate learning interface hosted
on the Campus LMS - Moodle, and is asynchronous.
-  Content will be released weekly and typically takes 30–60 minutes to complete.
-  Each week, we’ll let you know what to focus on - whether it’s something to reflect
on, apply in real life, or just be aware of. You don’t have to memorize anything.
Just bring your honest attention, and we’ll guide you through it.
-  Each week’s material will have a one-week deadline, except during campus
festival weeks, where deadlines will be set before the festival begins.
-  No content will be released one week before and during the mid-semester
exams, and the course will end one week before the comprehensive exams.
-  The content must be accessed by logging in to the campus LMS (Moodle).
-  Each week ends with a quiz on the learning interface. A full score is required to
proceed and multiple attempts are allowed.
-  Completing that quiz will unlock a corresponding Moodle quiz, which you must
attempt to mark the week’s content as complete.
-  Your progress is automatically saved on Moodle, so you can pause and return to
the material anytime. Closing the window/tab will not result in losing progress.
-  We encourage you to share your feedback! You can post your thoughts and
questions on the discussion forum, or use the feedback forms provided at the
end of each week’s content. Our instructor team will respond to queries.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
The course includes fundamentals and techniques of technical drawing and standard practices of
the same so that design ideas can be adequately communicated and produced. It introduces students
to the theories of projection and the concepts of engineering drawing using the most widely used
CAD application software, AutoCAD. Basic AutoCAD 2023 commands will also be introduced. The
course covers the following topics: Introduction to AutoCAD basic commands; theory of projections;
orthographic projections; isometric projections; projection of points, lines, planes and solids; section
of solids; developments of surfaces.

sections.heading: Scope and objective of the course
sections.text:
Computerized drafting provides accurate and easily modifiable graphics entities, easy data storage
and retrieval facility and enhances creativity.
Upon successful completion of this course, the student will be able to:
  Read and interpret engineering drawings
   Identify the three principal projection planes
  Draw 2-dimensional orthographic projections from given 3-dimensional views
  Create an isometric drawing using AutoCAD
  Comprehend orthographic and multiview projection
  Apply the concept of cutting planes to create the various types of sectional views
  Become conversant with appropriate use of AutoCAD software for drafting.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Concepts and laws of thermodynamics; thermodynamic properties; applications to closed and
open systems; entropy and entropy generation; availability.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
Thermodynamics deals with energy, matter, and the laws governing their interactions.
•  To learn usefulness of laws of thermodynamics in the design of processes, devices, and
systems involving effective utilization of energy and matter.
•  To understand the fundamentals and concepts of the laws of thermodynamics as applied
to control mass and control volume systems.
•  To apply the fundamentals and concepts of the laws of thermodynamics to control mass
and control volume systems and analyze them.
•  To examine  the  performance  of  engineering  devices  in  light  of  the  laws  of
thermodynamics.
3.    To define, understand, apply and analyze the concept of irreversibility and availability to
thermodynamic systems and to evaluate second law efficiency of thermodynamics systems
and devices.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
This course is designed to provide students with a
comprehensive understanding of how science and technology interact with societal structures,
economic  systems, and  global  governance. The  course  begins  with an  introduction  to
foundational perspectives on technological change and scientific knowledge systems, offering a
basic orientation  to how technologies are developed and adopted.  It then moves  to the
examination of Intellectual Property Rights and Innovation, focusing on real-world issues such
as patent disputes, corporate competition, and the strategic control of innovation. The third and
final module explores Science, Technology, and Social Stratification, encouraging students to
consider how power, inequality, and institutional interests influence technological priorities and
outcomes. Overall,  it  critically assesses the  societal  responsibilities and consequences of
scientific and technological work in contemporary settings.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Linear equations and matrices, Determinants, Basis of Rn , Eigen Value, Eigen
Vector, Linear transformations on Rn . Linear Programming: Geometric Solutions, Simplex Method,
Duality, Post optimal Analysis, Transportation and Assignment Problem. Nonlinear Programming
(Unconstrained optimization).

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The course is made for Pharmacy students keeping in mind the importance of Linear Algebra and Linear
programming problems and their possible applications in various fields of science and engineering. Linear
algebra begins with vectors and matrices – two of the most important practical concepts in mathematics.
Whereas Linear programming is a method to achieve the best outcome in a mathematical model whose
requirements are represented by linear relationships. Linear programming can be applied to various fields of
study. It is used in business and economics, but can also be utilized for some engineering problems. Industries
that use linear programming models include transportation, energy, telecommunications, and manufacturing.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
CLO1. Apply  the  concepts  of  matrix  algebra,  systems  of  linear  equations,  vector  spaces,  linear
transformations, and eigenvalues/eigenvectors to  solve mathematical problems  arising  in science and
engineering.
CLO2. Formulate and solve linear programming problems using graphical and simplex-based methods,
analyze duality and post-optimality, and apply optimization techniques to transportation and assignment
problems.
CLO3. Analyze and solve basic nonlinear optimization problems using appropriate numerical optimization
techniques, and interpret the results in the context of engineering and pharmaceutical applications.

title: PROCESS ENGINEERING

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
Basic concepts related to heat transfer, mass transfer and flow of fluid,
processes and equipment involved in extraction and filtration; mixing and granulation; size reduction
and  classification, evaporation and  distillation, drying and  crystallization, humidification and
dehumidification. Materials of construction. Theory of compression and consolidation of solids.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
This course introduces students to the fundamental principles and practical
aspects of pharmaceutical engineering, with a focus on key unit operations involved in the
development and manufacturing of pharmaceutical formulations. It covers a wide range of processes
including  size  reduction and  separation,  drying,  evaporation,  distillation,  mixing,  filtration,
centrifugation, extraction, compression, crystallization, and materials of plant construction. The
course emphasizes the selection, operation, and application of various equipment used in the
pharmaceutical industry.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
a.  Complete understanding of the principles of key pharmaceutical unit operations
b. Knowledge of the construction, working, and applications of various equipment used in
pharmaceutical unit operations such as size reduction, drying, distillation, mixing, filtration,
centrifugation, and extraction.
c.  Ability to apply principles of pharmaceutical engineering to analyze and optimize unit operations
for enhanced process efficiency, cost-effectiveness, and product quality in pharmaceutical
manufacturing.

and its conservation, environmental pollution, social issues and the environment, and environmental impact
assessment.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The United Nations Conference on Environment and Development
(UNCED) held in Rio De Janero in 1992, the 1994 conference on United Nations Framework Convention on
Climate Change (UNFCCC), and a very recent 2015 Paris Agreement have created awareness among the
people around the globe about the deteriorating condition of Earth’s environment. It has warned us not to be
ignorant of the environmental issues. In lieu of the situation, the Hon’ble Supreme Court directed the UGC
to introduce a basic course on environment for undergraduate students in India.
The course is designed to cover all aspects of environment [Ecological including biotic (flora- fauna) and
abiotic (air, water, soil & geography), social, economic and aesthetical]. The course is of interdisciplinary
nature dealing with social, biological & engineering aspects of environment. The role of biotic and abiotic
factors in the functioning of the environment, the impact of anthropogenic activities on the environment,
different environmental pollutants, its impact and management strategies; and ecological, socio-political and
economic issues will be discussed with appropriate real-life examples and case studies. The course would also
provide insight into practical solutions to different environmental issues. Finally, important concepts of
environmental impact assessment from all the above mentioned sources would be dealt with. The interested
students can take the learnings forward from this point and enrich themselves further by doing other
electives/projects in these areas.

title: Foundations of Data Structures and Algorithms

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Algorithm Analysis – Mathematical preliminaries, Sorting Algorithms, Search Algorithms, Linear
Structures, Non-Linear Structures, Hashing, Graphs and Algorithms.
(Open elective for non-B.E. Computer Science students)

sections.heading: Scope & Objective of the Course
sections.text:
A data structure is a way to organize large amounts of data, their relationships, and the opera-
tions that can be applied to them. This course focuses on applying data structures like stacks,
queues, linked lists, heaps, trees, and graphs, along with algorithmic techniques such as brute-
force, greedy, divide-and- conquer, and dynamic programming, to solve real-world problems, in-
cluding shortest paths in maps, spell checking, and social network analysis.
Objectives
• Apply basic data structures (stacks, queues, linked lists, trees) to solve programming prob-
lems.
• Implement advanced data structures (graphs, balanced search trees, hash tables, priority
queues) for complex applications.
• Use algorithmic techniques (brute-force, greedy, divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming)
to address real-world challenges.
• Develop skills to design and implement data abstractions for problem-solving.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
CLO1. Apply appropriate data structures such as arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees,
graphs, and hash tables to solve computational problems.
CLO2. Perform a basic analysis and comparison of algorithms based on correctness, effi-
ciency, and suitability for different problem domains.
1
CLO3. Design and implement solutions using fundamental algorithmic paradigms, including
divide-and-conquer, greedy, and dynamic programming.
CLO4. Develop efficient programs by selecting suitable data structures and algorithms for
real-world applications.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
This course provides students with a foundation in engineering design practice and prepares them for discipline-specific
advanced courses in engineering design. Students will gain experience in the use of digital design techniques and
management of larger open-ended, team-based engineering design tasks in a project-based learning environment.
Students will learn to create detailed designs of real-world products and systems by applying design thinking and
scientific principles. Students will learn a range of design techniques to contextualize, evaluate, and communicate
designs, from generating ideas via sketching to development of digital models and detailed technical drawings that meet
the international standards. Students will develop foundation skills in computer-aided design (CAD) techniques to
generate 3D models of products and assemblies and learn to integrate them in augmented and virtual reality tools.

sections.heading: Course Contents
sections.text:
Engineering Design process, Introduction to Engineering Drawing, Introduction to Orthographic
Projections, Projections of points, lines, planes, and solid objects, Sectional views, Manufacturing processes and
materials, Fits and Tolerances, Isometric Drawing, Introduction to Solid Modelling, Assembly drawings

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The scope and objectives of the course are as follows:
1.  Apply key elements of the design process and scientific principles to create detailed design of a product that
meets engineering requirements and standards.
2.  Generate and interpret engineering technical drawings of parts and assemblies according to engineering design
standards; and
3.  Use CAD software to generate a computer model of a well-defined part or assembly.

title: GAME THEORY & ITS APPLICATIONS

sections.heading: COURSE DESCRIPTION
sections.text:
This course introduces the fundamental concepts and analytical tools of game theory for studying strategic interactions
among rational decision-makers. It covers the construction and classification of games with complete and incomplete
Information, strategic behavior, and solution concepts, including dominant strategy equilibrium, iterated elimination of
strictly dominated strategies (IESDS), Nash equilibrium, mixed strategy equilibrium, and static and dynamic games with
and without complete Information. It also includes extensive-form games, finite- and infinitely-repeated games, Bayesian
games, and the integration of linear programming with game-theoretic analysis. Emphasis is placed on applications to
economics and public policy, including social choice and voting theory, trade, environmental economics, industrial
organization, auctions, negotiations, and other strategic decision-making problems.

sections.heading: SCOPE AND OBJECTIVE OF THE COURSE
sections.text:
Game Theory is a tool and is a beautiful mix of mathematics, economics, and psychology. Game theory is a technique for
analyzing strategic problems across diverse settings. The foundation of Game Theory was laid by John von Neumann, who
proved the fundamental minimax theorem in 1928 and published a book (co-authored with Oskar Morgenstern), Theory of
Games and Economic Behavior, in 1944. Game Theory became a buzzword and attained particular glamour, with the Nobel
Prize going to John Nash for his contributions to the Field, which has found applications in almost every branch of
knowledge. Broadly, Game Theory can be divided into cooperative and non-cooperative game theory. This course deals
only with non-cooperative games. The main objective is to introduce students to Game Theory & Its applications to the real
world as a tool for logical thinking in a strategic interaction setting.

sections.heading: COURSE LEARNING OUTCOMES
sections.text:
The course would aim to illustrate economic & other real-world concepts and to make students adept at approaching
financial problems from a game-theoretic perspective.
CLO1) Understand the Fundamentals of Game Theory, including game construction, analysis, and solutions.

sections.heading: Course Format & Weekly Workflow
sections.text:
The course will be conducted using a blended, student-centered, and outcome-based approach, incorporating
regular lectures (three per week to study core concepts and applications through the usage of Blackboard &
multimedia tools such as PowerPoint slides and video clippings) and interactive discussions during lectures (to
encourage discussion on real-life cases and to promote critical thinking). The students’ progress throughout the
course will be evaluated through a continuous assessment approach in accordance with the institute’s academic
regulations. The grading will be relative and in accordance with the BITS academic regulations. The course will
use NALANDA, a learning management system (LMS), to display course information, including lecture
slides/notes, practice sheets, solution materials, and other related materials. All notices will also be published on
NALANDA.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
This course provides a comprehensive introduction to artificial intelligence techniques for robotic systems with
emphasis on adaptive learning, machine learning, and cognitive decision making. Topics include: Evolution of
intelligent robotics; adaptive learning algorithms; biologically inspired learning using Dynamic Hebbian Learning
and adaptive oscillators; statistical learning and adaptive estimation; data-driven modelling of serial-chain
manipulator kinematics using neural networks; reinforcement learning for robot trajectory planning and decision
making; and high-level robot control through large language models/vision language models (using camera
sensors). Each module contains hands-on sessions and project-based learning to emphasize implementation of
intelligent algorithms for adaptation, learning, and autonomous algorithm for robotics.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
This course introduces the fundamental concepts of Artificial Intelligence for Robotics through the lens of
adaptive, data-driven, and cognitive robotic systems. Unlike conventional robotics courses that primarily focus on
analytical modelling and control, this course emphasizes how robots can learn, adapt, and make intelligent
decisions using modern AI techniques while remaining grounded in classical robotics principles.
Students will explore multiple paradigms of robot intelligence, ranging from adaptive learning algorithms and
biologically inspired learning mechanisms to neural networks, reinforcement learning, and high-level cognitive
reasoning using vision and large language models. Through hands-on experiments, students will investigate how
intelligent algorithms can be applied to serial-chain robotic manipulators for learning kinematics, trajectory
generation, sensor adaptation, and autonomous task execution.
Course Outcome:
Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:
CO1   Explain and compare adaptive, statistical, machine learning, and AI-based approaches for developing
intelligent robotic systems.
CO2  Develop and implement adaptive learning algorithms, including Dynamic Hebbian Learning and statistical
learning methods, for robotic sensing, adaptation, and motion generation.
CO3  Design and evaluate neural network and reinforcement learning approaches for solving robot kinematics
and trajectory planning problems in serial-chain manipulators.
CO4  Develop AI-enabled robotic applications that integrate vision to generate high-level task commands for
autonomous robotic manipulation.

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
Fuzzy sets, fuzzy binary relations, fuzzy logic, fuzzy reasoning, applications in decision making, control theory,
expert systems, artificial intelligence etc.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
The course aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the fundamental concepts of fuzzy sets, fuzzy relations,
fuzzy logic, and fuzzy reasoning, along with their applications in decision making, control theory, expert systems,
artificial intelligence, and other interdisciplinary areas. Emphasis is placed on developing analytical, computational,
and problem-solving skills through real-world applications. Each student is required to undertake a project involving
the application of fuzzy logic, which may be study-oriented, computer-oriented, simulation-based, or model-based, and
provides an opportunity to explore research articles and recent developments in fuzzy logic and its applications.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
CLO1. Explain the fundamental concepts and mathematical foundations of fuzzy sets, fuzzy numbers, fuzzy relations,
and fuzzy logic.
CLO2. Formulate and analyze problems involving fuzzy relations, fuzzy reasoning, fuzzy inference, and related
logical structures.
CLO3. Apply fuzzy logic techniques to real-world problems in decision making, control systems, expert systems,
artificial intelligence, and other interdisciplinary areas.
CLO4. Develop and evaluate a fuzzy logic-based project using appropriate computational tools, with reference to
relevant research literature and contemporary applications.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Introduction to HCI in the AI era; Understanding People: Perception, Motor control,
Cognition, Needs, and Experience; User Research:  Interviews, Field  research, and Survey  research;
Understanding Interaction: Usability Engineering, Information and control, Dialogue, Tool use, Automation,
and  Rationality; User  Interfaces:  Input  devices,  Displays,  Interaction  techniques, and  Reality-based
interaction; Design: Cognition, Practice, and Processes; Engineering: Systems, Design engineering, Safety
and risk, and Computational representations and models; Evaluation: Analytical methods, Think-aloud
studies, and Experiment.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
At the completion of this course, students will be able to:
•  Understand the concepts and theories of human-AI interaction. Furthermore, they will be able to
explain basic concepts from the relevant theories in cognitive and social sciences. (LO1)
•   Illustrate and compare methods of “user-centered engineering (UCE)”, involving future users in
various stages of the design and development process of AI systems. (LO2)
•  Apply “user-centered” methods appropriately, as a team; as part of design, development, and
evaluation of AI systems. (LO3)
•  Apply ethics procedures for user studies (e.g., privacy, consent) and FATE principles in design of
prototype based AI systems. (LO4)
•  Describe the perspectives and values of multiple stakeholders at different stages of the user-centered
engineering process (requirements, design, and evaluation). (LO5)

sections.heading: Course Description
Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
To develop the knowledge necessary for addressing issues of
gender equity and understanding gender roles. The course would help students get a greater insight
into women’s rights, their role in shaping political, social, economic and cultural institutions.
Emphasis would be laid on understanding the dynamics of gender relations in educational institutions,
work and home. The course would further aim at gender sensitization in the context of societal
stratifications.

sections.heading: Course Learning Outcomes
sections.text:
•   Familiarity with the foundational concepts, scope and relevance of Gender Studies as a
discipline.
•  Understanding of the historical trajectory of feminist movements and their theoretical
contributions.
•  Understanding of the social construction of gender, sex and sexuality through key theoretical
frameworks.
•  Understanding of intersectionality as a framework for analysing overlapping systems of
identity and inequality.
•  Evaluating the dynamics of gender discrimination within institutions of marriage and family.
•  Understanding the gendered dimensions of labour politics and workplace discrimination.
•  Evaluating the politics of unpaid domestic work and its relationship to gendered labour.
•  Understanding the impact of globalization on gendered labour, care work and emotion labour.
•  Understanding the ideal worker norm and the second shift as frameworks for analysing gender
discrimination in the workplace.
•  Evaluating media representations of gender and the concept of the male gaze.
•  Understanding theories of masculinity and their relationship to gender-based violence.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Nanotechnology is widely regarded as a transformative field with the potential to address
critical challenges in energy, healthcare, electronics, and advanced manufacturing. This
course is designed to introduce students to the fundamental concepts of nanoscience and
nanotechnology, preparing them for further academic research or industrial careers in this
rapidly evolving area. The course focuses on the fundamental science behind nanomaterials,
their synthesis and properties of nanomaterials, with emphasis on their size-dependent
physical, chemical, electrical, optical, and thermal properties. Applications of nanomaterials
in electronics, medicine, MEMS, photonics, catalysis, energy systems, and heat transfer will
be discussed. The course also introduces essential quantum mechanical concepts relevant to
nanoscale systems. In addition, emerging trends, large-scale manufacturing challenges, and
future directions in nanoscience and nanotechnology are covered.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The course is structured to provide a comprehensive and interdisciplinary overview
of nanoscience and nanotechnology. Students will learn common methods for the synthesis
of nanoparticles and nanostructures.
Special emphasis is placed on understanding the unique properties of nanomaterials
and the scientific principles governing their behavior at the nanoscale. The course highlights
real-world motivations and applications of nanomaterials across multiple technological
domains.
This course is well suited for students seeking foundational knowledge and practical
exposure to nanoscience and nanotechnology, and serves as an effective entry point into
advanced study or research in the field.

sections.heading: Course Learning Outcomes
sections.text:
After successful completion of this course, the student will be able to:

and quantum effects at the nanoscale.
◦Describe and compare common synthesis techniques used for nanomaterials.
◦Analyze the structure–property–application relationships of nanomaterials in areas
such as electronics, energy, catalysis, and biomedical systems.

title: Nanotechnology for Renewable Energy and Environment

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
This course provides an introduction to nanotechnology, emphasizing its applications in renewable energy and
environmental engineering. It covers fundamental concepts, including the distinction between the macro- and
nanoscale, nanoscale phenomena, and the distinctive properties of nanomaterials that enable them to outperform
many conventional materials. The course also discusses the fundamentals of fabrication, characterization, and
operating principles of advanced energy devices, including organic, quantum dot, and dye-sensitized solar cells,
fuel cells, batteries, and carbon nanotube-based energy storage systems, and the application of nanomaterials
for hydrogen production and storage. In addition, it examines the application of nanotechnology in improving
solar cells, nanoelectrodes, nanocoating, catalyst materials for fuel cells, and battery technologies. The course
further explores the role of nanotechnology in environmental sustainability, including groundwater remediation,
nanoadsorbents, ecotoxicology, nanomaterial toxicity, transport and fate of nanomaterials in the environment,
and the broader societal impacts of nanotechnology.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
Nanotechnology is widely regarded as a transformative technology with the potential to significantly benefit
society across diverse fields. This course is designed to equip students with the fundamental knowledge and
skills required for advanced academic research or industrial careers in nanotechnology, with particular
emphasis on applications in renewable energy and environmental sustainability. The course is divided into 3
modules as decribed below.
o  Module 1: General introduction to principles of nanoscience and technology
o  Module 2: Nanotechnology applications in the renewable energy sector
o  Module 3: Nanotechnology applications in the environmental sector.
The specific topics covered under each module are listed in the course plan (refer to section 6 of this handout).

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
o  Introduce the importance and application of nanomaterials and the origin of their unique properties.
o  Summarize the fabrication methods, characterization techniques, and operating principles of solar
cells, fuel cells, batteries, and CNT-based energy storage systems.
o  Explain the merits and motivation in the renewable energy and environmental sectors.
o  Define toxic effect of nanomaterials on human and environment, relative remediation and precautions.

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
Introduction of CAD/CAM systems, overview of FMS, system hardware and general
functions,  material  handling  system, work  holding  systems,  cutting  tools and  tool
management, physical planning of system, software structure functions and description,
cleaning  and  automated  inspection,  communications  and  computer  networks  for
manufacturing, quantification of flexibility, human factors in manufacturing, FMS and CIM
in action (case studies), justification of FMS, modelling for design, planning and operation
of FMS.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
In recent years the manufacturing industries are facing problems of survival. They find it
difficult to maintain a long term competitive advantage due to uncertainty in environmental
conditions. The ideal production system for such environment is Flexible Manufacturing
Systems (FMS), which are considered to meet the demand for a variety of products with
improvement of productivity in mid-volume manufacturing. This course will highlight the
fundamentals of FMS and modelling for design, planning and control of FMS.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
CLO1. Comprehend importance of adaptability of changes in product type and
quantity in industry.
CLO2. Understand how labor cost can be reduced by automated the manufacturing
system using FMS.
CLO3. Comprehend CNC technology and role of CAM in FMS.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Specifically designed for HD students, this course aims to improve students’ academic and
professional language skills. Science and engineering contexts will be used where necessary for
teaching writing and speaking skills. Technological tools like Grammarly, COCA and BAWE
are also included in the course so that students can learn to be accurate in their use of English
language.

•  Apply audience-aware writing style with clear purpose and organization.
•   Prepare structured technical reports using appropriate data collection methods.
•  Employ IMRD structure for research writing, including results, analysis, and
discussion.
•  Demonstrate competence in editing, oral presentation, and group discussion.
•  Build professional readiness through cover letters, CVs, and interview skills.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
This is a ﬁrst course on Pattern recognition.  It begins with an introduction to the fundamentals of
digital images and develops the theoretical background for the pattern recognition.   It goes on to
discuss the different aspects like the preprocessing of a digital image, segmentation, representation
and description and ﬁnally the object recognition. During the course, a ﬂavour of matlab programming
will also be given.

sections.heading: Scope & Objective of the Course
sections.text:
Over the past 30 years or so, pattern recognition and automation have evolved into a mature subject
embracing many topics and applications: these range from automatic (robot) assembly to automatic
vehicle guidance, from automatic interpretation of documents to veriﬁcation of signatures, and from
analysis of remotely sensed images to checking of ﬁngerprints and human blood cells.  Currently,
pattern recognition and automatic visual inspection are undergoing very substantial growth, neces-
sary improvement in quality, safety and cost effectiveness being the stimulating factors. The course
introduces the students to the fundamentals of digital images and various processing techniques that
are applied to them not only to improve their quality but also to recognize them.

Education Asia, 2007.

Ed., Thompson Asia, 2003.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
The purpose of this course is to not only study entrepreneurship but also practice it. Student teams are
expected to create a technology product-based or service/SaaS-based startup and complete the business
model canvas, including all the building blocks of creating a venture.
In order to create a successful startup, student entrepreneurs will be required to comprehend the five phases
of startup creation: (1) idea and problem validation; (2) solution validation and product market fit (PMF); (3)
go to market (GTM) and scalability; (4) operations and institutionalization; (5) Startup teams will work on
customer discovery, product development, market research, technology viability, fundraising, competitive
analysis, team formation, marketing & sales strategy, and storytelling. The course features workshops/guest-
lectures from entrepreneurs, investors and academicians with strong experience in creating and running
Startups. Participating teams will be assigned an experienced, dedicated entrepreneur mentor who will guide
them through the semester and can choose to mentor after the course is concluded. The top teams may be
invited to compete for seed funding in early 2027 to pursue their business idea for incubation after the
completion of the NVC course and thereby launch the business.

sections.heading: Scope & Objective of the Course
sections.text:
NVC’s mission is to empower student founders with the choice and tools to become entrepreneurs Hence,
the course aims to provide students with an opportunity to launch/ prepare to launch startups post-NVC. NVC
helps them to think and act entrepreneurially. The central mystery of entrepreneurship is how to transform
an idea into an organizational entity where people can channel their energy and creativity to produce a
reliable output that creates economic value. Some of the questions that will be addressed are: Which specific
market segment of customers should you focus on? How do you plan for a new venture? How do you build
an effective venture team? How do you establish your venture’s identity and legitimacy? How do you win
customers? How will your venture make money? How do you manage your venture’s dependence on key
external partners?

sections.text:
Fundamentals of Entrepreneurship; Elements of Leadership; Identifying
Business Opportunities; Market Study and Research; Business Plans; Finance, Issues in Raising
Finance, Venture Capitalist Evaluation of Business Plans, Technical Aspects for the Project;
Corporate Strategies for Growth; Legal Aspects to entrepreneurship; People Skills; Marketing and

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
This Course is about creating, managing, and leading an organization. This
course helps in creating an entrepreneurial mindset, developing entrepreneurial skills and
equipping students with the basic knowledge necessary for an entrepreneur.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
The course shall enable the participants to acquire and equip
themselves with requisite knowledge and skills to start and run a business successfully, which is
divided into personal skills (entrepreneurial skills) and those to start a company (Start-up tools).
The learning outcomes are:
a.  To  understand  about  entrepreneurship  and  getting  inspiration  from  successful
entrepreneurs.
b. To learn about idea generation, opportunity assessment and evaluation and the process to
create, build, and lead an entrepreneurial organization.
c.  To learn about nitty gritty of preparation of Business Plan.
d. To know about different sources of funding and identify an appropriate source of funding
for the venture.
e. To learn about launching a business venture and growing it to next level of growth.

sections.heading: Method of conduct of the course
sections.text:
The approach used in this course focuses on learning by doing
and learning by interactions.
The effort of the instructor in this course is to be on the following:
  Enable participants to understand the importance and relevance of entrepreneurship in the
present era.
  Motivating and inspiring them to take up entrepreneurship as a career option.
  Enable them to understand the traits of an entrepreneur with a view to diagnose their own
personality as to their strengths and weaknesses Vis-a- Vis ideal profile and to enable them
to work out strategies to consciously inculcate desired skills.
  Enabling  participants  to  identify  ideas, judge  their  potential as an  entrepreneurial
opportunity, select a particular opportunity within well-defined criteria, developing it further
to concretize it to give it a shape of a business, with a focus on implementation strategies.
  Develop skills to pitch their ideas for meeting their goals to raise finance.
   Inculcate communication and negotiation abilities to manage situations and people.
  Above all, to create an entrepreneurial environment that encourages participants to have
zeal to learn by interaction and asking questions.

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
Environment and global problems; Framing Environmental issues; effects of
infrastructure development on environment; prediction and assessment of environmental impacts of
infrastructure  projects:  technical  and  procedural  aspects,  guidelines  and  legal  aspects  of
environmental protection, impacts on air, water, soil and noise environment, valuation, strategic
assessment, mathematical modeling for environmental processes; social impact assessment (SIA),
dislocation/disruption impact of Infrastructure projects; Life Cycle Assessments (LCA) and risk
analysis  methodologies;  mitigation  of  environmental  impacts;  case  studies;  environmental
management plan (EMP), national and international certification and guidelines including ISO.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
The course focuses on understanding environmental issues linked to
infrastructure development, emphasizing technical, procedural, and legal aspects of environmental
impact assessment (EIA). It covers prediction and mitigation of impacts on air, water, soil, and noise
environments, supported by modeling tools. Strategic assessments, LCA, risk analysis, and SIA are
addressed alongside valuation and management frameworks. Case studies and EMP formulation are
discussed  with  reference  to  national  and  international  standards,  including  ISO,  ensuring
comprehensive exposure to certification protocols and regulatory compliance.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
a. Identify and frame environmental issues arising from infrastructure development, including
physical                    and                         social                      dimensions.
b. Apply procedural and technical approaches for impact prediction, assessment, and valuation using
modeling                  tools              and                  legal                 guidelines.
c. Formulate environmental management plans (EMP) and assess projects in line with national and
international frameworks, including ISO.

title: Research Practice

sections.heading: Aims and Objectives
sections.text:
This course  is designed  to  train  the  students towards acquiring competence  in research
methodologies. The course will be conducted in terms of actual participation in Research and
Development Work. Each student will be assigned to a faculty member to work on specified
projects. The student will be required to present a number of seminars in his research area in a
structured manner

sections.heading: Scope of the Course
sections.text:
The course broadly covers following aspects:
(i)   Research proposal
(ii)  Development related activities
(iii)  Research related activities
The 25% weightage would be for the project proposal, which the student would be required to
write, based on the skills acquired. For developmental activities, which carry 25% weightage,
the supervisor would assign to the student working with him an appropriate developmental work,
which can be related to Centers/ Laboratories/ Assistance in course development or in the R&D
activities of the supervisor. The student would have the teaching/research skills by assisting the
supervisor in teaching, evaluation and research activities of the supervisor. Under the research
related activities, which carries 50% weightage, a broad topic of research will be assigned to the
higher degree student by the Supervisor and the student would conduct literature search in the
specified area, learn various research methodologies/techniques for data collection and data
analysis, testing techniques/methods etc. and deliver seminars in his/her research area to the
supervisor. The student should also write research reports that along with the seminar/viva would
form part of evaluation component related to research related activities.

sections.heading: Operational Details
sections.text:
1. Within 2 weeks of registration, the student should prepare the work plan (research proposal)
for his research project and also for the developmental activities in consultation with the
supervisor.
2. Mid semester grading will be done by the supervisor based on the work done and progress
made towards planned objectives by the student in the assigned research area. The student is
required to submit mid semester report describing the work done and progress made by him. He
should also deliver a seminar to highlight these activities. Supervisors will grade the student for
mid semester on the basis of the mid semester report described above and the Seminar presented
by the student.
3. The student should submit mid-semester report in the 9th week of the semester to the

supervisor and this should be followed by seminar/presentation by the student. The supervisor in
turn is required to send mid-semester grades of all the students working with him to Head of
Department by the end of 9th week of the semester.
4. End semester report would provide details of work done by the student. End semester report
should be submitted to the supervisor and should be followed by seminar/presentation. Every
student would write a research proposal. This research proposal would form a part of the final
(end semester) report. The research proposal carries 25% weightage and should be written in the
proper format i.e. (i) Topic of Research (ii) Background and current status of research work in
the area as evident from the literature search/review, (iii) scope of the proposed research work,
(iv) methodology (v) work plan and time schedule  (vi) references and bibliography. The
references and bibliography should be written in standard format and should be cited within the
text of the research proposal.

sections.heading: COURSE DESCRIPTION
sections.text:
This course deals with the research and development work in assigned areas of professional
interest. Each student will work under the overall guidance and supervision of a faculty
member/professional. The course must end with a well defined Final Report outlining all the
investigations, achievements and conclusions  at the end of each semester. References and
bibliography in standard format are also to be included in the report.

sections.heading: SCOPE AND OBJECTIVE OF THE COURSE
sections.text:
The aim of this course is to carryout a research and development project in assigned areas of
professional interest. The course envisages student’s training in the methodology of research and
presentation of the research findings in the form of a scientific report.

sections.heading: OPERATION OF THE COURSE
sections.text:
a) The student should immediately chalk out a plan of work in Consultation with his Supervisor.
Current literature (journals, books, etc.) must be methodically reviewed and the status of the
work in the field must be considered. The detailed outline of work must reflect a survey of the
current literature in the same area and must include topic of research, objective, background of
previous work in the area, methodology and a work plan with a time schedule clearly indicating
the intermediate milestones and the  estimated  time  to  achieve  the  same  along  with
references and bibliography.
b) Within two weeks of registration, the student should give his Dissertation particulars to the
Head of Department in TS-1 Performa.
c) The student should regularly interact with his supervisor and present seminars and submit
reports on the scheduled dates. Proposed examiners and other faculty in relevant area may be
requested to attend the presentations.
d) Supervisor will announce the Mid-semester grade to his student and send the MID-SEM
Evaluation Form to the Head of Department.
e) Typed copy of Final Dissertation Report and Abstract are to be submitted to the supervisor on
or before the last day of class work in each semester.
f) Every student has to sign his attendance regularly with the supervisor or as per the alternative
arrangement made by the supervisor. An attendance sheet is being provided for this purpose to
the supervisor.
g) The candidate should apply and seek prior permission of his supervisor for going on leave for
any genuine needs. If leave of absence exceeds seven days in entire semester, recommended

i) A separate Dissertation topic has to be assigned to individual students. Wherever the broad
area is same, the aspects to be researched by an individual candidate should be clearly focused
and spelt out.
j) Utmost care should be taken in the preparation of the FINAL REPORT. A check-list of
various items is provided and students should carefully go through these. Supervisors are also
requested to examine the draft of the FINAL REPORT keeping in view the items in  the
checklist. Title of the thesis should be proper and should be indicative of the type of work done.

sections.heading: EVALUATION
sections.text:
Evaluation in this course is essentially individual oriented. The various instruments of evaluation
along with the weightage of components are given below:
Component             Weightage  Week in which due
Viva-I                 15            5th week
Mid. sem. Written report  15           10th week
Mid sem. presentation    15           10th week
Viva-II                15           15th week
Final Dissertation*      25          Last day of class work
Final viva-voce*        15          Actual date announced by DRC
*Final viva-voce examination and evaluation of the Dissertation is to be jointly done by the
Supervisor and the examiner appointed by the DRC. The other components are to be evaluated
by the supervisor and the details are to be made available to the examiner at the time of final
viva.
Supervisor will send the copy of Dissertation report to the examiner well in advance. Before
sending he should check the contents as per checklist and sign the ‘Certificate’ page. The
evaluation will recognize the day-to-day work involvement and punctuality of the student in his
work. Evaluation in various components shall take into account work progress and achievements,
technical/professional competence, documentation and expression,  initiative and  originality,
punctuality and reliability, self-reliance, and acquisition of special skills. The student should
extend full cooperation to his supervisor and interact with him in advance about the time, venue
2

and mode of each evaluation. He should be in constant touch with his supervisor. Supervisor
may require his student to sign the attendance sheet before a particular time on each working
day.
Grading will be done mainly on the basis of the progress made towards attaining the overall
objectives of the Dissertation. The supervisor shall evaluate various prescribed components of
evaluation before the submission of final Dissertation. He/she should seek utmost participation
of examiner by inviting him to the various seminars. Supervisor should maintain all pertinent
records of his student.
The final report and performance in the final viva are to be jointly evaluated by the Supervisor
and examiner appointed by the DRC. Evaluation in various components can be done on the basis
of marks or grades. However, the recommendations for the final award shall invariably be made
in terms of one of the prescribed letter grades, viz. A/A-/B/B-/C/C-/D/E. The student will have
to defend the work appearing in his/her Dissertation before the panel of examiners.
Immediately after the final viva, ONE copy completed Final Evaluation Form is to be submitted
to the Head of Department by the supervisor.

sections.heading: MID SEMESTER GRADING
sections.text:
This will be announced by the supervisor to his student sometime in the 10th week of the
semester. Mid-semester evaluation form should be returned by the supervisor to the Head of
Department during the 10th week of the semester.

Notices pertaining to this course will be displayed on respective Department Notice boards by

sections.heading: COURSE DESCRIPTION
sections.text:
This course deals with the research and development work in assigned areas of professional
interest. Each student will work under the overall guidance and supervision of a faculty
member/professional. The course must end with a well defined Final Report outlining all the
investigations, achievements and conclusions  at the end of each semester. References and
bibliography in standard format are also to be included in the report.

sections.heading: SCOPE AND OBJECTIVE OF THE COURSE
sections.text:
The aim of this course is to carryout a research and development project in assigned areas of
professional interest. The course envisages student’s training in the methodology of research and
presentation of the research findings in the form of a scientific report.

sections.heading: OPERATION OF THE COURSE
sections.text:
a) The student should immediately chalk out a plan of work in Consultation with his Supervisor.
Current literature (journals, books, etc.) must be methodically reviewed and the status of the
work in the field must be considered. The detailed outline of work must reflect a survey of the
current literature in the same area and must include topic of research, objective, background of
previous work in the area, methodology and a work plan with a time schedule clearly indicating
the intermediate milestones and the  estimated  time  to  achieve  the  same  along  with
references and bibliography.
b) Within two weeks of registration, the student should give his Dissertation particulars to the
Head of Department in TS-1 Performa.
c) The student should regularly interact with his supervisor and present seminars and submit
reports on the scheduled dates. Proposed examiners and other faculty in relevant area may be
requested to attend the presentations.
d) Supervisor will announce the Mid-semester grade to his student and send the MID-SEM
Evaluation Form to the Head of Department.
e) Typed copy of Final Dissertation Report and Abstract are to be submitted to the supervisor on
or before the last day of class work in each semester.
f) Every student has to sign his attendance regularly with the supervisor or as per the alternative
arrangement made by the supervisor. An attendance sheet is being provided for this purpose to
the supervisor.
g) The candidate should apply and seek prior permission of his supervisor for going on leave for
any genuine needs. If leave of absence exceeds seven days in entire semester, recommended
