and spelt out.
j) Utmost care should be taken in the preparation of the FINAL REPORT. A check-list of
various items is provided and students should carefully go through these. Supervisors are also
requested to examine the draft of the FINAL REPORT keeping in view the items in  the
checklist. Title of the thesis should be proper and should be indicative of the type of work done.

sections.heading: EVALUATION
sections.text:
Evaluation in this course is essentially individual oriented. The various instruments of evaluation
along with the weightage of components are given below:
Component             Weightage  Week in which due
Viva-I                 15            5th week
Mid. sem. Written report  15           10th week
Mid sem. presentation    15           10th week
Viva-II                15           15th week
Final Dissertation*      25          Last day of class work
Final viva-voce*        15          Actual date announced by DRC
*Final viva-voce examination and evaluation of the Dissertation is to be jointly done by the
Supervisor and the examiner appointed by the DRC. The other components are to be evaluated
by the supervisor and the details are to be made available to the examiner at the time of final
viva.
Supervisor will send the copy of Dissertation report to the examiner well in advance. Before
sending he should check the contents as per checklist and sign the ‘Certificate’ page. The
evaluation will recognize the day-to-day work involvement and punctuality of the student in his
work. Evaluation in various components shall take into account work progress and achievements,
technical/professional competence, documentation and expression,  initiative and  originality,
punctuality and reliability, self-reliance, and acquisition of special skills. The student should
extend full cooperation to his supervisor and interact with him in advance about the time, venue
2
BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani
Pilani Campus
AUGS/ AGSR Division
and mode of each evaluation. He should be in constant touch with his supervisor. Supervisor
may require his student to sign the attendance sheet before a particular time on each working
day.
Grading will be done mainly on the basis of the progress made towards attaining the overall
objectives of the Dissertation. The supervisor shall evaluate various prescribed components of
evaluation before the submission of final Dissertation. He/she should seek utmost participation
of examiner by inviting him to the various seminars. Supervisor should maintain all pertinent
records of his student.
The final report and performance in the final viva are to be jointly evaluated by the Supervisor
and examiner appointed by the DRC. Evaluation in various components can be done on the basis
of marks or grades. However, the recommendations for the final award shall invariably be made
in terms of one of the prescribed letter grades, viz. A/A-/B/B-/C/C-/D/E. The student will have
to defend the work appearing in his/her Dissertation before the panel of examiners.
Immediately after the final viva, ONE copy completed Final Evaluation Form is to be submitted
to the Head of Department by the supervisor.

sections.text:
This will be announced by the supervisor to his student sometime in the 10th week of the
semester. Mid-semester evaluation form should be returned by the supervisor to the Head of
Department during the 10th week of the semester.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
This is a course dealing with an advanced pursuit in terms of a study in assigned area
of professional interest.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The objective of this course is to train the Ph.D. students in the art of
research and involves various related aspects. This course helps the students in gaining deeper understanding
of fundamental concepts and acquiring the techniques of communicating at a professional level.

sections.heading: Operation of the course
sections.text:
All Ph.D. students will be assigned an on-going project generally drawn from the core courses of the
first/higher degree under the guidance of a senior faculty member. Several practice lectures will be held in
which each student will be given an opportunity. Besides the technical contents, the basic important pointsto
be focused during the lectures are.
a)  Planning
b)  Oral communication
c)  Audience awareness
d)  Style of presentation.
Each Ph.D. student will submit a Mid-Semester Report and a final report, which will include the following.
a)  Outline of lectures delivered or other related activities.
b)  References and bibliography of literature consulted
c)  Conclusions.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
This course introduces scientific and engineering inquiry through the principles
of measurement and experimentation. It covers fundamental concepts, such as accuracy, precision,
calibration, error analysis, and uncertainty, as well as the hands-on use of sophisticated instruments
across multiple disciplines. The course includes data acquisition, visualization, and analysis using
modern computational  tools.  It emphasizes experimental  design, hypothesis  formulation, and
experimental validation.  It also focuses on correlating measurements with real-world problems,
documenting and interpreting results, and communicating findings effectively with due consideration
to ethical practices in experimentation.

sections.heading: Scope & Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The course aims to provide a foundational understanding of
measurement as an essential element of engineering and scientific practice. It covers key measurement
concepts, exposure to a variety of instruments and sensors across disciplines, and methods for reliable
data acquisition and analysis. The objectives of the course are to enable students to:
(i) Understand fundamental measurement concepts such as accuracy, precision, resolution, cali-
bration, and uncertainty.
(ii) Use appropriate measuring instruments and sensors for acquiring experimental data across dif-
ferent domains.
(iii) Apply techniques for data acquisition, visualization, and analysis using modern computational
tools.
(iv) Develop an understanding of experimental methodologies, including hypothesis formulation,
experimental design, and validation.
(v) Interpret experimental results and correlate them with underlying scientific and engineering
principles.
(vi) Communicate experimental findings effectively and adhere to ethical practices in experimen-
tation and technical reporting.
1
BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani
Pilani Campus
AUGS/ AGSR Division

sections.heading: Course Learning Outcomes
sections.text:
By the end of the course, students will be able to:
CO1: Understand and apply fundamental measurement concepts such as accuracy, precision, resolution,
calibration, and uncertainty.
CO2: Use appropriate measuring instruments/sensors to solve a problem and acquire experimental data
across different disciplines.
CO3: Analyze experimental data using graphical and statistical methods, including error estimation and
uncertainty propagation.
CO4: Formulating hypotheses and their validation through design and conducting experiments.
CO5: Interpret experimental observations using fundamental scientific and engineering principles.
CO6: Document and communicate experimental findings effectively through structured reports and
presentations.

(iii) An Introduction to Error Analysis, John R Taylor, 2nd Ed, University Science Books, 1997.

Micro electro mechanical systems (MEMS), devices and technologies. Micro-machining and mi-
crofabrication techniques. Transduction mechanisms and modeling in different energy domains.
Analysis of micromachined capacitive, piezoresistive and thermal sensors/actuators and applica-
tions. Computer- aided design for MEMS layout, fabrication and analysis.

sections.heading: Scope & Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The course introduces the basic concepts in MEMS (Micro Electromechanical Systems) with a
view to address a class of students from science and engineering disciplines. The discussion
on topics like MEMS design, Microfabrication, Microfluidics, Sensors and actuators have been
structured in the course plan. The objective of the course is to equip the students from various
aspects and with basic knowledge of the area of MEMS.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
This course is designed to create an awareness on the basic concepts of biosafety and bioethics that are
essential for various branches of science which has had an great impact on quality of life and regulations
governing the experimentations on transgenic organisms and plants, prenatal diagnosis and related social
issues, handling and disposal of hazardous materials, environmental pollution concerns and ethics in need
based experimentation on animals and plants, would be addressed. Emphasis will also be made on health
care related issues.

title: Mechanics of Solids

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Introduction to mechanics of rigid bodies and deformable bodies, Thermal
stresses, Equilibrium of forces, Bending moment and shear force diagrams for determinate beams
and frames, Analysis of statically determinate trusses; Flexural and shear Stresses in beams,
combined stresses, Stresses and strains on inclined planes, Introduction to torsion, Torsion in
shafts, Slope and deflection in beams due to bending, Introduction to Energy Methods, Stresses in
thin cylindrical shells, Suspension cables, Failure theories, Buckling of columns using Euler’s Theory.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
This course aims at providing overall understanding of
various methods in understanding the behavior of structural elements under various loading
conditions. As a part of this course, understanding of behavior of key structural materials will also
be touched upon. Also, an overview of key structural components and their importance to
structure will also be covered.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
o  To comprehend the basic understanding of behavior of structural elements
o  To get a detailed understanding of different methods of approaching the problem
o  To gain the complete knowledge of stresses and strains developed in structural elements
o  To develop the comprehensive capability to analyze the structural elements

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Different types of cements, chemical composition, properties and tests, coarse and fine aggregate for concrete,
tests on aggregates, grading of aggregates and  its effect on concrete properties, chemical and mineral
admixtures, properties and tests on fresh and hardened concrete; transportation and placing of concrete, non-
destructive testing of concrete, durability of concrete, quality control and acceptance criteria of concrete,
Factors in the choice of mix proportions, Proportioning of concrete mixes by various methods – BIS method
of mix  design;  Introduction  to  special  concretes. Manufacturing/sources,  classification,  applications,
properties and testing of bricks, blocks, tiles, aggregates, lime, timber, paints, glass, bitumen, cutback,
emulsion, modified bitumen, steel, non-ferrous metals, polymeric materials, geo-synthetics, etc. Low cost and
waste material in construction. Latest, BIS, IRC & ASTM specifications and guidelines of all above-
mentioned material, and construction equipment.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
The course deals with properties, characterization, testing, selection and quality control of construction
material. For economical, durable and high performance of structure, it is imperative to have knowledge on
construction materials and their wider applications. This course provides a basic and enhanced overview of
various construction materials presently used in practice.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
By the end of this course, students will be able to:
a)  Identify and classify common civil engineering materials such as concrete, steel, wood, aggregates,
asphalt, and modern composites.
b) Explain the physical, mechanical, and chemical properties of construction materials and how these
properties affect material performance and selection.
1
BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani
Pilani Campus
AUGS/ AGSR Division
c) Perform standard laboratory tests to evaluate the properties and behaviour of civil engineering
materials, including tests for strength, and workability.
d)  Interpret test data and analyse results to assess material suitability for specific applications in civil
engineering.
e) Understand the influence of material properties on the structural performance, serviceability, and
durability of civil infrastructure.
f) Compare and evaluate materials based on environmental impact, cost-effectiveness, availability,
and sustainability.
g) Demonstrate awareness of current trends and innovations in civil engineering materials, including
smart materials, green materials, and recycled materials.
h) Apply appropriate material selection in the design and construction of civil engineering structures
in accordance with relevant codes and standards.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Fluid Mechanics  is an introductory course that covers the fundamental aspects of fluid mechanics,
especially the classical and well-established laws. This course emphasizes understanding these governing
laws and their widespread engineering applications in fluid related problems by covering the following
topics: Concepts and definitions, compressibility of fluids, fluid pressure and measurement, fluid statics,
buoyancy, rigid body motion, fluid kinematics, conservation laws: control volume approach, differential
analysis of fluid flow, study of flow pattern through orifices and mouthpieces, notches and weirs, analysis
of flow through pipes, viscous fluid flow analysis: analysis of flow through pipes, dimensional analysis and
similitude.
The contents of this course will enable the students to tackle real-life fluid mechanics problems and provide
a broad overview of the subject. Moreover, this course will be helpful to students as a prerequisite for further
advanced courses in fluid mechanics at undergraduate and graduate levels.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
•   Introduction to different fluid properties and their engineering applications
•  Learn about pressure exerted by fluids and pressure measurement techniques
•  Estimate hydrostatic forces on surfaces
•  Learn about buoyancy and evaluate stability of submerged and floating bodies
•  Understand concepts of fluid kinematics, methods of describing fluid flow, types of fluid flow,
control mass and control volume, rate of flow, continuity equation, potential and stream functions
•  Study dynamics of fluid flow, Euler’s equation, Bernoulli’s equation and its applications, Navier
Stokes equation, and pipe bend problems
•  Compute fluid discharge through orifices and mouthpieces, and flow over weirs and notches
•  Analyze flow of viscous fluids through pipes and plates, and compute head loss due to friction
•  Compute different types of energy losses and determine hydraulic gradient and total energy line for
flow through pipes. Become adept at solving problems pertaining to syphon, flow through pipes in
series, parallel and branched pipes, power transmission through pipes, and flow through nozzles
•  Perceive the concepts of dimensional analysis and similitude

sections.heading: Course Learning Outcomes
sections.text:
On completion of this course, the students will be able to,
1.  Demonstrate the difference between solid and fluid, its properties and properties in static and
dynamic conditions
2.  Estimate pressure exerted by fluids and experiment with pressure measurement devices
1
BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani
Pilani Campus
AUGS/ AGSR Division
3.  Apply conservation laws applicable to fluids and its applications through fluid kinematics and
dynamics
4.  Perceive and formulate relationship among the parameters involved in the given fluid phenomenon
and apply concepts of similitude in analyzing models and prototypes
5.  Estimate the losses in pipelines for both laminar and turbulent conditions and analysis of pipes
connected in series and parallel.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
This course introduces Civil Engineering students to the core concepts of hydraulic engineering, focusing
on the Behaviour of real fluids: boundary layer theory, turbulent flow through conduits; analysis of
closed-conduit hydraulic systems including pipes, valves, fittings, and pumps, water hammer in
pipes, pipe networks analysis: Hardy cross method; Open channel hydraulics: uniform and non-
uniform flow; flow past immersed bodies: drag and lift; Analysis of Impact of jets; Introduction to
fluid machinery.

sections.heading: Scope & Course Objective
sections.text:
The problems encountered by our society, such as water supply, irrigation, navigation, and water power,
resulted in the development of Fluid Mechanics and Hydraulic Engineering. The objective of this course is
to equip students with a fundamental understanding of the principles of fluid mechanics as applied to
hydraulic systems and structures. The course aims to achieve the following Course Objectives (Teacher's
perspective), aligned with the Course Outcomes (COs) (Students’ perspective):
1. To develop an analytical understanding of flow behavior in pipes and channels under varying conditions.
2. To apply fluid mechanics principles in analyzing hydraulic systems, including energy losses and force
impacts.
3. To introduce the working principles and performance of fluid machinery relevant to civil engineering.
4. To prepare students for practical problem-solving in the analysis, design, and assessment of water
infrastructures of Pipe networks, open channels, and structures submerged in fluid, like bridge piers,
dealt with by civil engineers.

sections.heading: Course Learning Outcomes (CLOs)
sections.text:
Upon the completion of this course, students will be able to perform the following:
1
BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani
Pilani Campus
AUGS/ AGSR Division
CLO1. Explain the behaviour of real fluids, including boundary layer development and turbulent flow
through conduits, and apply these concepts to practical hydraulic engineering problems.
CLO2. Analyze closed-conduit hydraulic systems by evaluating head losses, pipe flow characteristics,
pumps, valves, fittings, and the effects of water hammer in pressurized pipelines.
CLO3. Analyze and solve pipe network problems using the Hardy Cross Method for the design and
operation of water distribution systems.
CLO4. Analyze uniform and non-uniform flow in open channels using fundamental hydraulic principles and
empirical equations for engineering design and performance assessment.
CLO5. Evaluate fluid forces on immersed bodies, including drag, lift, and the impact of jets on stationary
and moving surfaces, for engineering applications.
CLO6. Explain the classification, operating principles, and applications of fluid machinery, particularly
hydraulic turbines and pumps, and relate them to hydraulic engineering systems.

sections.heading: Course Description
Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
In this course, the students will be introduced to the various design philosophies used in the design of
Reinforced Concrete (RC) structures, with a particular focus on the Limit State Design method. The
course will provide an in-depth discussion of the concepts of Limit State Design method. Subsequently,
the Limit State Design method will be employed to the design of singly and doubly reinforced
rectangular- and T-section beams and one-way and two-way slabs, for flexure, shear, anchorage, bond,
and serviceability requirement. Additionally, the course will cover the design of columns subjected to
axial loads, and axial load plus uniaxial and biaxial moments. Moreover, the course will explore different
types of staircases, with a specific emphasis on the design of dog-legged staircases. At the end of this
course, students will be able to design the basic structural elements of an RC buildings.

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
Environment and global problems; Framing Environmental issues; effects of
infrastructure development on environment; prediction and assessment of environmental impacts of
infrastructure  projects:  technical  and  procedural  aspects,  guidelines  and  legal  aspects  of
environmental protection, impacts on air, water, soil and noise environment, valuation, strategic
assessment, mathematical modeling for environmental processes; social impact assessment (SIA),
dislocation/disruption impact of Infrastructure projects; Life Cycle Assessments (LCA) and risk
analysis  methodologies;  mitigation  of  environmental  impacts;  case  studies;  environmental
management plan (EMP), national and international certification and guidelines including ISO.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
The course focuses on understanding environmental issues linked to
infrastructure development, emphasizing technical, procedural, and legal aspects of environmental
impact assessment (EIA). It covers prediction and mitigation of impacts on air, water, soil, and noise
environments, supported by modeling tools. Strategic assessments, LCA, risk analysis, and SIA are
addressed alongside valuation and management frameworks. Case studies and EMP formulation are
discussed  with  reference  to  national  and  international  standards,  including  ISO,  ensuring
comprehensive exposure to certification protocols and regulatory compliance.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
a. Identify and frame environmental issues arising from infrastructure development, including
physical                    and                         social                      dimensions.
b. Apply procedural and technical approaches for impact prediction, assessment, and valuation using
modeling                  tools              and                  legal                 guidelines.
c. Formulate environmental management plans (EMP) and assess projects in line with national and
international frameworks, including ISO.

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
Systems Engineering is an interdisciplinary field that focuses on
the structured development, integration, and management of complex systems
across their entire life cycle—from conceptual design and planning to operation,
maintenance, and retirement. In the context of infrastructure, it addresses technical,
organizational, and  stakeholder-related  complexities by employing a  holistic,
systems-oriented approach. This course introduces students to the fundamentals of
systems engineering with a focus on civil and infrastructure systems, preparing them
to think critically and act strategically in dynamic, real-world environments.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
The course is designed to build a strong foundation in systems
engineering methodologies while contextualizing their application to infrastructure
planning,  development,  and  management.  Students   will  explore  systems
architecture, modeling, simulation, optimization, and decision-support frameworks
relevant to the life cycle of infrastructure systems. The course also integrates modern
tools such as AI, IoT, digital twins, and life-cycle costing techniques to support
informed decision-making and innovation. The overarching objective is to develop
technically  sound,  system-aware  professionals  capable  of  solving  real-world
infrastructure problems through interdisciplinary thinking, structured analysis, and
evidence-based planning.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
a.  Understand systems engineering principles and their application to
infrastructure life-cycle management.
b.  Apply systems thinking and modeling techniques to analyze complex
infrastructure systems.
c.  Use optimization, simulation, and decision-support tools for infrastructure
planning and operations.
d.  Evaluate infrastructure projects using life-cycle costing and basic investment
analysis methods.
e.  Introduction to Integrating emerging technologies such as AI and IoT into
infrastructure systems design and management.

sections.heading: Text books and references
sections.text:

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
Systems Engineering is an interdisciplinary field that focuses on
the structured development, integration, and management of complex systems
across their entire life cycle—from conceptual design and planning to operation,
maintenance, and retirement. In the context of infrastructure, it addresses technical,
organizational, and  stakeholder-related  complexities by employing a  holistic,
systems-oriented approach. This course introduces students to the fundamentals of
systems engineering with a focus on civil and infrastructure systems, preparing them
to think critically and act strategically in dynamic, real-world environments.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
The course is designed to build a strong foundation in systems
engineering methodologies while contextualizing their application to infrastructure
planning,  development,  and  management.  Students   will  explore  systems
architecture, modeling, simulation, optimization, and decision-support frameworks
relevant to the life cycle of infrastructure systems. The course also integrates modern
tools such as AI, IoT, digital twins, and life-cycle costing techniques to support
informed decision-making and innovation. The overarching objective is to develop
technically  sound,  system-aware  professionals  capable  of  solving  real-world
infrastructure problems through interdisciplinary thinking, structured analysis, and
evidence-based planning.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
a.  Understand systems engineering principles and their application to
infrastructure life-cycle management.
b.  Apply systems thinking and modeling techniques to analyze complex
infrastructure systems.
c.  Use optimization, simulation, and decision-support tools for infrastructure
planning and operations.
d.  Evaluate infrastructure projects using life-cycle costing and basic investment
analysis methods.
e.  Introduction to Integrating emerging technologies such as AI and IoT into
infrastructure systems design and management.

sections.heading: CE G525 Course Description
Scope & Objective
sections.text:
The course CE G525 Water Resources Planning and Management aims to equip students with a comprehensive
understanding of the engineering, economic, and environmental aspects involved in the sustainable planning
and management of water resources.  It covers both quantitative and qualitative assessments of water
systems,  integrating  surface and groundwater  hydrology, water  quality  modeling, and watershed
management. The course emphasizes decision-making under uncertainty, project analysis, and the application
of mathematical modeling and optimization techniques, including linear, non-linear, and multi-objective
programming. Through the study of pollution sources, water conservation strategies, and demographic
considerations, students gain insights into integrated water resource planning. Modern computational tools
such as fuzzy logic and artificial intelligence are introduced alongside real-world case studies and laboratory
experiments, enabling students to address complex, multidisciplinary challenges in water resource systems.
The course ultimately prepares students to contribute effectively to socially and environmentally responsible
water resource development and policy-making.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:
a.  Understand the structure, components, and modeling approaches of water resource systems.
b.  Apply principles of engineering and economics in water resource planning and project evaluation.
c.  Analyze point and non-point source pollution using water quality modeling techniques.
d.  Assess groundwater resources and apply methods for sustainable groundwater management.
e.  Perform statistical and uncertainty analyses related to streamflow and water availability.
f.  Formulate and solve water resource problems using linear, non-linear, and multi-objective optimization
techniques.
g.  Plan and manage reservoir operations under both deterministic and stochastic environments.
h.   Utilize modern tools such as fuzzy logic and artificial intelligence in water resource management.
i.   Evaluate real-world case studies and apply integrated approaches to address complex water management
challenges.

*During the semester, each student will work in a team on a project dealing with water resources planning and
management. These projects will deal with some aspect of a real, complex water resources planning and analysis issue
of current interest to the world, nation, or a particular State. The projects typically are interdisciplinary and consider
such aspects of water resources planning and management as: engineering, law; economics; hydrology, climatology,
hydrogeology;  environmental  health; computer  modeling;  population  growth;  land use  planning;  regional
development; or politics. Each group will make an oral presentation of their progress and outcome to the class during
Mid-semester presentation and final presentation and submit the reports accordingly.
The purposes of the term project are:
1.  To enable you to explore in-depth an aspect of the subject of water resources planning and management.
2.  To provide experience in the formulation, execution and presentation of an engineering investigation in the
area of water resources planning and management.
3.  To provide a teamwork experience dealing with the interdisciplinary nature of water resources planning and
management.
Steps in Carrying out the Project
The steps in carrying out the project are:
1.  Prepare a proposal in MS Word and email it to the instructor specifying the objective of your project and
outlining how you plan to go about executing it. Before beginning your project, you need to prepare a project
proposal and submit it to the instructor for approval and feedback. This proposal should be about 1-2 page in
length. The instructor will review the proposals and provide comments for the student to revise the proposal
for final submittal and approval. The proposal should contain:
•   Title of the project,
•  Team members.
•   Scope, Definition of the problem and Background of the study,
•   Objectives,
•   Plan work,
•   Discussion (preliminary) of the proposed methods of solution of the problem.
•   Anticipated data needs.
•   Anticipated problems in carrying out the project.
•  Assignment of tasks to team members.
•   Anticipated outcome
•  A minimum of 5 bibliographic/references citations relevant to your proposed project.
2.  Present an oral report in class on the date posted on the class assignment web page.
3.  Send a written report (in MS Word) to the instructor on the date posted on the class assignment web page.

sections.heading: CE G525 Course Description
Scope & Objective
sections.text:
The course CE G525 Water Resources Planning and Management aims to equip students with a comprehensive
understanding of the engineering, economic, and environmental aspects involved in the sustainable planning
and management of water resources.  It covers both quantitative and qualitative assessments of water
systems,  integrating  surface and groundwater  hydrology, water  quality  modeling, and watershed
management. The course emphasizes decision-making under uncertainty, project analysis, and the application
of mathematical modeling and optimization techniques, including linear, non-linear, and multi-objective
programming. Through the study of pollution sources, water conservation strategies, and demographic
considerations, students gain insights into integrated water resource planning. Modern computational tools
such as fuzzy logic and artificial intelligence are introduced alongside real-world case studies and laboratory
experiments, enabling students to address complex, multidisciplinary challenges in water resource systems.
The course ultimately prepares students to contribute effectively to socially and environmentally responsible
water resource development and policy-making.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:
a.  Understand the structure, components, and modeling approaches of water resource systems.
b.  Apply principles of engineering and economics in water resource planning and project evaluation.
c.  Analyze point and non-point source pollution using water quality modeling techniques.
d.  Assess groundwater resources and apply methods for sustainable groundwater management.
e.  Perform statistical and uncertainty analyses related to streamflow and water availability.
f.  Formulate and solve water resource problems using linear, non-linear, and multi-objective optimization
techniques.
g.  Plan and manage reservoir operations under both deterministic and stochastic environments.
h.   Utilize modern tools such as fuzzy logic and artificial intelligence in water resource management.
i.   Evaluate real-world case studies and apply integrated approaches to address complex water management
challenges.

Methods, Models and Applications, UNESCO Publishing, 2005.

Examination
*During the semester, each student will work in a team on a project dealing with water resources planning and
management. These projects will deal with some aspect of a real, complex water resources planning and analysis issue
of current interest to the world, nation, or a particular State. The projects typically are interdisciplinary and consider
such aspects of water resources planning and management as: engineering, law; economics; hydrology, climatology,
hydrogeology;  environmental  health; computer  modeling;  population  growth;  land use  planning;  regional
development; or politics. Each group will make an oral presentation of their progress and outcome to the class during
Mid-semester presentation and final presentation and submit the reports accordingly.
The purposes of the term project are:
1.  To enable you to explore in-depth an aspect of the subject of water resources planning and management.
2.  To provide experience in the formulation, execution and presentation of an engineering investigation in the
area of water resources planning and management.
3.  To provide a teamwork experience dealing with the interdisciplinary nature of water resources planning and
management.
Steps in Carrying out the Project
The steps in carrying out the project are:
1.  Prepare a proposal in MS Word and email it to the instructor specifying the objective of your project and
outlining how you plan to go about executing it. Before beginning your project, you need to prepare a project
proposal and submit it to the instructor for approval and feedback. This proposal should be about 1-2 page in
length. The instructor will review the proposals and provide comments for the student to revise the proposal
for final submittal and approval. The proposal should contain:
•   Title of the project,
•  Team members.
•   Scope, Definition of the problem and Background of the study,
•   Objectives,
•   Plan work,
•   Discussion (preliminary) of the proposed methods of solution of the problem.
•   Anticipated data needs.
•   Anticipated problems in carrying out the project.
•  Assignment of tasks to team members.
•   Anticipated outcome
•  A minimum of 5 bibliographic/references citations relevant to your proposed project.
2.  Present an oral report in class on the date posted on the class assignment web page.
3.  Send a written report (in MS Word) to the instructor on the date posted on the class assignment web page.

performers in the class, or 40% of the median of the class, whichever is lower to clear the course. This shall be
considered as the minimum performance criterion to clear/pass the course. If any student gets the marks lower than
the prescribed standard mentioned above, he/she will be awarded NC.
Attendance Clause
As BITS Pilani is a fully residential university with an internal and continuous evaluation system, it is expected that
every student demonstrates a high level of responsibility by maintaining 100% attendance in all classes and laboratory
sessions. Regular attendance and class participation are integral components of the learning process, and students are
expected to appear in all scheduled tests and examinations and complete assigned academic tasks sincerely and on
time.
While 100% attendance is the expected norm, under no circumstances should a student’s attendance fall below 60%
in this course. A student falling short of this minimum attendance requirement shall not be permitted to appear in the
comprehensive examination and will be considered as not having cleared the course.
Students are therefore advised to remain fully aware of their academic responsibilities and ensure consistent
attendance throughout the semester.
Academic honesty and integrity Policy:
Academic honesty and integrity of high quality is expected to be maintained by all of the students throughout
the Semester and any kind of academic dishonesty or indulgence in illegitimate practices is not acceptable.

construction, and the project lifecycle; and of the concepts, theories, principles, and techniques

objectives while meeting required standards of ethics and governance.

lifecycle.

construction project

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
[as per the Bulletin]
This course covers topics related to characterization of pavement materials including  soil,
aggregates,  bitumen,bituminous  mixtures  and  pavement  quality  concrete  (PQC).  Soil
characterization includes description of characteristics and desirable properties, classification,
compaction, strength and modulus of subgrade  soil. For aggregates, origin and production,
mineralogy, physical properties and aggregate properties for mix design would be discussed.
Detailed description of bituminous binder would include origin, production and  it application,
chemical composition, physical and rheological properties, grading system, modification of
bitumen, cutbacks and emulsions. Bituminous mixtures include production, desirable properties,
mix design and performance testing. For PQC, materials and selection of mix proportions would
be covered along with design example.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
The main objective of this course is to understand the different material components typical
in pavement and learn about the importance of the properties of these components for
effective functioning of the pavement. In this course, we would also look into the
guidelines outlined for testing, specifications and characterization of various material used
in pavements (both nationally and internationally). A brief about the ongoing worldwide
research on various material aspects of pavements will also be covered as a part of different
lectures.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
a.   . To characterize pavement materials
b.   . To perform bituminous mix design
c.   . To perform mix design of concrete

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
The course deals with complete planning and design of airports with greater emphasis
on planning not restricted to airports, but air transport at large. The course will also touch base on several other
connected aspects of air transportation such as forecasting air transport demand, evolution of aircraft and
pavements, air transportation business, sustainability aspects etc.,

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The scope of the course is to know the various aspects of airport
planning and design. This course is expected to provide a broad overview on various topics as mentioned
below.
➢ To understand briefly air transport and aviation industry [Module I]
➢ To understand the need to forecast air transport demand [Module II]
➢ To get the overall idea about aircraft and its influence on entire planning [Module III]
➢ To get a comprehensive overview about airport system and master planning [Module IV]
➢ To get an overview about the factors affecting the airport capacity [Module V]
➢ To comprehensively analyze the airside configuration and geometric design [Module VI]
➢ To understand the structural pavement design and airport drainage [Module VII]
➢ To get a quick overview about different visual aids in airport and in airspace [Module VIII]
➢ To acknowledge the importance of maintenance and rehabilitation of pavement [Module IX]
➢ To know the parameters influencing the airport performance including benchmarking [Module X]

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
o  Complete comprehensive understanding of airport planning process
o  Structural pavements, maintenance and failures
o  Detailed insights into various guidelines and standards

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
This course covers topics related to pavement failure, evaluation and rehabilitation such as pavement
deterioration, distress and different types of failures, methods of measurement and treatment, use of modern
equipment  for pavement surface condition measurements,  analysis  of  data,  interpretation,  Structural
deterioration of pavements: causes, effects, methods of treatment, structural evaluation of flexible pavements
by rebound deflection method, analysis of data, design of overlay, use of FWD and other methods for
evaluation of flexible and rigid pavements and their application, pavement testing under controlled conditions,
test track studies, Instrumentation for pavement testing.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The course includes the determination of causes of failure in flexible and concrete pavement. The different
techniques for evaluation and rehabilitation of different types of distresses will be taught to the students. The
use of modern equipment’s for structural evaluation of pavement, and design of overlay with the help of data
collected by using the equipment will be covered in this course. The accelerated test facilities constructed
worldwide and instrumentation used in these test facilities for pavement evaluation will be taught to the
students.

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
Network planning, accessibility and mobility; road alignment and survey; geometric design: cross
sectional elements, sight distance, horizontal and vertical alignments; road materials and use of
marginal materials; pavement design, drainage, culverts and small bridges; construction and
specifications; quality control in construction; pavement failures; maintenance; preparation of
detailed project report (DPR); community participation in planning, design, construction and
management.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
Rural roads are the key components for the development of rural community. In this regard, the
Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) was launched by the Govt. of India to provide
connectivity to unconnected Habitations as part of a poverty reduction strategy. Subsequently, the
various strategies have been adopted in planning and construction of rural roads with the aid of
technologically advanced construction practices. The scope of the course is to know the various
aspects rural roads construction and the various processes associated with the construction. In the
recent past, special emphasis is on the use of green technology for road construction in many states.
Rural road technology is fast evolving at an urban pace. The course aims to cover various
technological advancements that have taken place not only in India, but also on the global stage.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
a.   . To perform the geometric design of rural roads
b.   . To design the flexible and rigid pavement
c.   . To prepare the detailed project report

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
Introduction and Scope of dynamic analysis of structures;
origins of vibration theory and experiment; review of earlier concepts: D’Alembert’s
principle, equations of motion. Elements of a structural system: springs, dashpot,
mass; Springs in parallel and series; methods to formulate equations of motion;
Formulation (equation of motion) and solution of undamped and damped free
vibration analysis of S.D.O.F system; Formulation (equation of motion) and solution
of undamped and damped forced vibration analysis of S.D.O.F system; Forced
vibration under harmonic, periodic, impulse, step, ramp, general dynamic forces
(time and frequency domain analysis) and response spectrum load, support excited
vibration, seismic pickups; Numerical techniques for evaluation of dynamic response
of SDOF  system; time domain  analysis;  direct  integration  techniques;  finite
difference method (Central Difference method); Newmark beta method; average
and linear acceleration method; Development of equation of motion and solution
for two degree of freedom systems; Free vibration analysis of MDOF systems;
frequencies; mode shapes and response; orthogonality condition of mode shapes;
Approximate methods for obtaining natural frequencies and mode shapes; Holzer
method;  Stodola’s method;  Rayleigh’s method;  Rayleigh-Ritz method;  Inverse
iteration method; Vector iteration method; Rayleigh’s Quotient  iteration method;
Matrix  iteration method; Generation of damping matrix  for MDOF; dynamic
properties; modal damping; classical damping; damped response with Rayleigh and
Caughey damping.Mode superposition method; mode acceleration method; modal
combination rules using absolute sum, SRSS and CQC method.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
Natural phenomena and human activities impose forces of time-dependent variability on
various civil engineering structures. This course deals with analysis and design of structures
subjected to dynamic loads, which involve consideration of time-dependent forces. Based on
this scope, the following objectives have been listed:
  To make this course necessary for students who are desirous of joining design offices/
industry related to buildings, industrial plants, bridges, tanks, offshore structure,  tall
chimneys etc.
  To determine the behavior of structures under dynamic loading and design a structure
which is resistant to dynamic loading such as seismic, wind, seawave, vehicle induced
vibration force etc.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
a. Development of software for the analysis of framed/skeleton structures.
b.  Capability development for the use of structural dynamics concept and its
applications for framed structural analysis and design under dynamic loading.
c.  Determine the behavior of structures under dynamic loading and design a
structure, which  is resistant to dynamic loading such as seismic, wind,
seawave, vehicle induced vibration force etc.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Basic concepts in transportation planning, accessibility and mobility, land use
interaction, government role in transportation planning, characteristics of travel and transport problems;
transportation survey and data collection: planning, design and implementation, travel analysis zone (TAZ)
development, traditional four-step modelling process; analysis of travel behaviour and demand: studying
travel behaviour, analysing urban travel markets; innovations in transportation modelling: travel behaviour
model, activity-based models, econometric modelling using r-studio, modelling travel demand with cube,
transportation demand management (TDM),  transportation  system management (TSM),  smart  city
transportation planning: transit-oriented development (TOD),pedestrian-oriented development, liveable street
planning,  multimodal  transportation  planning,  shared  mobility  concepts,  integrated  transportation
management and planning, transportation and energy, climate change, fuel choice and green mobility.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The course aims at imparting knowledge on understanding of urban
transportation problems from planners’ perspective, definition of the problem, setting clear goals and
objectives to serve as guiding factors in the planning process, identification of the causal factors influencing
the demand for urban travel and development of relationship between the factors and the travel demand.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
a.  The candidates will understand the process of planning transportation infrastructures,
b.   . The candidates will learn to model and analyze demand of transportation infrastructures.

sections.heading: Text Books
sections.text:
TB1. Sarkar, P.K., Maitri, V., and Joshi, G.J. Transportation Planning, Principles, Practices
and Policies, PHI Pvt. Ltd., latest edition.
TB2. Chakroborty, P. and Das, A. Principles of Transportation Engineering, PHI Pvt. Ltd.,
latest edition.
RB1. Papacosta, C.S., and Prevedouros Transportation Engineering and Planning, PHI Pvt.
Ltd., latest edition.
RB2. Kadiyali, L. R. Traffic Engineering and Transport Planning, Khanna Publishers, latest
edition.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
The course deals with various aspects of concrete structures with emphasis on design
of various elements and exposure to different code provisions.
Materials; high strength concrete, flexure analysis and design; shear and diagonal tension; bond and
anchorage; serviceability; torsion; columns; joints; indeterminate beams and frames; yield line analysis; strip
method for slabs; composite construction; footing and foundations; concrete building system; concrete tall
buildings, detailing in concrete structures

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The concrete structures are quite common in India for both low-rise
and high-rise buildings due to the strong performance in the last many decades even during strong wind &
earthquake ground motion. The concrete structures are used in most of the infrastructure applications such as
construction of buildings, bridges, roads, airport structures, stadiums, water tanks, chimneys, storage bins,
nuclear  reactors  etc., The codal provisions  are continuously changing with changing times due  to
technological advancements and our improved understanding of the behavioral characteristics of concrete.
Though concrete structures are design are not anything new, but certain aspects of design and construction
still needs further research and understanding. The beam-column joint is hardly 50 years old and was totally
unexplored before 1970s. Today, it was observed that beam-column failure is one of the most important
reasons for the failure of RC framed structures. On the other hand, RC structures are only framed form, but
different structural configurations evolve over the years to accommodate the tall buildings with safety and
economy. The present course aims to highlight the design and construction aspects of wide range of
structures, ranging from traditional RC framed structures to tall buildings to certain specialized structures
such as chimneys and water tanks. The emphasis will be more on the performance of structure under
earthquake loading conditions. The codal provisions will be discussed for the better understanding.
➢ To understand the concrete structures and its applications [Module - I]
➢ To study different structural configurations for the concrete structures [Module-II]
➢ To understand and design few important components of RC framed structures including beam-column
joints and other vital structural elements [Module-III]
➢ To understand the concept of shear wall frame structures [Module IV]
➢ To understand the behavioral and design aspects of shell structures and folded plates [Module V]
➢ To understand the ductile behavioral aspects of structures under earthquake [Module VI]
➢ To understand the design and detailing aspects of water tanks and chimneys [Module VII]
➢ To understand the design aspects of RCC poles and pipes [Module VIII]

Pilani Campus

➢ To discuss the case studies of different RC structures and its failures [Module IX]
➢ To discuss the various advancements in concrete structures and the research scope [Module X]

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Introduction to basic concepts of prestressing; prestressing systems; analysis of prestress; losses in
prestress; deflection; design of anchorage zone, design of prestressed concrete girders.

sections.heading: Scope and Objectives
sections.text:
The universal use of prestressed concrete as a versatile construction material is well established due
to its suitability in multifarious types of structural applications. The application of prestressed concrete
is increasing with the development of technology. Prestressing is the application of an initial load on a
structure to enable it to counteract the stresses arising from subsequent loads during its service
period. In this course, the students will be introduced to prestressed concrete and its applications.
The course would cover important topics of prestressed concrete, including the design of structural
elements based on the limit state philosophy of design. It would partially fulfill the requirements of
practicing structural design engineers.
The course integrates science and engineering principles to design prestressed concrete members and
structural systems. The application of scientific and engineering knowledge would be demonstrated in
solving engineering problems associated with the design of precast prestressed building members.
This course would be quite helpful for students who want to join the structural design or construction
industry. At the end of the coursework, students will be able to determine the behavior of prestressed
concrete structures.

sections.heading: Course Learning Outcomes
sections.text:
Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to understand the fundamental
concepts of prestressing and the different systems used in prestressed concrete construction. They
will gain the ability to –
▪  Understand the basic principles of prestressing and identify various prestressing systems including
pre-tensioning and post-tensioning methods.
1
BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani
Pilani Campus
AUGS/ AGSR Division
▪  Analyze the behaviour of prestressed concrete members under axial loads and bending, including
the use of pressure/thrust lines and load balancing concepts.
▪  Calculate different types of prestress losses and understand their causes and effects on structural
performance.
▪  Evaluate the flexural and shear strength of prestressed concrete members and design appropriate
reinforcements.
▪  Analyze the transfer of prestress in pre-tensioned members and anchorage zone stresses in post-
tensioned members.
▪  Design prestressed concrete sections for flexure using limit state concepts and apply methods
such as Magnel’s approach.
▪  Compute short- and long-term deflections in prestressed concrete members and assess crack
width control under service loads.
▪  Analyze statically indeterminate prestressed concrete structures, including secondary moments
and concordant cable profiles.
▪  Understand and design composite structures involving prestressed and in-situ cast concrete under
different support conditions.
▪  Apply engineering knowledge and analytical skills to solve real-world structural design problems
involving prestressed concrete.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
Bridges are an inseparable part of any communication network as they are the key elements in roadways
and highway networks. This course intends to impart skills for analysis & design of various types of bridges.
This course will mainly focus on the design of three types of bridge superstructures namely Slab
culverts/bridges, T-beam bridges, and Composite bridges. The design of the bridge substructure will include
the design of elastomeric bearings and the design of abutments and piers. Moreover, the course will include
the design aspects of continuous bridges. At the end of this course, the students would be equipped with the
complete analysis and design of slab, T-beam and composite bridges, along with the design of substructures
for them.

[as per the Bulletin]
Flexibility Method; stiffness method; beam curved in plan; two dimensional and three
dimensional analysis of structures; shear deformations, shear wall analysis; interactive
software development for analysis of structures.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
Advanced structural analysis techniques and methods provide efficient means and tools
for analysis and design of framed structures using matrix approach. Hence learning
advance structural analysis will be very useful for structural analyst and designers using
computer oriented approach. The basic objective of  this course  is to acquire the
fundamental concepts of matrix methods of structural analysis and their implementation
in development of computer programs for computer aided structural analysis of structures.
By the end of the course, the students will be familiar with matrix methods of structural
analysis using self-developed computer programs wherein both the concepts of flexibility
method and stiffness method of structural analysis will be emphasized

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:

b.  Capability development for the use Matrix based structural analysis
principles and formulations for framed structure.
c.  Development of capability to analyze curved members and non-prismatic
members using stiffness matrices derived from flexibility matrices.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Fundamentals of the finite element method (FEM); basic formulations of FEM; steps in FEM; 1-D, 2-
D and 3-D elements; axi-symmetric elements, isoparametric formulations; programming aspects in
FEM; plate bending elements; shell elements; material and geometric nonlinearity; Buckling and
Vibration problems, application of FEM to civil engineering problems.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
Finite element method is the most powerful numerical method widely used for solving problems in
different branches of engineering especially Civil Engineering. This method is usually used to solve
complex problems with regard to complexity in material, geometry, boundary, and loading
conditions, such as non-homogeneous material, irregular geometry, boundary conditions, and static
& dynamic loading conditions. The finite element formulation from the weak form of the governing
differential equations is also covered. The course is aimed to enable students to understand the
advanced concept of finite element method and its application to Civil Engineering.

sections.heading: Text Book
sections.text:
R. D. Cook, D. Malkus, M. E. Plesha, and R. J. Witt, Concepts and Applications of Finite Element
Analysis, Wiley India, Fourth Edition, 2003.

sections.heading: Reference Books
sections.text:
1.  O. C. Zienkiewicz, R. L. Taylor and J. Z. Zhu, The Finite Element Method: Its Basis & Fundamentals,
Butterworth-Heinemann, 6th edition, Elsevier India, New Delhi, 2005.
2.  Huebner and Thornton, The Finite Element Methods for Engineers, 2nd Edition, Mc-Graw-Hill.
3.  Chandrupatla and Belegundu, Introduction to Finite Elements in Engineering, 2nd Edition,
Prentice-Hall

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
Environment and global problems; Framing Environmental issues; effects of
infrastructure development on environment; prediction and assessment of environmental impacts of
infrastructure  projects:  technical  and  procedural  aspects,  guidelines  and  legal  aspects  of
environmental protection, impacts on air, water, soil and noise environment, valuation, strategic
assessment, mathematical modeling for environmental processes; social impact assessment (SIA),
dislocation/disruption impact of Infrastructure projects; Life Cycle Assessments (LCA) and risk
analysis  methodologies;  mitigation  of  environmental  impacts;  case  studies;  environmental
management plan (EMP), national and international certification and guidelines including ISO.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
The course focuses on understanding environmental issues linked to
infrastructure development, emphasizing technical, procedural, and legal aspects of environmental
impact assessment (EIA). It covers prediction and mitigation of impacts on air, water, soil, and noise
environments, supported by modeling tools. Strategic assessments, LCA, risk analysis, and SIA are
addressed alongside valuation and management frameworks. Case studies and EMP formulation are
discussed  with  reference  to  national  and  international  standards,  including  ISO,  ensuring
comprehensive exposure to certification protocols and regulatory compliance.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Historical overview of Chemical Engineering, Principles of balancing with examples to illustrate differential and
integral balances lumped and distributed balances, Material balances in simple systems involving physical
changes and chemical reactions, Systems involving recycle, purge and bypass, Properties of substances: single
component & multicomponent, single and multiphase systems. Ideal liquid and gaseous mixtures, Energy balance
calculations in simple systems, Introduction to Computer aided calculations-steady state material and energy
balances for chemical plants

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
This course provides an introduction to the basic fundamentals of chemical engineering. It deals with calculations,
which form the basis of the design of a chemical industrial plant or process. It aims to inculcate conceptual
knowledge as well as systematic and sound problem solving skills in the student. The concept of material and
energy balances are introduced, explained, and worked with the help of examples from the real world chemical
process plants. Fundamentals of  this course would be required for other courses like Chemical Process
Technology, Chemical Reaction Engineering, Separation Processes and Process Modelling and Simulation.

sections.heading: Course Learning Outcomes (CLO)
sections.text:
CLO1. At the end of this course, the students must be able to apply important definitions and conventions in
chemical processes.
CLO2. They can solve material and energy balances for single and multiple units with or without chemical
reaction and feedback/bypass.

sections.heading: Method of Conduct of the Course
sections.text:
The course Chemical Process Calculation  is organized  into three weekly lectures of 50 minutes each,
complemented by tutorials, self-study, and continuous assessment. Weekly tutorials emphasize numerical
problem-solving to strengthen analytical skills. Independent study is encouraged through assigned readings,
problem sets, and use of our Learning Management System (NALANDA) for lecture notes, resources, and
discussion forums.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Fundamental  Concepts,  Fluid  Statics,  Integral and  Differential  Analysis  for  Fluid  Motion,
Dimensional Analysis, Internal and External Fluid Flow, Fluid Machinery, Flow through Packed Bed,
Agitation, Introduction to Compressible Flow.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
This course is an introduction to the field of fluid mechanics. It mainly covers the basic principles of
fluid mechanics. It introduces the student to the fundamental and practical aspects of fluid flow
operations that a practising chemical engineer encounters regularly. The physical concepts of fluid
mechanics and analysis methods, beginning from basic principles, shall be dealt with in this course.

sections.heading: Learning Outcomes
sections.text:
  Recognize and define key fluid properties (such as pressure, density, temperature, viscosity, and
velocity fields), calculate shear stresses and viscous forces, and apply fundamental fluid laws including
the ideal gas law, surface tension, and speed of sound.
  Evaluate  pressure  distributions  in  hydrostatic  fluids and submerged  surfaces  across  various
geometries, and predict buoyancy forces on floating bodies.
  Apply the Reynolds transport theorem to establish conservation laws and solve problems involving
the Conservation of mass and momentum using integral and differential analysis.
  Apply Bernoulli and Euler equations to solve incompressible inviscid flow problems, and develop key
dimensionless groups using principles like the Buckingham Pi Theorem.
  Analyze fully developed laminar and turbulent pipe flows, calculate pipe losses using the Moody chart,
and evaluate pressure drops across fittings, valves, and sudden expansions or contractions.
  Apply boundary-layer concepts (including calculating thickness and pressure gradients), evaluate
Drag on immersed bodies, analyze fluid flow through solid beds, and determine minimum fluidization
velocities.
  Understand the characteristics and operations of pipes, fittings, and valves, and select and design
pumps based on specific process requirements.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Applications of first and second laws; relations between state properties; chemical equilibria in reacting and
non-reacting systems; statistical concepts, and brief exposure to irreversible thermodynamics; extensive
problem assignments throughout. [Review of work, heat, reversible and irreversible processes, First Law
applications to closed and open systems, Second Law, Entropy, Heat effects, Equations of state and
generalized correlations for PVT behavior, Maxwell relations and fluid properties estimation; Residual and
excess properties, Partial molar quantities; Gibbs-Duhem Equation, Fugacity and Activity Coefficient
models, Vapor-Liquid equilibria, chemical reaction equilibrium.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
  Understanding laws of thermodynamics and applying the concept for heat, work and energy
calculations.
  Analyze essential conditions (temperature, pressure, composition, etc.) for simple physical and chemical
changes.
  Thermodynamic properties calculation for ideal and real fluids.
  Apply thermodynamic principles in estimation/calculation of thermodynamic efficiency
   Application of thermodynamic principals for understanding the criterion (G, equilibria constant, etc.)
of simple chemical reaction at equilibria, degree of conversion, composition and effect of P, inert gas
addition, excess reactants, products on conversion, etc.
  VLE calculations for phase-equilibria.

sections.heading: Students learning outcomes
sections.text:
1.  Develop ability to analyze heat, energy, and work requirement/transfer for simple physical
and chemical processes using laws of thermodynamics.

sections.heading: Applying principles of thermodynamics to chemical engineering systems.
sections.text:
3.  Industrial  design  of  reactors,  separators  and   utilities  using  principles  of
thermodynamics.
4. Thermodynamic efficiency calculation for chemical engineering processes.

title: Engineering Chemistry

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Introduction to basic principles of various branches of chemistry and their applications in chemical
Industries. Organic chemistry (Important functional groups and their reactions, Some important name
reactions commonly used in the chemical industry); Physical chemistry (Thermodynamic processes,
Thermochemistry, Electrochemistry, Adsorption, Catalysis), Chemical methods of analysis (volumetric
analysis: neutralization, redox, complexometric titrations), Instrumental methods of analysis ( IR, UV-
vis spectroscopy, Chromatography), Engineering materials (cementing materials, refractories, polymers),
Metals and alloys (Iron and steel), Corrosion (types of corrosion and corrosion control methods), Water
treatment (Hardness of water, water analysis and water treatment), Fuels and combustion (Classification
of fuels, Analysis of coal, Combustion, Calorific value and its determination).

sections.heading: Scope & Objective
sections.text:
The course aims  to introduce various aspects of chemistry as applied  to
engineering. The course also aims to bridge the theoretical concepts and their practical engineering
applications, thus highlighting the role of chemistry in the field of chemical engineering.

sections.heading: Course Learning Outcomes
sections.text:
Upon successful completion of this course, the student will be able to:
   Identify and illustrate key functional groups and industrially important organic reactions used in
chemical synthesis.
  Explain the principles of thermodynamics and apply them to evaluate energy changes in
chemical processes.
  Analyze  electrochemical  systems  and  interpret  electrode  potentials,  electrochemical  cell
behavior, and battery performance.
  Describe adsorption processes and interpret isotherms and breakthrough curves relevant to
industrial separations.
  Perform and  evaluate chemical and  instrumental  analytical techniques such  as  titrations,
spectroscopy (IR, UV-Vis), and chromatography.
   Classify polymers and engineering materials and assess their structure-property relationships for
industrial use.
  Distinguish between various metals and alloys, especially steel, and justify their use based on
physical and chemical properties.
  Assess the types and characteristics of fuels and calculate their calorific values using standard
methods.
   Identify different types of corrosion and propose suitable prevention and control methods.
  Analyze water samples for impurities, determine hardness, and recommend appropriate water
treatment techniques.
   Integrate chemical  concepts  to  solve  practical problems  in  industrial and environmental
engineering contexts.
  Demonstrate  scientific  thinking,  analytical  reasoning, and  technical communication  skills
through tests, quizzes, and project work.

sections.heading: Course Description
Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
This course is an introduction to the chemical reaction kinetics, design and performance of various types of chemical
reactors for chemically reacting systems, which yield industrially important products. The emphasis in this course will
be to understand the fundamentals of kinetics of homogeneous reactions, design and analysis of ideal reactors; and
non-ideal flow.

sections.heading: Learning Outcomes
sections.text:
By the end of this course the student will be able to,
  Develop performance equations for reactors and design the reactors
  Apply design principles to decide on reactor for appropriate processes/reactions.
   Understand the basics of catalysis and develop equations for catalyst effectivness, design catalytic reactors
   Understand how non ideal reactors (reactors in the real world) operate differently from ideal reactors.
   Learn how the chemical engineering industry depends on reactors and their design.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
The course comprises of experiments in three major areas of chemical engineering, i.e., fluid mechanics, heattransfer
and mass transfer. The course involves experiments designed to cover the areas related to the theory of

sections.heading: Fluid flow
sections.text:
flow through packed and fluidized beds, major and minor losses associated with fluid flow, flow
characteristics, continuity principle, boundary layer theory and fluid moving machinery,

sections.heading: Heat transfer
sections.text:
conduction, convection, radiation and heat exchange equipments such as heat exchangers (shell
and tube, double pipe, plate type, finned tube) and condensers.

sections.heading: Mass transfer
sections.text:
Vapor liquid equilibrium (VLE), separation based on volatility, mass transfer equipments such
as distillation column, packed bed adsorber, and mass transfer with reaction and other relevant concepts.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The main objective of this course is to familiarize the students on different principles of chemical engineering through
hands on experimentation. The experiments are designed to enable students to apply the theoretical background
assimilated in the relevant chemical engineering courses to practice in a laboratory environment. Emphasis is laid on
employing scientific methodology in practice: each experiment requires planning, data collection, calculations based on
chemical engineering principles, critical analysis, discussion and presentation of the observed result. Additionally, the
students will also learn the operation of laboratory scale scientific equipment.

sections.heading: Course Learning Outcomes
sections.text:
  Gain fundamental hands on experience working with Chemical Engineering laboratory conditions and
equipments.
   Learn how to apply important Chemical Engineering theory for calculations and performing experiments.
   Learn how to get proper data, how experimental data can be analyzed and how suitable conclusions can be
attained.

sections.text:
9.1 Lab Report:
Guideline for Laboratory Report Submission
●  At the beginning of the semester, all students will be encouraged to form a group of 3 or 4 amongst
themselves. Please note that due to operational constraints, a group size smaller or larger than prescribed
may not be feasible.
●  On the day of conduction of the lab experiment, a datasheet with experimental results will be noted by each
group member. Based on the observation sheets, the students will compile a report which should include the
following:-
○  Aim & Objectives of the experiment: 1 mark
○  Laboratory Observations: 1 mark
○  Sample Calculations: 2 marks
○  Results and Discussion: 1 marks
○  Conclusions and Understanding: 1 mark
3
BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani
Pilani Campus
AUGS/ AGSR Division
●  Students are encouraged to utilize the lab hours for carrying out sample calculations, data visualization
and building insights for the discussion part of the lab report, particularly since both faculty and TAs are
available live during this time to solve your doubts on spot.
●   It’s expected that every group will submit a lab report as a hardcopy (printout) at the lab and attach it to a master
file maintained at the lab for this purpose. Please make sure you write name and ID of all group members on
top of each page. You are free to use any platforms/software for report generation,data analysis and visualization.
Use of technology is encouraged. Handwritten and scanned reports won’t be accepted!
●  The students are encouraged to work along with  their groupmates to draft the report. However, the
“Conclusions and Understanding” section of the report needs to be individually written by each group
member. This means that each report will have 3 or 4 separate conclusion and understanding (i.e., one by each
student in the group)
●  Lab report will be due one week after the completion of the experiment. Only those lab reports which are
received on the due date will be evaluated.
●  Plagiarism: As highlighted, you’re requested to submit a professional quality digitally printed lab report.
Plagiarism might be construed as academic dishonesty and your submitted lab reports may be subjected through
plagiarism detection software(s). While we understand there might be a few technical phrases common in all
the lab reports, hence there won’t be any penalty for similarity up-to 20%. However, there would be 50% marks
deduction for those whose reports are 20%-40% similar. If found more than 40% similarity, zero marks will be
awarded for involved students. Decision of I/C will be final in all such cases.
9.2 Cylce-1/Cycle-2 Lab Exam:
  The mid/end sem lab exam will be a closed book lab exam, where the students will perform
experiments at the lab on their own and submit a report in the designated time slot.
  The students will be asked to pick an experiment (through lucky draw) from a pool of experiments relevant
to their cycle.
 A handwritten report (similar to the lab report) needs to be written and submitted for evaluation in given
time slot.
  The experiments will be shortened to enable timely completion of the experiment and report writing.
  No separate make-up for the Lab Exams will be allowed.
9.3 Comprehensive Quiz:
9.3.1 A comprehensive quiz will be conducted on the designated date as a closed book exam. Questions and
options (in case of multiple choice questions) would be randomized and it’s in your best interest to focus on
your questions in hand since the time would be limited.
9.3.2 The quiz will be based on the theory behind the experiments covered in the lab and may include question on
concepts pertaining to the chemical engineering principles involved in the experiments.
9.3.3 No separate make-up for the quiz will be allowed.

9.4.1 Viva will be closed book and you will be tested on clarity of concepts related to the experiments conducted,

9.4.2 A panel of all instructors will take the viva and give individual marks. Average of those marks would then be
taken and communicated to you. Please note that we may not be able to give you individual break-up of marks

9.4.3 Only genuine requests for viva make-up backed by paperwork/evidence/proof will be entertained. A

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Special equilibrium-based separations like humidification and water cooling, drying of wet solids, adsorption,
crystallization  etc., Mechanical  separations  like  filtration,  centrifugation,  froth  floatation  etc.,  Solid
separations based on size reduction including sieving operations and related equipment like crushers, mills,
pulverizers etc., special separation processes like ion-exchange, membranes, chromatography etc.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
This course gives the basic understanding of Mechanical Operations, which involves size reduction, size
separation, filtration, etc. and certain Mass Transfer Operations like humidification, drying, adsorption,
membrane separation, and crystallization.  It covers the fundamentals, application of each of these unit
operations and the equipment used is discussed in detail. The objective of the course is to orient the students
to the industrial practices, which involve both mechanical operations and mass transfer operations, so that they
can understand them better.
