Pilani Campus
Instruction Division
value decomposition (EVD), singular value decomposition (SVD)) and their uses, Hilbert spaces and
norms, projections, inequalities, orthogonalization. The fifth and final module (module-4) consists of an
introduction to optimization: convex sets and convex functions; unconstrained and constrained optimization,
Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, duality, and optimization techniques such as Lagrange multipliers,
numerical optimization (non-convex) techniques.
The objectives of the foundational course are to lay strong foundations for i) probability and random
signals and related theory,  ii)  linear algebra, matrices  iii) optimization techniques and  their uses in
communications and signal processing.

sections.heading: Course Outcomes
sections.text:
At the end of the course Signal theory and optimization, students learn useful mathematical and probability
concepts, tools (transforms, matrices, optimization), and techniques to model several phenomena that occur in
communication systems and networks, and analyze and design them better. Specifically, they learn the
significance of signal theory, fundamental laws of probability, finding moments of random variables, modeling
using random variables, and random processes and their applications. Furthermore, generation and simulation
of random variables using software tools like MATLAB/Python are also one of the essential practical outcomes
of this course. In addition to strong random signal theory foundations, students learn useful techniques of linear
algebra and matrices, optimization, which are useful in understanding and analyzing machine learning-aided
next generation communication networks.

sections.text:
Probability theory and random variables; joint, conditional, and marginal distributions; functions of
random variables; moments, expectation, and statistical inequalities; introduction to random processes;
stationarity, autocorrelation, ergodicity, and power spectral density; basic concepts of linear algebra:
vector spaces, inner product spaces, linear operators and transformations, spectral decomposition;
matrix factorizations including SVD, LU, and QR; positive definite matrices; orthogonal projections
in Hilbert spaces; introduction to optimization: convex sets and convex functions; unconstrained and
constrained optimization; Lagrange multipliers, Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, duality, and
numerical optimization techniques.

sections.heading: Scope and Objectives
sections.text:
The instructor presents the content of the course "Signal Theory and Optimization" in five modules. The
first module (module-0) comprises preliminaries covering signals classification, definitions, properties,
limitations, and applications. The subsequent module (module-1) consists of axiomatic probability theory and
random variables, joint, conditional, and marginal distributions of random variables, first and second order
statistics, Moment generating function, characteristic function, functions of random variables, and statistical
inequalities, generation and simulation of random variables.
The third module (module-2) mainly introduces stochastic processes, specifications, concepts such as
stationarity, autocorrelation, crosscorrelation, ergodicity, energy, and power spectral densities. The fourth
module (module-3) consists of basic concepts of linear algebra, namely, vector spaces, linear independence
and dependence, inner product spaces, linear operators and transformations (matrices), standard matrices (for
example, positive definite and semidefinite matrices), matrix decompositions (for example, LU, and QR, Eigen

value decomposition (EVD), singular value decomposition (SVD)) and their uses, Hilbert spaces and
norms, projections, inequalities, orthogonalization. The fifth and final module (module-4) consists of an
introduction to optimization: convex sets and convex functions; unconstrained and constrained optimization,
Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, duality, and optimization techniques such as Lagrange multipliers,
numerical optimization (non-convex) techniques.
The objectives of the foundational course are to lay strong foundations for i) probability and random
signals and related theory,  ii)  linear algebra, matrices  iii) optimization techniques and  their uses in
communications and signal processing.

sections.heading: Course Outcomes
sections.text:
At the end of the course Signal theory and optimization, students learn useful mathematical and probability
concepts, tools (transforms, matrices, optimization), and techniques to model several phenomena that occur in
communication systems and networks, and analyze and design them better. Specifically, they learn the
significance of signal theory, fundamental laws of probability, finding moments of random variables, modeling
using random variables, and random processes and their applications. Furthermore, generation and simulation
of random variables using software tools like MATLAB/Python are also one of the essential practical outcomes
of this course. In addition to strong random signal theory foundations, students learn useful techniques of linear
algebra and matrices, optimization, which are useful in understanding and analyzing machine learning-aided
next generation communication networks.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
This course covers analysis of series and parallel resonant converters, load dependent properties of resonant converters
with ZVS/ZCS boundary. Operation of these converters for Zero-current Switching and Zero-Voltage switching is
discussed in detail. The concept of resonance is extended to analyze the soft switching mechanism of semiconductor
devices Diode, MOSFET and IGBT to reduce the switching loss and possible mitigation of EMI. The zero-current-
switching and the zero-voltage-switching quasi resonant switch cell is discussed for full bridge converter. Design example
of zero-current-switching and zero-voltage switching class E-inverter is also covered in this course.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
a.  Understand the concept of resonant tank network
b.  Analyze the dependence of ZVS/ZCS boundary on load resistance
c.  Design ZVS/ZCS switch cell for DC-DC converter
d.  Analysis of switching loss and EMI under soft switching

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
This ME course is meant for equipping students with knowledge of
prevalent power quality issues in the modern power distribution system, their causes and classifications
covering voltage and current based power quality problems such as sag, swell, unbalance, harmonics
and poor power factor. Various standards on power quality and their monitoring techniques are also
covered. The course also majorly deals with power quality compensation techniques including both
passive and active compensation, their design, analysis and modeling. The control techniques for active
power compensators and active filters are also discussed. The lab component is designed to enrich
students’ knowledge of power quality with practical hands on and simulation exercises.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
A ME course focusing on electric power quality typically
covers the analysis, mitigation, and improvement of power quality issues, including voltage variations,
harmonics, and other disturbances, preparing graduates for careers in power utilities and industries.
The objectives of this course are designed to help students to:
a.  Understand various power quality issues and their impact.
b.  Learn about power and power factor in single-phase and three-phase systems.
c.  Study conventional and active compensation techniques for power factor correction and
load voltage regulation
d.  Gain knowledge of active filter techniques for harmonics elimination.
e.  Understand power quality improvement in power supplies, drive systems, and renewable
energy systems.
Learning outcomes of the course have been incorporated in the course plan on next page.

sections.text:
a.  T1: B. Singh, A. Chandra, K.A. Haddad, “Power Quality: Problems and Mitigation Techniques”,
Wiley, 2015, 1st Edition.
b.  T2: R. C. Dugan, M. F. McGranaghan, S. Santoso, H. W. Beaty, “Electrical Power Systems
Quality”, McGrawHill, 2012, 3rd Edition.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
This ME course is meant for equipping students with knowledge of
prevalent power quality issues in the modern power distribution system, their causes and classifications
covering voltage and current based power quality problems such as sag, swell, unbalance, harmonics
and poor power factor. Various standards on power quality and their monitoring techniques are also
covered. The course also majorly deals with power quality compensation techniques including both
passive and active compensation, their design, analysis and modeling. The control techniques for active
power compensators and active filters are also discussed. The lab component is designed to enrich
students’ knowledge of power quality with practical hands on and simulation exercises.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
A ME course focusing on electric power quality typically
covers the analysis, mitigation, and improvement of power quality issues, including voltage variations,
harmonics, and other disturbances, preparing graduates for careers in power utilities and industries.
The objectives of this course are designed to help students to:
a.  Understand various power quality issues and their impact.
b.  Learn about power and power factor in single-phase and three-phase systems.
c.  Study conventional and active compensation techniques for power factor correction and
load voltage regulation
d.  Gain knowledge of active filter techniques for harmonics elimination.
e.  Understand power quality improvement in power supplies, drive systems, and renewable
energy systems.
Learning outcomes of the course have been incorporated in the course plan on next page.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Semiconductor fundamentals for Nanotechnology, Introduction to low dimensional nano-structures and
Quantum Mechanics ,Scaling and nanoelectronics, Nano electronic device materials and circuits, Strain
engineering and high speed quantum electronic devices, Optical properties of nano-structures, Linear and
non linear effects of optical materials and structures, Nano photonic devices, Electronic Devices based on
nano structures in evolution of Silicon Base Devices, Integrated photo electronic devices and systems and
its applications, New Trends in Nano devices and technology.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
This course provides a blend of electronic and photonic fundamentals and their applications to the fast
moving technology involved in high-speed electronics, optical electronics and optical communication
systems in terms of nano structures. Electronics and Photonics are becoming increasingly important as
limitations of speed, size and bandwidth affect many electronic devices and systems. Moreover,
integration of electronics and photonics becomes an important issue related to modern technical aspects
like optical interconnects, integrated optical circuits etc. Here the fundamentals of semiconductors,
quantum structures and transport properties related to quantum structures will be first discussed. That will
be followed by electronic and optical properties and details of strain engineering. Finally all these basic
concepts will be applied in understanding modern and photonic and electronic devices useful for
engineering applications. Students will also be encouraged to learn hands-on-training in analysis/
simulation of some electronic-photonic devices using MATLAB/ SILVACO TCAD software.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Evolution of wireless cellular technologies to 5G and beyond, review of matrix and signal theory for
communication applications, introduction to stochastic geometry for performance analysis of wireless
networks, D2D communications- modeling and analysis, cooperative communications-buffer-aided relaying
and performance analysis, modulation and multiple access techniques-NOMA, OTFS, OAM. Introduction to
potential technologies for beyond 5G/6G communications: IRS, molecular communications, and AI in
wireless communications.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
a)  This course aims to introduce the students to the advances in wireless communications and expose
them to the research options available for applications in the real-world implementation of the next-
generation wireless networks.
b) The course will introduce the students to current trends in the wireless industry with a specific focus
on the 5G and beyond 5G communication networks.
c) The course aims to equip students with tools for designing the engineering aspects of wireless
communications.
d) New techniques envisaged  to be a  part of the next-generation wireless networks,  like D2D
communications, NOMA, OTFS, and stochastic geometry applied to wireless communications, to
name a few, will be covered to make the student industry and research-ready.

sections.heading: Course Learning Outcomes
sections.text:
a)  Evaluate the trade-offs in system design parameters (e.g., power, bandwidth, latency, mobility) in
the context of modern wireless networks.
b)  Design and evaluate advanced modulation, coding, and diversity techniques for improving link
reliability and spectral efficiency in various wireless environments.
c)  Analyze complex wireless channel models (e.g., time-varying fading, spatially correlated MIMO
channels) and assess their implications on communication system performance.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Evolution of wireless cellular technologies to 5G and beyond, review of matrix and signal theory for
communication applications, introduction to stochastic geometry for performance analysis of wireless
networks, D2D communications- modeling and analysis, cooperative communications-buffer-aided relaying
and performance analysis, modulation and multiple access techniques-NOMA, OTFS, OAM. Introduction to
potential technologies for beyond 5G/6G communications: IRS, molecular communications, and AI in
wireless communications.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
a)  This course aims to introduce the students to the advances in wireless communications and expose
them to the research options available for applications in the real-world implementation of the next-
generation wireless networks.
b) The course will introduce the students to current trends in the wireless industry with a specific focus
on the 5G and beyond 5G communication networks.
c) The course aims to equip students with tools for designing the engineering aspects of wireless
communications.
d) New techniques envisaged  to be a  part of the next-generation wireless networks,  like D2D
communications, NOMA, OTFS, and stochastic geometry applied to wireless communications, to
name a few, will be covered to make the student industry and research-ready.

sections.heading: Course Learning Outcomes
sections.text:
a)  Evaluate the trade-offs in system design parameters (e.g., power, bandwidth, latency, mobility) in
the context of modern wireless networks.
b)  Design and evaluate advanced modulation, coding, and diversity techniques for improving link
reliability and spectral efficiency in various wireless environments.
c)  Analyze complex wireless channel models (e.g., time-varying fading, spatially correlated MIMO
channels) and assess their implications on communication system performance.

sections.heading: Course  Description
sections.text:
Introduction  to  digital communication  systems;  signal  characterization and
representation of bandpass and low-pass signals; signal space analysis; fundamentals of source coding and entropy;
digital modulation techniques and constellation design; optimum receivers for additive white Gaussian noise
channels; maximum likelihood (ML) and maximum a posteriori (MAP) detection; symbol error probability
analysis; non-coherent detection methods; carrier and symbol synchronization techniques; communication over
band-limited channels; ISI, Nyquist criteria, and signal waveform design, equalization; multicarrier modulation
systems, effects of intercarrier interference (ICI) and carrier frequency offset (CFO); channel capacity limits and
fundamentals of channel coding.

sections.heading: Course Scope and Objective
sections.text:
1. To provide fundamental knowledge to model, design, and analyze advanced digital communication
systems, with applications in both industry and R&D.
2. To reinforce theoretical concepts through practical assignments using MATLAB, Python, and USRP.
3.  Requires prior knowledge of Linear Systems, Probability Theory, Stochastic Processes, and basic
Communication Systems.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
This course deals with the system-level design of embedded systems comprised of both hardware and
software. It investigates topics ranging from system modeling to hardware-software implementation. This
course also teaches analysis and optimization processes for supporting algorithmic and architectural
design decisions. It also helps the student gain design experience through different case studies. The
course emphasizes a top-down design methodology driven by bottom-up constraints. The topics covered
will include co-design of hardware and software involving key aspects like partitioning, mapping and
optimization.

sections.heading: Course Learning Objectives (CLOs) are as follows
sections.text:
a. Analyze embedded system requirements and develop suitable hardware–software co-design solutions by
applying system-level modeling, partitioning, and synthesis techniques.
b. Evaluate and optimize hardware–software architectures using partitioning algorithms, mapping
strategies, and performance estimation methods to satisfy design constraints such as speed, area, power,
and cost.
c. Design and implement hardware–software co-designed embedded applications using contemporary
design methodologies and FPGA-based platforms to address real-world engineering problems.

steady state and transient (2) Electronic Devices: Diode, BJT and OPAMP.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:

calculation) techniques for DC and AC (1-phase) circuits using Kirchhoff’s
current law (KCL), Kirchhoff’s voltage, law (KVL), Ohms law, Nodal analysis,
Mesh  analysis,  Network  theorems  (Thevenin’s  theorem,  Norton’s
theorem, Maximum power transfer theorem, Superposition theorem) etc.
2. Students will able to perform circuit analysis on electronic circuit
consisting of elements such as diode, BJT transistor, OPAMP.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Feedback control is a central aiding tool in a wide range of engineering and even
some non-engineering applications. This is a second UG level course on the subject, which takes the so-
called Modern approach as opposed to the Classical approach taken in the previous compulsory course
on the subject. This course discusses the basic analytical and design techniques using the concept of state
variables; the techniques of optimal control and estimation theory and an introductory level treatment of
nonlinear systems. The underlying mathematical concepts of these techniques will be emphasized and
also some flavor of applications will be given through examples, exercises and take home assignments
drawn from various engineering domains.

sections.heading: Scopes and Objectives
sections.text:
After completing this course the students will be able to
1)  Analyze various properties (E.g. stability) of linear and nonlinear dynamic systems
2)  Design linear state and output feedback controllers in time domain
3)  Design linear optimal controllers in both deterministic and stochastic domains
4)  Design Kalman Filter and Extended Kalman Filter (widely used signal processing tool)
5)  Design nonlinear state feedback controllers using backstepping algorithm
6)  Simplify higher order LTI models to lower order ones

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Dimensions, units, dimensionless ratios, hydraulic similarity and the testing of models, Continuity and
Bernoulli's equations, fluid properties, Reynolds experiment, laminar and turbulent flow in pipes, major and
minor losses in flow through pipes, Flow in pipelines between reservoirs, open channel flow, Pumps, flow
and velocity measurement devices.

sections.heading: Scope & Objective
sections.text:
This course introduces the foundational principles of fluid mechanics and their practical applications in
hydraulic systems used in water and wastewater treatment plants and sewerage networks.  It covers the
behavior  of  fluids  in motion and  at  rest, emphasizing both  theoretical frameworks and  engineering
applications. Topics include flow regimes, pressure losses, open channel flow, pump performance, and
hydraulic modeling. Students will develop analytical skills to solve real-world fluid flow problems and design
efficient hydraulic systems.

sections.heading: Course Learning Outcomes (CLOs)
sections.text: Upon the completion of this course, students will be able to perform the following:

sections.heading: Fundamentals of Fluid Mechanics
sections.text:
Understand physical dimensions, units, and dimensionless analysis using
Rayleigh and Buckingham π methods; Grasp the concept of hydraulic similarity and model testing

sections.heading: Fluid Properties and Flow Regimes
sections.text:
Analyze dynamic and kinematic viscosity; Distinguish between laminar
and turbulent flow using Reynolds experiment and Reynolds number.

sections.heading: Flow in Pipes
sections.text:
Apply Poiseuille’s law for laminar flow pressure drop; Analyze velocity profiles and
pressure loss in laminar and turbulent pipe flow; Use Moody diagram and Darcy’s law to determine friction
factors.

sections.heading: Complex Pipe Flow Systems
sections.text:
Evaluate flow in non-horizontal and variable diameter pipes; Estimate minor
losses due to expansions, contractions, and fittings.

sections.heading: Pipeline Flow Between Reservoirs
sections.text:
Assess head losses and solve problems involving series and parallel
pipelines.

sections.heading: Open Channel Flow
sections.text:
Define hydraulic parameters like wetted perimeter and hydraulic mean depth; Use
Chezy’s and Manning’s equations to calculate discharge and flow depth.

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
Accounting is the language of business. Through this language, the business (i.e. the Company) not
only maintain the records of transactions it undertakes during the course of its existence but also
communicates with the outside world by publishing various financial reports that summarize
transactions undertaken by the company. Therefore, it is important to note here that this course entails
two important and interrelated aspects, i.e.,
a. Recording transactions, and
b. Preparing financial statements such as balance sheet, income statement, etc.
Since b. follows a., it is important to learn the recording of transactions first to learn preparing
financial statements.
The course will introduce you to the following key concepts: introduction, standards and basic rules
of accounting, double-entry accounting system, identifying and recoding transactions, preparing trial
balance, dealing with incomplete transactions, preparing the balance sheet, types of ownership,
credibility and role of auditing, measuring income, adjustments to the accounts, preparing the
statement of cash flows, recording sales revenue, reporting inventories and cost of goods sold,
recording capital assets, liabilities and interest, stockholders' equity and valuation of financial assets.
This course is specifically designed to meet the educational needs of second year Economics students
and students pursing Finance minor program. To complete the program requirement, the students from
Economics and Finance background require a basic understanding on accounting principles and
financial statement analysis. This course serves that purpose, and it is prerequisite to other advanced
courses that students from (MSc) Economics and Finance (minor) undertake in the subsequent
semesters. Hence, being elementary in nature this course has got its relevance and importance.
Besides, a few students also take this course as an elective to pursue their academic interests in the
field of finance.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
The scope of this course largely encapsulates an introduction to the reporting system used by
businesses to record and convey financial information to investors, analysts, and regulators. This
reporting system is referred to as financial accounting. The key learning objectives that this course
accomplishes enables participants in learning:
a. how companies identify and record transactions that have a financial impact and are critical
to day-to-day functioning of the company.
b. how using a systematic procedure, the recorded transactions are summarized into
meaningful and standardized reports (financial statements) such as the balance sheet, statement
of income etc.
c. the key components that form part of these financial statements.
d. how these financial statements are analyzed and what information do they convey
about the financial well-being and prospects about the company.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
Students who complete this course would be able to
a. Understand the accounting methods for recording the business transactions.
b. Evaluate various financial concepts and preparation of financial statements-balance sheet,
income statement, and cash flow statement.
c. Identify the financial position and performance of the companies.
d. Make better economic decisions while undertaking investments in financial assets.

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
Security Analysis and Portfolio Management addresses two connected
problems: what a financial asset is worth, and how much of it a particular investor should hold.
The first half of the course develops valuation. Students examine the characteristics and risk-return
profiles of the major asset classes – equity, fixed income, and derivatives – and the fundamental,
quantitative and technical techniques used to estimate intrinsic worth. Analysis of economy,
industry, and stock specific fundamentals are carried out for valuing stocks. Hence, asset valuation
forms a major component of this course.
Another important aspect of the course is on modern portfolio concepts, where the criterion changes:
a holding is no longer judged on its own merits but by its contribution to the risk and return of the
whole. This covers modern portfolio theory, diversification and correlation, asset allocation, and the
construction of portfolios aligned to a stated investor's objectives, constraints and risk tolerance.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
The objectives of the course are to provide an introduction to:
•  Types of financial securities and their salient characteristics.
•  Investment philosophy and its role in asset allocation and long-term personal finance
management.
•  Modern portfolio theories and their applications in portfolio design and evaluation.
•  Equity and debt valuation using fundamental analysis and relative valuation techniques.
•   Technical analysis.
•   Financial derivative contracts and their applications.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
• Distinguish the major classes of financial securities — equity, fixed income, derivatives and
alternatives — by their claim structure, risk-return profile and role within a portfolio.
• Value individual securities using techniques appropriate to the instrument, including discounted
cash flow and relative valuation for equity and yield-based measures for fixed income, and state the
assumptions on which each valuation rests.
• Measure and decompose investment risk, separating systematic from unsystematic components,
and evaluate investments on a risk-adjusted basis rather than on raw return.
• Construct a diversified portfolio using correlation and modern portfolio theory, and justify the
resulting asset allocation against a specified investor's objectives, time horizon and risk tolerance.
• Apply derivative instruments to hedge or modify portfolio exposure, and explain the payoff
profile and risk of each strategy employed.
• Assess portfolio performance using risk-adjusted measures and attribution analysis, and determine
when a portfolio requires rebalancing as market conditions change.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Financial Management is a foundation course offered to finance minor students and as
a disciplinary and open elective. The Financial Management course has several practical applications to financial
decision-making and encompasses topics having a varying degree of complexity. It is usually taught at the graduate
level such as MS/MBA or at the PhD. This course ECON/FIN F 315 is designed to suit the level of academic
experience and exposure in finance for undergraduate students having just taken a first course on Fundamentals of
Finance and Accounting. The course’s learning objectives focus on the primary financial decisions undertaken by
the financial manager of an organisation to achieve the principal objective of the firm.
In an increasingly competitive and globally integrated world marked by all-pervasive technological advancements,
the roles and responsibilities of financial managers are expanding in response to the explosion in the number of
firms striving for success. On the one hand, corporations are hungry to fulfil their financing needs, so on the other
are the investors, looking for the best return on the buck they invest. The wide range of investment avenues available
to investors explains the extent of innovations happening in the financial markets worldwide. However, with
uncontrolled growth comes the risk of an uncontrolled collapse and the financial crisis of 2008 is a classic case of
fault lines in the financial markets.
To retain the confidence and faith of investors and forge robust and sustainable growth, the firms must impress
suppliers of capital (investors) with adequate rewards to compensate them for the risks they undertake. More
importantly, the modern viewpoint of the roles and responsibilities of the board of directors and the C-suite
managers has departed from the traditional profitability perspective to the wealth maximisation principle. The firm
must protect and strengthen the rights of its stakeholders, such as employees, suppliers, customers, the environment,
investors, etc. Hence, the wealth maximisation principle influences the decisions firms make about their financing
policy, investment policy, and dividend distribution policy.
The role of the financial manager - which is central to the decision-making concerning finances (money, capital,
investment etc.) – plays a critical role in ensuring seamless day-to-day operations, maintaining profitability and
sustaining reliable long-term performance along with adherence to the company’s ESG (sustainability) policies.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
This course introduces students to the fundamental Corporate Finance
concepts, theories, and the financial decision-making process. The structure of the course enables students to:
a. Develop an understanding about the variety of financial instruments and their valuations,
b. Learn globally adopted practices on corporate investment and risk management and
c. Gain deeper insights into modern corporate finance principles and practices.
Primarily, the course objectives hover around key decisions made by financial managers, including financing,
investing, capital structure, and shareholder rewarding policies. The contents of this course enable the participants
to appreciate the interdependencies between these decisions and their impact on the firm's survivability.
Important: The course assumes that students have done a basic course on accounting (prerequisite), have strong
foundation on financial statements, and have elementary familiarity with financial markets, financial securities,
statistics, and MS-Excel.

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
This course focuses on the concept of financial risk in modern finance. Despite market
volatility and irrational exuberance, effective risk quantification and management remain
crucial. Regulators have imposed safeguards to curb excessive risk-taking by financial
institutions. As a result, risk management has become a core function in the finance industry.
The course is designed to prepare students for the growing demand in financial risk
management roles.
Financial risk (which includes interest rate risk, credit risk, foreign exchange risk and
portfolio risk), Application of Asset price Theory, CAPM and Modern Portfolio Theory,
Multifactor models of risk and return, Capital adequacy, BASEL Norms; Comprehensive
Capital Analysis and Review, Basel Committee on Banking Supervision guidelines, Value at
Risk (VaR), VaR from regulator perspective, Responsive VaR Model, Addressing VaR
weakness, Back testing Concepts - Checking the Strength of VaR Model, Issues with the
Standard VaR models, Risk Not in VaR (RNIV) to VaR migration of risk, Volatility Clustering,
Quantifying and Modeling volatilities, Hedging techniques, Options Greeks, Managing Risk
with Derivatives.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
The three core focus areas dealt with in this course are (i) Risk Identification, (ii) Risk
Measurement, and (iii) Risk Management, in the context of modern-day finance. The scope and
objective of the course is to enable students learn essentials of financial risk management. The
three core focus areas along with the functions and workings of financial institutions
encompass the entire coverage of this course. To meet the stated objective of the course, a
detailed course plan is designed which students can refer in section 6 of this document.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
a.  Understand and classify financial risks such as interest rate risk, credit risk, foreign
exchange risk, and portfolio risk in modern financial markets.
b.  Analyze and implement risk measurement tools such as Value at Risk (VaR),
Responsive VaR, and backtesting techniques.
c.  Interpret and evaluate regulatory frameworks like Basel norms and its guidelines for
capital adequacy and systemic risk control.
d.  Develop risk mitigation strategies using derivatives, including hedging techniques
and options Greeks, to manage exposure effectively.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
 Concepts of State, Nation, Rights and Duties, Civil Society, Democracy, Citizenship and Justice.
  Ideologies of Modern Politics: Social Contractualism, Liberalism, Socialism, Communism,
Maoism, Anarchism, Secularism.
 Selected Readings from key texts of leading thinkers in the History of Modern Western Political
Philosophy including Machiavelli’s Prince, Hobbes’ Leviathan, Locke’s Second Treatise of
government, Rousseau’s Discourse on the origin of inequality, Marx and Engels’ Communist
Manifesto.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
This Course  introduces  certain  select concepts  of  Politics  that  are  relevant  to  the Modern/
Contemporary period. The course helps in unravelling the contexts from which these concepts emerged
through a study of ideologies as well as first-hand reading of key texts in the history of political
thought.
This course prepares the students to be informed active citizens. The design and  its execution
emphasize the comprehension of political thinking, the application of communication and analytical
skills, and the understanding of human diversity.
Modern political concepts enhance the knowledge of the political science discipline by offering the
conceptual vocabulary along with various methods of inquiry. This course not only increases students’
knowledge of the history of classical and modern political thought but also enlightens them with the
fundamental values and ethical issues contested in politics over time. This course informs about the
alternative moral and ethical frameworks for (re)interpreting and evaluating contemporary political
discourses.
Scope: As an introductory course in Politics, this is based on lectures and reading texts. However, the
students are encouraged to move beyond the textbook and familiarize with the research studies by
eminent scholars. This course encourages to use critical thinking and evidence to understand and
evaluate rival theories and interpretations. Accordingly, Students are expected to participate in the
classroom discussions as well as initiate and moderate discussions on political issues that may have
captivated their interest. This practice enables students to develop a critical understanding of various
political discourses and equip them to address political theories and questions of political life and
1

Pilani Campus
AUGS/ AGSR Division
values. Most significantly, this Course facilitates students’ engagement with various political debates
of contemporary India and the world.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
This course focuses on the concepts of environment, development, and climate
change in the contemporary world. The nature and causes of environmental problems in developing and
developed countries will be explored. Attention is given to both the causes and solutions of environmental
problems and the role of state and non-state actors interacting at local, national and global scales. The goal
of this course is for the learners to appreciate the people-environment relations and to understand the
anthropocentric dynamics of development and climate change.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The objective of the course is to make the students aware of the
debates and issues relating to sustainable development and climate change, so as to sufficiently challenge
them to come up with practical solutions. The course covers theory and practice at the global and local
levels and examines the contemporary policy and practice regarding environment, development and
climate change.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
This course focuses on the concept of development, development theories and
practices in the modern world. Interplay between theory and practice and the outcome of this relationship are
also explored in the syllabus. The course provides an overview of development thinking from ‘classical’
development ideas to alternative and post development theories. The course then attempts to critically review
contemporary debates about development, including the link between the current world order and the
Development goals of the developing countries.

debates and issues relating to development and post development. The course covers development theory
and practice at the global and local levels and examines the practice in contemporary times.
. Text Books: John Rapley (2010), Understanding Development: Theory and Practice in the Third World
Viva Books. (Reading material will be given by the IC through classroom portal)

sections.heading: Scope and objective of the course
sections.text:
The main objective of the course is to enhance both the  oral and written communication skills of the
students, required for various managerial activities such as conducting and participating in interviews,
discussing in groups, presenting in teams, speaking in public, giving instructions, conducting meetings, etc.
It would enable the students to understand and demonstrate the use of proper and advanced writing
techniques that today's technology demands including anticipation and audience reaction.

professional presentations, giving instructions, and conducting meetings.
CLO2. Participate confidently and effectively in interviews, group discussions, and team presentations.
CLO3.  Understand  the  communication  process  and  apply  the  principles  of  effective  business
correspondence.
CLO4. Demonstrate the use of advanced writing and communication techniques including the effective and
responsible use of contemporary digital and AI-enabled tools.

sections.text:

Media with its evolutionary and operational details. The course would impart a broad knowledge of the
developments, operations, types and impact of mass media.

covering diverse range of Media such as Cinema, Social Media and Digital media.

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
The course  is planned to give a comprehensive working
knowledge of Advertising and Marketing communication and how they inter-relate.
It offers modules, case studies and do-it your own assignment opportunities. The
main feature of the course is that it is constantly evolving, keeping itself relevant to
the needs of the advertising industry. Today’s student is expected to understand all
the major marketing functions: advertising,  its process, integrated marketing
communication  involving  across  multimedia:  podcast/podcasts,  newspaper,
magazine, television, and via Internet. It aims to enable the students to familiarize
the advertising communication process and how it works in relation to market and
the consumers.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
a.  To introduce advertising with IMC perspectives
b.  To engage the students through various hands-on activities relating to Advertising
Media
c.  To prepare the students to learn advertising concepts and theories in practice
d.  To expose the students to the traditional and digital media for advertising
e.  To familiarize the students about global advertising and promotion scenario along
with rural marketing
f.  To sensitize them about various ethical issues when planning and
implementing advertising and promotional programs
g.  To underscore the implications of AI within advertising realm

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
a.  Grasp the nuances of advertising world and how it works
b.  Build the best business ideas and translate them into campaigns
c.  Differentiate the power of different advertising media and apply accordingly
d.  Design the advertising campaigns keeping in mind the target audience and
respective media
e.  Judge and adhere to the advertising regulations and ethical standards to be
fair in practice

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
Psychology as a science, Perception, its nature, determinants, and
measurement; Biological bases of behaviour; Consciousness, Motivation, and Emotion;
Learning and behaviour modification; Memory and forgetting; Thought processes, Problem-
solving, and Creative thinking; Individual differences—Intelligence, Gender, Personality,
Stress, and Coping; Social thought and Social Behaviour; with an emphasis on psychological
assessment, behavioural data, research analytics, and evidence-based decision-making.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
To develop a conceptual framework for understanding the human
behaviour; relevance of psychology in daily life and its application in social, educational,
industrial, personal and other spheres.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
CLO1. Explain the major concepts, theories, and principles of psychology, including
the biological, cognitive, emotional, developmental, personality, and social
foundations of human behaviour.
CLO2. Apply psychological principles to analyse everyday individual and social
behaviour, decision-making, learning, motivation, stress, and interpersonal
interactions.
CLO3. Compare and critically evaluate major psychological perspectives, theories,
and empirical evidence to explain human thought, emotion, and behaviour.
CLO4. Demonstrate an understanding of psychological research methods, ethical
principles, basic research design, and the interpretation of psychological data.
CLO5. Evaluate individual differences in perception, intelligence, personality,
emotion, and behaviour using evidence-based psychological concepts and
appropriate assessment approaches.
CLO6. Integrate psychological knowledge to promote self-awareness, effective
communication, well-being, problem-solving, and responsible decision-making in
academic, professional, and social contexts.

title: Public Policy

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The objective of the course is to make the students aware
of the art and craft of policy analysis. This course covers theories, processes and techniques of
public policy making, monitoring and evaluation. The course also covers the international agencies
and the globalization of policy agenda.

sections.heading: Text Book
sections.text:
R.K. Sapru, Public Policy: Art and Craft of Policy Analysis, Second Edition, PHI
Learning Private Ltd., New Delhi, 2011.

sections.heading: Reference Material- Books/Papers
sections.text:
Eugene Bardach and Eric M. Patashnik, A Practical
Guide for Policy Analysis: The Eightfold Path to More Effective Problem Solving by. CQ Press,
2019.
Book chapters, Journal papers, and newspaper reports will be given in advance as reading materials
before each session. Students should be prepared to think out of box for maximizing their learning
curve.

sections.heading: Course Format
sections.text:
The course format will be interactive with regular class discussions and several
group exercises and presentations. Students are expected to prepare in advance with the help of
reading material provided and through self-initiative.

sections.heading: Course Outcomes
sections.text:
By the end of this course, students will be able to understand the nature,
scope and significance of Public Policy as a scientific activity; students will be able to analyse
various contemporary public policies being made in India and elsewhere; through exposure to this
course, students will gain the knowledge required for working in the public and private sector on
various policy related issues.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Principles of creative writing, stimulating creative activity, techniques of creating images, constructing
events and creating characters, writing short stories, digital storytelling and multimodal narratives, plays
and poems, adaptation of creative writing across digital and social media, writing critical essays on works
of art, AI and digital writing tools, authorship and ethics

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The objective of the course is to familiarize students with the nature and functioning of creative writing.
Besides basic tenets of creative writing, the course will not only encourage the students to acquire
techniques of constructing events, characters, writing poems, short stories and one act plays but also
develop in them the ability to appreciate writings of all sorts. References to the related and contemporary
works will be made from time to time during discussion and workshop.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Introduction to, Importance and scope of Current Affairs; Domains of Current Affairs-Political, Social, Religious,
Scientific, Developmental,  etc.;Issues  in  Current  Affairs-Controversial,  Non-controversial,  Neutral; Sources  of
Information in Current Affairs-newspapers, Magazines, Posters, Pamphlets, Manifestoes, recently published books,
etc.; Reading: Skimming & Scanning, Extensive vs. Intensive, comprehension;Understanding current issues, events and
information; Interpreting current issues, events and information; Opinion formation-factors and materials influencing
opinion formation;Balancing and expressing opinion.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the course
sections.text:
The objectives of the course are to instill in students the habit of keeping themselves updated on a host of
issues that relate not only to an individual but the society at large and also to inculcate among the students
the skills of reading, understanding, interpreting and forming an opinion on national and international events
and issues of different nature and of various domains.

sections.heading: LearningOutcomes
sections.text:
Having successfully completed all the modules of the course, students will be able to
a.    Read about, listen to, interpret and understand current issues covered in print,
visual and electronic media
b.     Analyze an issue from various perspectives and understand their implications for
an individual, a nation and the society at large
c.     Identify ideological biases in people’s opinion
d.    Form informed opinion on any given issue
e.     Express opinion in an effective manner

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Goals of Public Speaking, differences and similarities between Public Speaking and General Purpose
Speaking, Role of Critical Thinking in Successful Public Speaking, Speaker’s Credibility; Different phases
of Nervousness, dealing with Nervousness; Non- Verbal Communication, Using Body and Voice for
communication, paralinguistic features; Using visual aids; Speech Writing and delivering- Effective
Introductions and Conclusions; Speeches for Special Occasions; Team Presentations; Group Discussion
and Job Interviews

sections.heading: Scope and Objectives of the Course
sections.text:
The course aims to familiarize students with the art of public speaking and help them become confident,
ethical, and effective speakers in academic and professional contexts. Students will learn to manage public
speaking anxiety, construct logical arguments, organize speeches, and deliver presentations using appropriate
content, structure, language, paralinguistic features, kinesics, and visual aids.
The revised course also enables students to use AI-assisted tools in a limited and responsible manner for idea
generation, outline development, rehearsal feedback, and slide improvement, without replacing independent
thinking or original expression. Students will be encouraged to assess AI output critically for accuracy,
audience suitability, bias, and ethical use.

sections.heading: Classroom Methodology
sections.text:
The classroom methodology includes lectures, group and pair work, practical activities, guided rehearsal,
and performance-based tasks. The course remains strongly practice-oriented and develops speaking skills
through JAMs, extempore speaking, storytelling, parliamentary debates, group discussions, interviews, and
presentation tasks.
Video clips and model speeches will be used for illustration. In addition, selected classroom activities may
include AI-supported speech brainstorming, AI-assisted audience adaptation tasks, and guided reflection on
AI-generated feedback, while preserving the same teacher-led, practice-based format intact.

sections.heading: Overall Learning Outcomes of the Course
sections.text:
Knowledge and Understanding
Having successfully completed the module, students should be able to demonstrate knowledge and
understanding of:
✓  Basic components of public speaking.
✓  Reasons for and symptoms of stage fright, and ways to combat it.
✓  Steps involved in preparing outlines and organizing speeches.
✓  Different modes of delivery and the use of connective devices.
✓  Drafting different types of speeches.
✓  Basic principles of responsible AI use in speech preparation, practice, and review
Application of Knowledge and Skills
Having successfully completed the module, students should be able to:
✓  Plan, prepare, and deliver different types of speeches, JAMs, and presentations.
✓  Capture and maintain audience attention.
✓  Participate constructively and meaningfully in group discussions and parliamentary debates.
✓  Perform effectively in job interviews.
✓  Use AI tools selectively to brainstorm topics, refine outlines, rehearse delivery, and improve presentation design
while retaining authorship and accountability
Communication Skills and Analytic Techniques
Having successfully completed the module, students should be able to:
✓  Listen effectively.
✓  Speak confidently.
✓  Demonstrate oratory skills.
✓  Use body language appropriately.

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
Nature and dynamics of conflict; characteristics of conflict; theories of
conflict; reasons and sources of conflict; value of conflict in social change; different
approaches to addressing and managing conflict; conflict analysis through socio-economic
class; class-based dimensions of conflict; culture and globalization perspectives; role of
culture in propagating conflict; role of globalization in nation-state conflict; workplace and
organizational conflict dynamics; conformity theories and conflict; power of
communication; identity-based perspectives on conflict; AI, technology, and conflict
resolution; algorithmic and digital dimensions of conflict; negotiation techniques;
mitigation and resolution techniques; conflict management styles.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
To develop the knowledge and professional skills necessary to facilitate resolution of conflicts.
Emphasis  would  be  laid  on  skills  and  specific  techniques  to  resolve  inter-personal,
organizational and community-based conflicts. At the conclusion of the course, the student will
understand the basic dynamics of conflict, most significant interventions used to manage
conflict,  benefits and  costs of  conflict, recognize  his or her preferred  style of  conflict
management and develop an understanding and appreciation of the conflict management styles
of others.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
•  Focus and familiarity with the theories and theorists in the conflict school of thought.
•  Understanding of the basis of conflict in society from the lens of structures like socio-
economic class.
•  Understanding the debates around conflict from the standpoint of gender.
•  Understanding conflict from the point of view of culture.
•  Evaluating shaping  of  conflict from systems  of  globalization and  ethnocentric
tensions.
•  Understanding conformity theories and their association with conflict.
•  Understanding the power of communication and the development of self.
•  Evaluating the power of communication with respect to conflict resolution.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
This course aims to introduce undergraduate students to key concepts of Marxist theory. After
beginning with a brief survey of the dominant narratives on inequality and exploitation, students will be introduced to
the critique of bourgeois history developed by Marx and Engels, particularly in their writings on dialectical and
historical materialism. In order to get a clearer view of how capitalism produces surplus value, Marx’s Labor Theory
of Value and other related concepts will be read and discussed. At regular intervals, this conceptual framework will be
applied to analyze cultural texts (films, advertisements, popular culture etc.) in order to develop analytical skills that
surpass conventional wisdom in the study of social and economic structures.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
Considering that Marxist theory and practice is a vast field, this course has
limited itself to some of the central concepts and questions that are timely and relevant to students in these modern
times [Refer to the Modules]. The primary objective is to understand the Marxist critique of capitalism, and based on
that understanding, examine if it is possible to forge another kind of society, more egalitarian and without
fundamentally exploitative structures.
​

title: ​   ​          ​          : Critical Analysis of Literature and Cinema

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
Creativity and Aesthetics; Overview of Approaches to Literature, Interpretation of Selected
Works; Cinema; Understanding Drama: Theme, Character, Plot, Form; Understanding
Fiction: Setting, Point of View, Plot and Character; Understanding Short Fiction and Novel:
Meaning and Message, Style and Coherence; Understanding Comics; Understanding Cinema:
Relationship of Form and Meaning, Image Construction, Shots, Scenes, Sequences,
Mise-en-Scene, Codes, Frames, Signs, Syntax; Sound: Diegetic & Non-diegetic Sound,
Silence; Linear and Non-linear Narrative Structure.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
The course attempts to inculcate in students a critical insight required to interpret a work of
literature or cinema. To enable the students to imbibe such perception and critical judgment,
the subtle nuances of such works will be taught extensively. Students will also be introduced
to different forms, terminologies and trends prevalent in such artistic ventures to enable them
to place a work of art in the proper context.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Copywriting is the corner stone of ALL successful marketing. Copywriting empowers you with the ability to
turn words into dollars. Effective copy can play an important role in shaping perceptions about products,
services and brands. The course requires a sound knowledge of advertising communications and will explore
all aspects of writing for print, radio, television and online. It extensively prepares the students to write and
develop ad copy for various media while selecting tone(s), style(s) and approach(es) for ad copy.…It further
equips the students to communicate the strategy and specific assignments to a team using a Creative Brief.

sections.heading: Scope and Objectives
sections.text:
•  To introduce the concept of copywriting in advertising
•  To connect the various advertising concepts and theories to the art of copywriting
•  To generate ideas for successful business copy
•  To prepare the students to learn business content writing
•  To uncover the basics of the traditional and digital media for copywriting
•   to expose the students through various hands on copy activities relating to different media
•  To learn to write ethically and value driven copy for sustainable business

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
Drama as a distinct genre; History of drama; Performance and stagecraft; Evolution of drama
from a theocentric to a logocentric plane; Distinct characteristics of Western and non-Western
dramas; Aristotle’s Poetics and the genre of tragedy; Bharat Muni’s Natyashastra and the
idea of comedy; Adaptation of myths as Drama; Modern drama.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
The objective of the course is to introduce students to different types and forms of drama. In
doing so, this course will familiarize students with various dramatic forms spanning different
geographical spaces and time, thereby helping them to have a deeper understanding of the
same. It will also enable the students to connect various dramatic forms through the study of
visuals, timelines, and biographical and contextual readings that allow them to delve further
into the history and conventions of the time period when these dramatic works were
produced.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
1) Understand and analyze various dramatic forms keeping in mind recent trends and
theoretical underpinnings.
2) Apply acquired knowledge in critically appreciating dramatic texts and performances.
3) Exhibit methodological proficiency to formulate research problems and write research
papers.

title: LINGUISTICS

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Linguistics as a field of study and its relationship with other disciplines; nature of language; its varieties and role in
society; concepts of structure, system, unit and class; theories of linguistic analysis.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the course
sections.text:
The objective of the course is to acquaint students with the nature and functioning of language and the role it plays in
the society. The fundamental linguistic concepts will be exemplified through English. Reference to Indian languages
will also be made whenever possible.

sections.heading: Learning Outcomes
sections.text:
Having successfully completed all the modules of the course, students will be able to understand
✓ the properties and important characteristics of a human language
✓ the structure of a language
✓ how meaning is derived
✓the use of language in various contexts
✓ the role of human brain in language production and perception
✓ the differences in language acquisition and language learning
✓ how a language changes over a period of time
✓ the relationship between language, society and culture
✓ the types and use of sign languages

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
An overview of major philosophical traditions from the Western and Indian worlds. The course traces the
nature and purpose of philosophy from classical Greek thought through modern rationalism, empiricism,
and existentialism before turning to the classical Indian schools.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
A critical survey of major Western and Indian philosophical viewpoints, from antiquity to contemporary
thought. The course aims to equip students with the tools to critically evaluate philosophical arguments
and to appreciate their relevance to questions of knowledge, ethics, and selfhood in human life.

sections.heading: Course Learning Objectives
sections.text:
Upon completion of the course students will have
•  An understanding of the various philosophical schools of Indian and Western traditions.
•  A critical and comparative grasp of the philosophical viewpoints & debates.
•  An ability to build theoretical constructions and extend philosophical thinking to other disciplines.
•  An ability to practice the habit of thinking rationally and critically in leading an ethical and meaningful
life

title: Popular Literature and Culture of South Asia

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
South Asia as a region; culture and its representation through
literature and cinema; politics of representation, breaking the stereotypes; bringing in
the marginalized voices; writings of women; identity formation; concept of majority
and minority; commonality in spite of all the differences, violence, migration and
dislocation.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
The objective of the course is to introduce students to Literature
and Popular Culture of South Asia. In doing so, it will familiarize students to
perspectives and scenarios that differ from their own culture, thereby, helping them to
have deeper understanding of other cultures. This course aims to bridge the gaps in our
understanding of our neighbors and enable us to have broader perspectives.

sections.heading: Course Learning Outcomes
sections.text:
After completing the course, the students would be able
to:
•  Have basic concepts of South Asia as a region
•   Understand, analyze different productions from the region and ponder on the implications of
such representations
•  Apply acquired knowledge in real life scenarios by acknowledging common history, heritage
and culture, as well as, the diversity of the region

title: Organizational Psychology

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
This course is floated to provide a brief understanding of how humans behave the way they
do in an organization. This will be a highly informative course for people who want to understand the psychology of
organizations and gain an in-depth understanding of the management functions of an organization at an individual level.
The course would be highly relevant and suitable for students who wish to pursue a master’s in business schools because
it will give them a sound theoretical understanding.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
To develop a conceptual framework for understanding organizations and
their various functions from a psychological viewpoint. The course would help students understand the behavior of
humans at different levels of hierarchy in an organization and the relevant issues and processes imbuing them.

sections.heading: Course Learning Outcomes (CLOs)
sections.text:
a) Students will know about what happens after they join the world of work.
b) Students get to know what all operates and how to tackle various issues at workplace.
c) Students will get first hand practical information related to adjusting in their respective workplaces.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Key concepts and histories of science fiction; major theoretical frameworks in SF; utopias,
dystopias, and speculative futures; science fiction in relation to technological and ecological change; feminist,
postcolonial, and global interventions in SF; engagements with artificial intelligence, posthumanism, and the animal;
and the reimagining of cultural and ecological futures through speculative storytelling.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
i) Introduce students to science fiction as a literary mode that critiques technological and social change.
ii) Explore how science fiction engages with questions of environment and the posthuman through
narrative.
iii) Examine connections between science, technology, and ethics through speculative imagination.
iv) Develop interdisciplinary skills by linking literary analysis with perspectives from history of
science and cultural studies.

title: Human Resource Development

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
This course is floated to provide a brief understanding of the practical ramification (or better
subfield) of human resource management and deals with the significant issues related to developing human resources
with special reference to  its tripartite foundations of human betterment, organizational enhancement, and societal
development. The course will help clarify the subtle difference between HR Management & HR Development. This will
also enable curious minds to learn more about how training programs are planned, conceived, constructed, and delivered
to potential stakeholders. HRD focuses on this core idea as to how the capabilities and credentials (and ultimately
productivity) of the employees can be enhanced.

sections.heading: Course Learning Outcomes (CLOs)
sections.text:
a) To develop a conceptual framework for understanding human behavior in organizations and develop human capital
(manpower) in various sectors and spheres of the world of work.
b) The course would be very beneficial for students trying to understand the management functions of one very
significant department of any organization.
c) To get a superficial idea about various training/skill development exercises and processes encompassing such
activities.

Preliminary Lecture, Logic and Science working behind music, Interval of Frequencies and interval of time,
Scales- Hindustani, Carnatic and Western, Musical Streams, Notation Systemes, Principles of Thaat, Raga

sections.text:
The course aims to acquaint the students with the how and why of Music. It introduces the concepts of
Musicology, Applied Theory, Rasa-Bhava and the working of Raga, Acoustics, some aspects of
the textual and contextual development of music, the semantics of music, influence of music over mind
and body, composers and compositions.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
This course introduces students the timeless wisdom spoken by Lord Krishna in the Bhagavad Gita
and enables them to appreciate and apply those in daily life. Beginning with the fundamentals of the
need to understand spirituality, the content includes science of soul, various types of yogic practices,
viz., karma-yoga (action in God consciousness), jnana-yoga (philosophical research for truth),
dhyana-yoga (meditative practice), astanga-yoga (eightfold yoga system) and culminates with bhakti-
yoga (devotional service to God). Adopting a topical approach, the course also touches upon these
subject matters: the most confidential knowledge, three modes of material nature, nature, enjoyer and
the consciousness, divine and demoniac qualities, and the perfection of knowledge.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
Meant for anyone who wants to make his or her life peaceful, blissful and perfect by aligning oneself
to the principles set forth in Srimad Bhagavad Gita. The prime objectives of this course are to
understand our relationship (sambhandha) with God, the process of reviving that relationship
(abhidheya), and the goal of that process (prayojana). In this context, the 5 important subject matter
isvara, jiva, prakriti, kala and karma are discussed in detail.

sections.heading: Course Learning Objectives
sections.text:
Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to:
1.  Explain the principal philosophical concepts of the Srimad Bhagavad Gita, including isvara,
jiva, prakriti, kala, and karma, and the relationship among them.
2.  Differentiate and analyse the major paths of yoga—karma-yoga, jnana-yoga, dhyana-yoga,
and bhakti-yoga—along with their purpose and practical significance.
3. Apply the teachings of the Bhagavad Gita to improve time management, stress management,
concentration, emotional balance, self-discipline, decision-making, and overall well-being in
academic and personal life.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
An introduction to the ethical concepts, theories, and codes that govern professional life. The course traces the
foundations of ethics and the profession, before applying this framework across business, management,
education, engineering, and computing.

sections.heading: Scope & Objective
sections.text:
This course provides a formal acquaintance with the concepts and frameworks of ethics; recognize the codes of
ethics relevant to the experience of being a professional and develops an understanding of the ethical issues
relating to professions generally, and to business, management, education, engineering, and computing in
particular. Through the analysis of real-time case studies, students learn to appreciate the role of moral reasoning
in issues of professional life.

sections.heading: Course Learning Objectives
sections.text:
Upon completion of the course students will have
●  An understanding of the core concepts of ethics, the profession, and professional ethics, and their
specific application across business, management, education, engineering, and computing.
●  A critical and comparative grasp of competing ethical theories and professional viewpoints such as rule-
following versus professional judgment.
●  An ability to apply ethical theories and frameworks to real, contested professional dilemmas, extending
this reasoning across multiple professional domains rather than any single one.
●  An ability to practice the habit of sound ethical judgment and professional responsibility in one's own
future career and conduct.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
  Introduction-A survey of the international politics since the 20th century; Rise of Nationalism;
World Wars, Emergence of IR as a discipline and the nature of its subject matter.
  Key Defining Events in IR: Creation of United Nations, Cold War, Fall of USSR, September 11,
China’s entry into WTO.
  Key theoretical frameworks: Classical IR thinkers and their location within the existing IR canon
that include realism, liberalism, constructivism, critical theory, and Asian theory of IR.
  Key Agents of IR: State, Empire, International and sub-national agents, foreignpolicy.
  Key Structures in IR: State-system, Eurocentrism, Post-colonialism, Globalization, Security and
Global Governance
  Key Institutions in IR: International Society, International Diplomacy, Great Powers, Balance of
Power, War, International Law and Human Rights Regime and the Climate Change Regime.
  Assorted Themes: Global Health Regime- Pandemic and IR
 India’s Foreign Policy: Locating India’s space in the contemporary global order: identifying the
opportunities and Challenges (India-Pakistan-China), India and China in South Asia; India and
United States.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
International Relations is the study of an international system that is constituted by territorial states
who enjoy sovereignty over matters of vital interests to them. This course offers the history of the
international system, its functioning, theoretical frameworks, and the nature of the changing relations
between the  states and non-state actors. This course offers a  critical reflection and analytical
understanding of key defining events and the topical issues that not only shaped but also confronted
the existing international order. The course encourages students to engage in debates on the nature of
international order as well as the responses to the challenges of the current international order. The
course is designed to offer both the theoretical frameworks and critical reflections on the contemporary
affairs. Moreover, the students will be able to make a clear perception of the relationship between the
international relations as a discipline and the practice of world politics. Considerable sessions are
devoted to understanding India’s role in the contemporary world too.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Ecocriticism has found its place in the Indian academy only in the last twenty years
or so. The course is intended to familiarize the learners with ecological, deep ecological and tinai critical
principles and show them how these could be effective critical tools. The course gives a humanistic perspective
on how ecology is a new paradigm in cultural and literary texts. The learners will be exposed to recent
ecocritical concepts which will challenge conventional attitudes and values which are detrimental to the well-
being of our planet.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
1. To introduce the learners to one of the major postmodern critical trends.
2. To familiarize the learners with some key ecocritical concepts.
3. To equip the students to create ecocritical documents in literary, cinematic and other artistic forms.
4. To train the learners in the application of the critical concepts to various cultural texts.

sections.heading: Text Books
sections.text:

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Transformer: Constructional features, equivalent circuit and phasor diagram - regulation and efficiency, parallel
operation. Three phase  transformer  connections; Harmonic  in  transformers;  Testing; Phase  conversion;
Autotransformer. D.C Machines: Construction, armature windings, armature voltage and torque equations,
classification. D.C generators, performance characteristics; D.C motors  - torque/speed characteristics, speed
control and braking. Testing and efficiency. Induction machines: Constructional features and rotating magnetic
field. Circuit model and phasor diagram. Steady state characteristics. Testing, starting and speed control. Time
harmonics and space harmonics. Wound rotor induction motors, Single phase induction motors - classification and
equivalent  circuit. Synchronous  machines:  Constructional  features; synchronous  generators and  motors;
equivalent circuit and phasor diagram; power and torque characteristics and capability curves. Parallel operation.
Salient pole synchronous machine - phasor diagram and determination of synchronous reactances; starting and
speed control of synchronous motors. Special machines- universal motors, Induction generators.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
Electrical Machines are the work horse in almost all industries ranging from few watts’ power to several mega watt
power applications. The scope of this course  is to study of working principle & operating characteristics of
Electrical Machines for the mode of Generation, and Utilization of Electrical Power. The specific objective of this
course is to gain better understanding of various conventional electrical-magnetic devices such as Transformer,
DC Machines and AC Machines. The course covers theory as well as detailed experimental component for better
understanding of the concepts.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
The students  will learn about the operating principles, constructional features,
equivalent  circuit diagram,  efficiency, testing & control and  different type of performance characteristics of
transformers, DC machines, induction and synchronous machines. The further details are given in the course plan.

sections.heading: Course Description (as per the Bulletin)
sections.text:
Crystal  structure and growth of semiconductor,  electrical conduction  in  solids, Elementary quantum physics
(Photoelectric effect, uncertainty principle, Schrodinger wave equation and tunneling), energy bands in solids, charge
carriers in semiconductors, excess carriers in semiconductors, Fabrication of p-n junctions, equilibrium conditions,
forward and reverse biased junctions, metal-semiconductor junctions Bipolar junction transistors, field effect transistors
(JFET, HEMT, MOSFET), Special diodes (varactor diode, solar cell, LEDs, Tunnel diode and HBT).

sections.heading: Scope and Objectives
sections.text:
The course provides a comprehensive understanding of the characteristics, operation and limitations of semiconductor
devices. This  course  starts with  explanation on  crystal  structure, semiconductor  materials, fundamentals  of
semiconductors. This course helps in developing the understanding about excess carriers in semiconductors and its
application. In-depth study on ‘junctions’ prepares the students for even a detailed study on devices to be studied later
like FET, BJT, MOSFET viz. commonly employed in Integrated Circuit (IC) technology. Concepts of optoelectronic
diodes will also be discussed in this course.

sections.heading: Course Learning outcomes
sections.text:
At the end of this course, students will be able to:
  CLO1: Explain the fundamentals of semiconductor materials, crystal structures, electrical conduction,
quantum physics concepts, and energy band theory governing electronic devices.
  CLO2: Analyze charge carrier transport, excess carrier behavior, and the electrical characteristics of
semiconductor materials under equilibrium and non-equilibrium conditions.
  CLO3: Evaluate the operation and characteristics of semiconductor junctions, including p-n junctions,
metal-semiconductor junctions, and their behavior under forward and reverse bias conditions.
  CLO4: Explain the operating principles, characteristics, and applications of major semiconductor
devices, including BJTs, JFETs, HEMTs, MOSFETs, and special semiconductor diodes.
  CLO5: Apply the fundamental principles of semiconductor device physics to analyze the performance
and limitations of electronic and optoelectronic devices used in modern integrated circuits and
electronic systems.
