sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
An introduction to measurement techniques and instrumentation design and operation, the basic concept of units,
measurement error and accuracy, Instrument design aspects, techniques and specifications of electronic instruments, the
construction and design of measuring devices and measuring instruments such as Analog/ Digital meters, DSO, signal
generators, signal analyzers, data loggers and recorders, electronic counters with their proper applications, Industrial
Communication techniques, safety methods and instrumentation in hazardous areas. The course will also consist of
laboratory practice and lab assignments.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
 An introduction to measurement techniques and instrumentation design and operation
 The basic concept of units, measurement error and accuracy, the construction and design of measuring devices
and circuits, measuring instruments and their proper applications
 To learn about instrument design aspects, techniques and specifications of various electronic instruments
 To know various aspects of Industrial Communication techniques

sections.heading: Learning outcomes
sections.text:
  Analyze the functionalities and operations of electronic measuring devices and instruments
  Know basic building blocks of electronic measuring instruments
   Excel in operating electronic measuring instruments, such as, DSO, Multimeter, Function generator, LCR
meter and all other instruments.
  Know how to use electronic measuring instruments efficiently.
  Have knowledge about various industrial safety standards and bring insight into various industrial
communication techniques.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
INSTR F312 Transducers and Measurement Systems
Importance and types of measurement, generalized measurement system, functional elements,
static and dynamic  characteristics, primary sensing elements, modulating transducers,  self
generating transducers, inverse transducers, fiber optic transducers, measurement techniques for
motion, seismic, pressure, flow, temperature, level, humidity, pH, viscosity; charge, isolation
amplifier, MEMS based transducers;

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the course
sections.text:
The objective of this course is to have a detailed study of
measurement systems and to understand their application in the areas of monitoring, control and
experimental engineering analysis.

sections.heading: Learning Outcomes
sections.text:
   Analyze the functionalities and operations of sensors and measuring instruments techniques.
   Define static and dynamic performance metrics of sensor and instrumentation systems.
   Understand Working Principles of different sensing elements, such as Resistive sensing, Capacitive
sensing, Inductive sensing, Electromagnetic sensing, Thermoelectric sensing, Hall effect and many other
elements.
  Know how to select measurement devices for physical quantities like temperature, pressure, motion, and
flow etc.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
This course introduces students to the principles and practical aspects of designing integrated circuits using
CMOS technology. It covers both analog and digital VLSI design methodologies, exploring circuit-level
building blocks, layout considerations, and performance trade-offs. Emphasis is placed on low-power, area-
efficient, and high-performance  circuit techniques, along with exposure to modern CAD tools and
fabrication-aware design strategies. Students will gain experience designing critical components, including
logic gates, adders, amplifiers, and mixed-signal interfaces.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
⮚ The course is designed to familiarize students with different design principles used in the Design
of Digital & Analog VLSI Circuits & Systems using CMOS logic.
⮚  Understanding of CMOS technology fundamentals and their impact on design.
⮚  Design and analysis of digital logic circuits: static, dynamic, sequential.
⮚  Design and analysis of analog CMOS circuits: Op-Amplifiers, Advance current mirrors, Reference
Circuit.
⮚  Exploration of Technology scaling trends, noise, and power-performance trade-offs.
⮚  Exposure to EDA tools for schematic capture, simulation, and layout.
⮚  Bridging theory with practical insights via Lab/Design assignments.
⮚ VLSI design activity will be understood by Synthesis and then Analysis at several successive levels
of design abstraction.
1
BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND SCIENCE, Pilani
Pilani Campus
AUGSD/ AGSRD Division

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Object orientation concepts, theories and principles; fundamental concepts of the object model: classes, objects,
methods and messages, encapsulation and inheritance, interface and implementation, reuse and extension of
classes, inheritance and polymorphism; overloading and overriding; static and dynamic binding; multithreaded
programming; event handling and exception handling; process of object oriented requirements specification,
analysis and design; notations for object-oriented analysis and design; case studies and applications using some
object  oriented programming  languages.  Object  Oriented  Design  Patterns:  Behavioural,  Structural and
Creational.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
a)  Gives an in-depth understanding of object-oriented programming using the java programming language, object-
oriented analysis and design, and design patterns.
b)  In the classroom, the course will be taught with live demonstrations, running and debugging several examples on
tools like Eclipse.
c)  The latter part of the course focuses on designing object-oriented software.

sections.heading: Course Learning Outcomes (CLOs)
sections.text:
On successful completion of this course, students will be able to:
CLO1. Explain the principles of object-oriented programming and apply core concepts such as abstraction,
encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism in software development.
CLO2. Design, implement, test, and debug medium-sized Java programs using classes, objects, interfaces,
collections, generics, exception handling, file I/O, and multithreading.
CLO3. Analyse object-oriented software requirements and represent software designs using appropriate
UML diagrams and object-oriented design principles.
CLO4. Apply commonly used object-oriented design patterns to develop software that is modular, reusable,
extensible, and maintainable.
CLO5. Evaluate alternative object-oriented design and implementation choices based on software quality
attributes such as maintainability, flexibility, and reusability.
1

sections.heading: Course Description
Scope & Objective of the Course
sections.text:
Mathematics, described as a language of science, has acquired its unique position due to its precision and
rigour. This makes essential the development of the sense for mathematical rigor as well as the habit of math-
ematical thought process. The course will achieve this by introducing students to propositional and predicate
logic. As an important follow-up, various methods of proof will be discussed. Several mathematical struc-
tures like relations and orderings are studied due to their importance, not only in mathematics but also applied
subjects like computer science. The course is also useful for the preparation for the study of computational
concepts, techniques, and skills necessary to comprehend the structure of problems encountered in the design
and analysis of algorithms.

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
Groups, subgroups, a counting principle, normal subgroups, and quotient
groups, Cayley’s theorem, automorphisms, permutation groups, Sylow’s theorems, Rings, ring of
real quaternions, ideals and quotient rings, homomorphisms, Euclidean rings, polynomial rings, and
polynomials over the rational field.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The objective of this course is to provide an introduction to abstract algebraic structures, including
groups and rings. The abstract setting allows for the study of disparate mathematical objects together.
We can derive properties and structures that apply to concrete examples. We will see examples from
number theory, linear algebra and geometry.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
CLO1. Understand and apply the fundamental concepts of groups to solve algebraic problems
CLO2. Analyze the structure of rings, integral domains and fields using algebraic theorems

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Mathematical Modeling in Biology, Epidemiology, Model for Various Problems and
Situation Using ODE and PDE, Classic Models in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, Equilibria and Stability
Analysis, Dynamics of Class-Structured Populations, Techniques for Analyzing Models.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The principal objective of this course is to familiarize students with
the theory of population and a basic understanding of mathematical modelling of a real-world problem.
Students will gain enough background to read theoretical population and evolutionary ecology literature, do
simple modelling, and springboard to more complex theory if desired. Students will develop techniques for
understanding and analysing simple, multivariate, and nonlinear models will be explored.

sections.heading: Course Learning Outcomes
sections.text:
CLO1. Develop mathematical models of physical and biological systems using ODE.
CLO2. Understanding the concept of qualitative analysis of the model equations. Particularly,
equilibria analysis, linear stability analysis and bifurcation theory.
CLO3. Analyze ecological and epidemiological models to interpret their dynamical behaviour and
derive meaningful biological insights.
CLO4. Implement and simulate mathematical models using MATLAB and interpret the
computational results..

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
This course provides a foundational introduction to multivariable calculus and vector analysis, which
are essential tools in engineering and the physical sciences. Students learn to analyze functions and
geometric objects in two and three dimensional spaces, studying local behavior through differentiation
and global properties through integration. Compared to single variable calculus, multivariable calculus
introduces new ideas and describes behaviour in multiple directions and dimensions. These concepts
play a central role in areas such as probability and statistics, fluid mechanics, electrical sciences and
numerous other applications.
The course develops mathematical techniques required to model real-world phenomena such as
motion, flow, and fields. Key topics include polar coordinates, convergence of sequences and series,
power  series, Taylor and Maclaurin series,  partial derivatives, and vector calculus, leading to
fundamental integral theorems such as those of Green, Stokes, and Gauss.

sections.heading: Scope and objectives of the course
sections.text:
  To develop a solid conceptual understanding of functions of several variables.
  Introduce partial derivatives and their applications in modelling and optimization.
  To study multiple integrals and their use in computing areas, volume and mass.
  Build geometric intuition via visualization of surfaces and vector fields.
  To strengthen problem solving skills required for advanced engineering courses.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:
 CLO1. Determine if an infinite series is convergent or divergent by selecting the appropriate tests.
 CLO2. Apply techniques for plotting and analyzing curves in polar coordinates, including converting
between polar and Cartesian forms, sketching polar graphs.
 CLO3. Interpret parametric curves as trajectories described by position vectors, and compute associated
velocity and acceleration vectors to analyze motion.
Please Do Not Print Unless Necessary
BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND
SCIENCE, Pilani
Pilani Campus
AUGS/ AGSR Division
 CLO4. Develop a deep understanding of the gradient vector, including its geometric meaning, its
relationship to level curves and level surfaces, its role in directional derivatives, and its use in linear
approximation and sensitivity analysis.
 CLO5. Compute partial derivatives using the chain rule and total differentials, and apply these tools to
model changes in multivariable systems.
 CLO6. Formulate and solve optimization problems involving multiple variables, both unconstrained
and constrained, using techniques such as Lagrange multipliers.
 CLO7. Compute multiple integrals using appropriate coordinate systems, including rectangular, polar,
cylindrical, and spherical coordinates.
 CLO8. Perform change of variables in multiple integrals and understand the role of the Jacobian
determinant.
 CLO9. Set up and evaluate line integrals (for work and circulation), surface integrals (for flux), and
volume integrals, and interpret their physical significance in applied problems.

sections.heading: Method of conducting the course
sections.text:
The instructional approach for this course integrates theory, practice, and computational exposure. Core
concepts and mathematical derivations will be introduced through classroom lectures, while tutorial
sessions will be devoted to reinforcing these ideas through guided problem-solving and application-based
exercises. To supplement in-class learning, three video lectures will be made available, showcasing the
use of computational software (MATLAB) for visualization and problem-solving. Student learning will
be evaluated on a continuous basis through quizzes, assignments, and examinations, ensuring both
conceptual understanding and practical competence.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
This course presents the study of differential equations with the objective of introducing the
classical methods for solving boundary value problems. It also serves as a basis for the applications
of differential equations, Fourier series and Laplace transform in the various branches of
engineering and sciences. Furthermore, it emphasizes on the role of orthogonal polynomials in
dealing with Sturm-Liouville problems.

sections.heading: Scope and Objectives
sections.text:
•  To understand the theory of first and second order ordinary differential equations and to
learn methods to solve them.
•  To understand the series solution of second order ordinary differential equations and their
interval of convergence.
•  To understand the Laplace transform, its properties, and applications for solving IVPs
and BVPs.
•  To understand the Fourier series expansion of a function.
•  To understand the concept of eigenvalues and eigenfunctions and to use them in solving
heat and wave equations.

sections.heading: COURSE LEARNING OUTCOMES
sections.text:
After completing this course, the student will be able to
1)  solve differential equations appearing in modeling of various processes in their respective
engineering or science stream.
2)  understand whether a given initial value problem is solvable or not.
3)  understand the region in which the solution is valid (like in series solution approach).
4)  solve the problems involving linear system of first order differential equations.
5)  understand the eigenfunction expansion/Bessel series expansion of a function using
respective orthogonality properties which can be further helpful in solving various
problems in their engineering and science streams.

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
Introduction to optimization; linear programming; simplex methods; duality
and  sensitivity analysis; transportation model and  its variants; integer linear programming
nonlinear programming; multi-objective optimization; evolutionary computation techniques.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
Engineers, scientists, analysts, and managers often face the challenge of
making trade-offs between different factors to achieve desirable outcomes. Optimization is the
process of making these trade-offs in the best possible way. Over the years, optimization problems
have become well-established and are encountered  in the physical sciences, engineering,
economics, industry, planning, and many other areas of human activity. The objective of this course
is to familiarize students with standard methods of solving optimization problems.
This course covers various aspects of optimization, including a description of techniques such as
Linear Programming and Nonlinear Programming, and their applications in various engineering and
science disciplines, including economics and finance. Multi-objective optimization, which addresses
optimization with more than one objective, is also discussed. Additionally, the course provides a
brief and informative overview of the non- traditional optimization technique, Genetic Algorithms.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
CLO1: Understanding of the formulation and solution of LPP
CLO2: Understanding of the duality theory and post optimal analysis with their applications in
transportation, assignment and integer LPPs
CLO3:  Understanding  of  multi-objective  LPP,  Nonlinear programming and  non-traditional
optimization techniques

sections.heading: Course Description
Scope & Objective of the Course
sections.text:
Mathematics, described as a language of science, has acquired its unique position due to its precision and
rigour. This makes essential the development of the sense for mathematical rigor as well as the habit of math-
ematical thought process. The course will achieve this by introducing students to propositional and predicate
logic. As an important follow-up, various methods of proof will be discussed. Several mathematical struc-
tures like relations and orderings are studied due to their importance, not only in mathematics but also applied
subjects like computer science. The course is also useful for the preparation for the study of computational
concepts, techniques, and skills necessary to comprehend the structure of problems encountered in the design
and analysis of algorithms.

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
Groups, subgroups, a counting principle, normal subgroups, and quotient
groups, Cayley’s theorem, automorphisms, permutation groups, Sylow’s theorems, Rings, ring of
real quaternions, ideals and quotient rings, homomorphisms, Euclidean rings, polynomial rings, and
polynomials over the rational field.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The objective of this course is to provide an introduction to abstract algebraic structures, including
groups and rings. The abstract setting allows for the study of disparate mathematical objects together.
We can derive properties and structures that apply to concrete examples. We will see examples from
number theory, linear algebra and geometry.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
CLO1. Understand and apply the fundamental concepts of groups to solve algebraic problems
CLO2. Analyze the structure of rings, integral domains and fields using algebraic theorems
CLO3. Construct rigorous mathematical proofs to solve computational and theoretical problems

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Topology and topological spaces, Metric spaces, Product and Quotient
topology,  Continuity  and  Homeomorphism,  Connectedness,  Compactness,  Normal  spaces,
Classification of compact surfaces.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
To introduce the students to the concepts of logical thinking
in abstract terms using formal and axiomatic methods and to lay the foundations for further studies in
abstract Mathematics.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:
CLO1. Define and analyze basic topological concepts, including topologies, bases, subspace topologies,
product topologies, and quotient topologies, to construct and classify fundamental topological spaces.
CLO2. Evaluate continuity and homeomorphisms to determine topologic equivalence between abstract spaces and
investigate topological invariants.
CLO3. Demonstrate a rigorous understanding of topological properties such as connectedness, compactness,
countability, and separation axioms (including Hausdorff and Normal spaces).
CLO4. Apply and construct formal mathematical proofs utilizing key structural theorems, including Urysohn's
Lemma, Urysohn Metrization Theorem, and Tietze Extension Theorem.

sections.heading: COURSE DESCRIPTION
SCOPE & OBJECTIVE
sections.text:
Ordinary Differential Equations frequently occurs as mathematical models in many branches of science,
engineering and economy. For a mathematician confronted with such a model there are a number of issues
to address and various approaches to choose from:
Is the problem well-posed? Do you expect the differential equation to have a solution? If so, is there a
unique solution satisfying the given initial or boundary conditions?
Can you find an explicit, analytical solution? This is only possible in rare circumstances.
Geometric or qualitative methods: These methods give insights into general, qualitative features of
solutions and do not require solving the differential equation.
Stability and dependence on parameters: Having obtained a solution by any method, we would like to
know how the solution changes if we change the initial data by a small amount (stability analysis) and if we
change  parameters  in  the  differential  equation  (parameter  dependence).  Course  helps  deeper
understanding of the complicated models that are there in the real life.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
CLO1. Existence and uniqueness of ODEs of nth order
CLO2. Linear and nonlinear behavior of system of ODEs
CLO3. Applications of ODEs in real-world problems

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Solution of non-linear algebraic equations; interpolation and approximation; numerical
differentiation and quadrature; solution of ordinary differential equations; systems of linear
equations; matrix inversion; eigenvalue and eigenvector problems; round off and conditioning.

sections.heading: Scope and objectives of the course
sections.text:
Enables one to devise algorithms for the numerical solutions of mathematical problems. Also discusses
the error analysis of different algorithms.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:
• CLO1. Explain the fundamental concepts of numerical analysis, including sources of computational
errors, floating-point arithmetic, error propagation, and conditioning.
• CLO2. Apply appropriate numerical methods to determine the roots of nonlinear equations and evaluate
the convergence, accuracy, and efficiency of different iterative algorithms.
• CLO3. Solve systems of linear and nonlinear equations using direct and iterative numerical techniques
and analyze the stability and conditioning of computational methods.
• CLO4. Construct interpolation polynomials using standard interpolation techniques and estimate
interpolation errors for function approximation.
• CLO5. Compute numerical derivatives and definite integrals using finite difference and quadrature
methods and assess the associated approximation errors.
• CLO6. Obtain numerical solutions of ordinary  differential equations arising from  initial value
problems using single-step and multistep numerical methods.
• CLO7. Solve boundary value problems using finite difference methods and interpret the numerical
solutions obtained.
• CLO8. Determine dominant eigenvalues and eigenvectors of matrices using numerical algorithms such
as the power and inverse power methods.
• CLO9. Apply weighted residual techniques, including the Rayleigh–Ritz, Collocation, and Galerkin
methods, to obtain approximate solutions of boundary value problems and compare their applicability
and effectiveness.

sections.heading: Method of conducting the course
sections.text:
The instructional approach for this course combines theoretical concepts, analytical problem-solving,
and computational practice. Classroom lectures will introduce the fundamental principles, mathematical
formulations, and derivations of numerical methods. Tutorial sessions will reinforce these concepts
through guided problem-solving, analytical exercises, and discussion of practical applications. Selected
numerical methods  will be implemented  using MATLAB  to  provide  hands-on  computational
experience,  facilitate  visualization, and enhance problem-solving  skills. Student learning will be
assessed  continuously  through  quizzes,  assignments,  laboratory/computational  exercises,  and
examinations to ensure the development of both conceptual understanding and practical proficiency.

sections.heading: Course Desccription
sections.text:
This course on Time Series Analysis and Forecasting covers introductory concepts of trend, seasonality,
and cyclicity in time series data.  It reviews extrapolative and decomposition models and smoothing
techniques. Discussions include autoregressive error structure – auto-covariance and auto-correlation, ACF,
and PACF. Linear stationary model analysis, such as AR, MA, ARMA is included along with error
diagnostics. It includes Box-Jenkins time series analysis and linear non-stationary models, such as ARIMA,
SARIMA, and ARFIMA. Finally, we study some models with stochastic variance – ARCH and GARCH.
The course includes discussions on multivariate time  series models and associated techniques.  It
necessarily involves the use of statistical software and programming languages for hands-on practice.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
This 4th level course introduces time series analysis and associated forecasting techniques, in which students
will be equipped with various forecasting techniques and knowledge on modern statistical methods for
analyzing time series data. The course reviews extrapolative and decomposition models, introduction to
Box–Jenkins time series analysis, and ARIMA models. The remainder of the course considers various
practical aspects of the principles behind modern forecasting techniques. Students will study and develop
the ability to select appropriate model to carry out forecasting. A one-hour lab will be conducted every
week. Students will learn how to explore and analyze different types of time series data using R
programming.

title: Applied Statistical Methods

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Applied Statistics is an exciting sub-area of Statistics. It has application in almost all science disciplines
which deal with data and uncertainty. This course builds up fundamental concepts of various key statis-
tical methods necessary to analyze/interpret a variety of practical business/engineering problems. This
course emphasizes the role of statistics in one’s own field of study by making sense of data, developing
self-ability to apply appropriate statistical methods, performing experimental designs and above all, re-
alizing the limitations/inherent assumptions in a statistical test to avoid over interpretation or misinter-
pretation. The thrust areas covered in this course include probability distributions, statistical inference,
analysis of variance (ANOVA), regression and correlation, discriminant analysis, factor and cluster
analysis, time series analysis and forecasting, nonparametric methods and statistical quality control. The
theoretical learning will be complemented with various case studies and hands-on training in excel/R.

sections.heading: Scope and objective of the course
sections.text:
This 4th level course is designed with a two-fold purpose. First, it will provide an exposure to various
theoretical univariate/multivariate methods and their practical applications. Second, this course will
improve methodological/analytical maturity to attempt a variety of problems using MS-excel and R.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
This course provides a foundational introduction to multivariable calculus and vector analysis, which
are essential tools in engineering and the physical sciences. Students learn to analyze functions and
geometric objects in two and three dimensional spaces, studying local behavior through differentiation
and global properties through integration. Compared to single variable calculus, multivariable calculus
introduces new ideas and describes behaviour in multiple directions and dimensions. These concepts
play a central role in areas such as probability and statistics, fluid mechanics, electrical sciences and
numerous other applications.
The course develops mathematical techniques required to model real-world phenomena such as
motion, flow, and fields. Key topics include polar coordinates, convergence of sequences and series,
power  series, Taylor and Maclaurin series,  partial derivatives, and vector calculus, leading to
fundamental integral theorems such as those of Green, Stokes, and Gauss.

sections.heading: Scope and objectives of the course
sections.text:
  To develop a solid conceptual understanding of functions of several variables.
  Introduce partial derivatives and their applications in modelling and optimization.
  To study multiple integrals and their use in computing areas, volume and mass.
  Build geometric intuition via visualization of surfaces and vector fields.
  To strengthen problem solving skills required for advanced engineering courses.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:
 CLO1. Determine if an infinite series is convergent or divergent by selecting the appropriate tests.
 CLO2. Apply techniques for plotting and analyzing curves in polar coordinates, including converting
between polar and Cartesian forms, sketching polar graphs.
Please Do Not Print Unless Necessary
BIRLA INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY AND
SCIENCE, Pilani
Pilani Campus
AUGS/ AGSR Division
 CLO3. Interpret parametric curves as trajectories described by position vectors, and compute associated
velocity and acceleration vectors to analyze motion.
 CLO4. Develop a deep understanding of the gradient vector, including its geometric meaning, its
relationship to level curves and level surfaces, its role in directional derivatives, and its use in linear
approximation and sensitivity analysis.
 CLO5. Compute partial derivatives using the chain rule and total differentials, and apply these tools to
model changes in multivariable systems.
 CLO6. Formulate and solve optimization problems involving multiple variables, both unconstrained
and constrained, using techniques such as Lagrange multipliers.
 CLO7. Compute multiple integrals using appropriate coordinate systems, including rectangular, polar,
cylindrical, and spherical coordinates.
 CLO8. Perform change of variables in multiple integrals and understand the role of the Jacobian
determinant.
 CLO9. Set up and evaluate line integrals (for work and circulation), surface integrals (for flux), and
volume integrals, and interpret their physical significance in applied problems.

sections.heading: Method of conducting the course
sections.text:
The instructional approach for this course integrates theory, practice, and computational exposure. Core
concepts and mathematical derivations will be introduced through classroom lectures, while tutorial
sessions will be devoted to reinforcing these ideas through guided problem-solving and application-based
exercises. To supplement in-class learning, three video lectures will be made available, showcasing the
use of computational software (MATLAB) for visualization and problem-solving. Student learning will
be evaluated on a continuous basis through quizzes, assignments, and examinations, ensuring both
conceptual understanding and practical competence.

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
Review of coordinate geometry, Rational Fractions, Complex Numbers and quadratic
equations, Matrices and determinants, Progression and series, permutations and combinations, Binomial
theorem, Functions: Polynomial, Trigonometric, exponential, logarithmic etc., One variable Calculus: Limit and
continuity, Differentiation, Integration. Applications of derivatives and definite integration. Program-specific
applications of the above mathematical concepts.

sections.heading: Scopes and objective of the course
sections.text:
This Course deals with intermediate mathematics that is essential for PCB students who joined BE (E&S
engineering). Course covers set theory, Functions, Coordinate geometry, basic algebra & theory of equations,
permutations and combinations, Binomial theorem, Trigonometry, One Dimensional Calculus: Limit and
continuity, Differentiation, Integration, Application of derivatives and definite integration.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
CLO1. Apply concepts of algebra, trigonometry, matrices, and discrete mathematics to solve mathematical
problems.
CLO2. Analyze and solve problems in coordinate geometry, three-dimensional geometry, and differential
calculus.
CLO3. Apply integral calculus and related mathematical techniques to solve real-world problems.

sections.text:
  Determination of strength, deformation and stability of structural and machine elements.
  Understand the material properties and Idealization of stress-strain curves.

elements, which involve calculation of stress, strain and deformation. This is an essential feature in any
design process.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
This course covers the following topics: Mathematical preliminaries; Fluid statics and forces on
submerged bodies; Integral relations for a control volume; Mass, Momentum and Energy Con-
servation; Reynolds Transport Theorem; Differential relations for fluid flow, Analytical solution of
Navier-Stokes equation; Dimensional analysis and similarity; Inviscid potential flows; Bernoulli’s
Equation; Internal and external viscous flows; Basic compressible flows.

sections.heading: Scope & Objectives of the Course
sections.text:
The objectives of the course are to learn about the following topics:
• Introduction to fluid mechanics and establish its relevance in mechanical engineering.
• Derivation of the equations governing mass, momentum and energy transport.
• Application of the governing equation to solve simple fluid mechanics problems.
• Non-dimensionalization of governing equations and identification of dimensionless
numbers, Modeling and similarity concepts.
• Two dimensional, inviscid, potential flows; Stream function, Velocity potential.
• Analyze laminar and turbulent flows inside pipes, External flow past immersed bodies,
Intro- duction to Boundary layer theory
• One dimensional, compressible flow inside ducts of variable cross-section, normal and
oblique shocks.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Introduction, Structure of Materials (Metal and Ceramics), Dislocations, heat treatment of steel and
strengthening Mechanisms of Metals, Phase diagrams, Iron-carbide phase diagram, Phase transformation
in Metals, Mechanical and thermal properties of Metals, Polymers (Structure, processes and properties),
powder metallurgy.

sections.heading: Scope and Objectives
sections.text:
CO1. Develop  familiarity with  the  different  levels of  structure  (atomic,  crystal, microscopic)  in
engineering materials and deviations from “perfect” structure (structural defects).
CO2. Introduction to characterization method like optical microscope, XRD, SEM, TEM
CO3. Understand the effects of microstructure on the mechanical properties of materials.
CO4. Understand the basis for microstructure development in materials.
CO5. Understand how materials are processed.
CO6. Selection of Materials for specific application

Course Objectives:
  To determine the power output and evaluate the performance of simple thermodynamic
cycles for power generation technologies in terms of thermal efficiency.
  To analyze and evaluate the performance of coal based or gas based power generations
technologies.
  To analyze and evaluate the performance of vapor compression and vapor absorption
refrigeration cycle.
  To analyze and evaluate gas turbine cycle with multistage compression with intercooling,
multistage expansion with reheat and regeneration terms of its efficiency.
  To estimate air conditioning requirements of a space using various air-conditioning
processes.
Course Plan
Module 1: Vapor Power Cycles
Learning Objectives
  To analyze ideal Rankine cycle for a vapor power plant using T•s plot and evaluate thermal
efficiency by applying first law and second law of thermodynamics.
  To evaluate performance of Rankine cycle considering isentropic efficiencies of turbine and
pump.
  To represent the Rankine cycle processes on the Mollier diagram (enthalpy•entropy chart).
  To analyze reheat Rankine cycle for a vapor power plant using T•s plot and evaluate its
performance by applying first law of thermodynamics.
  To evaluate performance of regenerative Rankine cycle using feed water heaters.
  To study boilers their mountings and accessories.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
The course introduces students to concepts and nuances of Mechanical Engineering Design. Content includes
materials, standards and design of machine elements and application of scientific principles, technical knowledge,
and imaginative skills to be developed in a student. The machine elements covered are Shafts, Screw fasteners,
Welded joints, Springs, Brakes & Clutches, Bearings and Gears.
The Tutorial classes of the course will be mainly used for assisted problem solving, consultation and evaluation.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
To prepare a student of mechanical engineering to apply theory and practice of Design of Mechanical Elements.
It is an introductory course laying foundation on design ground rules, application of strength of material principles,
selection of components, and selection of materials for a given application.

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
Unconventional manufacturing processes and analysis, micro-manufacturing technologies,
introduction to computer-aided manufacturing, CNC machines, CNC Part programming,
additive manufacturing, modelling and simulation of manufacturing processes, surface
technologies, related laboratory exercise and fabrication project.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
This course introduces students to advanced manufacturing technologies for fabricating
components across multiple length scales. It focuses on the challenges of machining difficult-
to-machine materials and transforming them into high-value products. The course emphasizes
hands-on learning through CNC  part programming, CNC machine  operation,  additive
manufacturing, and  digital-to-physical manufacturing workflows.  Lectures complement
laboratory sessions by covering the fundamentals, process capabilities, numerical methods, and
optimization techniques required for the analysis and development of advanced manufacturing
processes.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
CLO1.  Explain the  principles,  capabilities,  limitations, and  applications  of advanced
manufacturing processes, including CNC machining, additive manufacturing, and non-
traditional machining.
CLO2. Develop CNC part programs and implement digital manufacturing workflows to
fabricate engineering components using advanced manufacturing systems.
CLO3. Analyze the influence of process parameters, material properties, and machine
characteristics on product quality, productivity, and process performance.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Introduction to manufacturing systems, forecasting, life cycle concepts, facility location and layout planning,
aggregate and batch production planning, scheduling, inventory control, material requirement planning, and
enterprise resource planning,  just-in time and lean manufacturing,  total quality management, supply chain
management and Industry 4.0.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The objective of this course is to impart important decision making processes and analytical tools in design, planning
and control of manufacturing / service processes. At the end of the course the students shall be able to establish routes
and schedules for work that will ensure the optimum utilization of men, materials and machines in a manufacturing /
services.
•   Familiarize fundamental concepts in production / operations management
•   Understand the decision making process in design, planning and control of manufacturing / service systems
•  Develop skills for decision making in conversion process / manufacturing systems

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
This course introduces the necessity, classification, operating principles, and applications of various energy
storage technologies used in modern energy systems. Mechanical, thermal, electrochemical, electrical, and
chemical energy storage systems will be discussed with emphasis on their design, operation, performance
characteristics, advantages, limitations, and practical applications in electric vehicles, renewable energy
integration. The course also covers emerging storage technologies including advanced battery systems,
supercapacitors, hydrogen energy systems, and phase change material-based thermal storage systems.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The objective of  this course  is to provide students with a strong understanding of energy storage
technologies and their role in sustainable energy systems. The course covers fundamental thermodynamic,
electrochemical, and mechanical aspects of energy storage systems along with their design considerations,
performance evaluation, safety issues, and practical applications. The course also aims to familiarize
students with recent advancements, technical challenges, economic considerations, and future prospects of
modern energy storage technologies. The course also introduces Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) as a
simulation tool for the design, analysis, and performance evaluation of energy storage systems, with
emphasis on thermal management and flow behavior.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
The course essentially prepares engineering students to utilize their existing technical knowhow for
sports applications. The specific topics will include, working with human and human movement
patterns,  qualitative and  quantitative  techniques  for  analysis  of human movement.  Sports
performance measure and  analysis. Anthropomorphy, Ergonomics and Task  design. Computer
application in sports, computerized performance measure. Sports surface and its impact on sports
performance, surface testing methods. Sports and training equipment case study, business around
sports

sections.heading: Scope & Objective
sections.text:
This is an introductory course to impart knowledge and skill set related to working with human in
sports  engineering  application.  Understanding human movement  pattern  and  performance
measurement. Understand, assess and analyze effect of equipment, sports surfaces and environment
on sports performance. Use of ergonomic concepts, image processing, smart sensors and data analysis
in sports engineering. Standard techniques of evaluation and testing of sports equipment and sports
surfaces and appreciation of business around sports industry.

sections.heading: Learning outcome
sections.text:
Course Learning Outcomes:
By the end of this course, students will be able to:
Understand the fundamentals of human movement and apply engineering principles to analyze sports
performance.
Appreciate the role of ethics, human factors, and design considerations in sports technology.
Utilize modern computing tools for motion analysis and performance evaluation in sports.
Gain insights into sports infrastructure, surface design, and their impact on athlete performance.
Explore the  business,  innovation, and marketing  potential within the  sports ecosystem from an
engineering perspective.

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
This is a first-level course offered to advanced first degree and higher degree students to understand
the essential concepts in compressible flows. The course contents include Introduction to Gas
Dynamics, Basic equations for compressible flow, Flow with friction and heat addition, Normal shock,
Quasi one-dimensional flow, Oblique shock, Prandtl-Meyer Flow, Potential equation for compressible
flow, Linearized flow solution, and Hypersonic flows.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
a.  Introduce students to important concepts and mathematical formulations of Gas Dynamics
b.  Enable students to formulate and solve engineering problems in Gas Dynamics

sections.heading: Course Learning Outcomes
sections.text:
Upon successful completion of this course, the students will have the following learning outcomes:
a.  Develop a broad understanding of the basic concepts and theories in gas dynamics
b.  Develop an in-depth understanding of various gas dynamic concepts such as flows with heat
addition and friction, normal and oblique shock waves, Prandtl-Meyer expansion waves, Quasi
1D flow in nozzles and diffusers, Linearized solution theory and applications, and Hypersonic
flows

sections.heading: Textbooks and Reference Books
sections.text:
TB:    Ethirajan Rathakrishnan, Gas Dynamics, 7th Edition, Prentice, PHI Learning, 2020.
RB:   John D. Anderson Jr., Modern Compressible Flow: With Historical Perspective, 4th
Edition, McGraw Hill Education, 2021.

sections.heading: Method of Conduct of the Course
sections.text:

The former would involve instructor-led class lectures and problem solving exercises while the latter

sections.text:
Introduction to tensors, tensor algebra and tensor calculus. Kinematics of deformation (displace-
ment, velocity, deformation gradient, material and spatial ﬁeld descriptions, description of local
deformation, linearized kinematics, kinematic rates), left & right Cauchy-Green deformation ten-
sor, Cauchy-Lagrangian strain tensor.  Traction and stress (ﬁrst Piola-Kirchhoff stress, second
Piola- Kirchhoff stress, Biot stress etc). Mechanical conservation and balance laws (conservation
of mass, conservation of linear momentum, conservation of angular momentum, conservation of
energy, work done by stresses and the principle of virtual work, BVP, IVP, calculus of variation).
Constitutive relations (constraints on constitutive relations, frame indifference, objectivity, material
symmetry, constitutive models for linearly elastic, hyperelastic solids and ﬂuid ﬂows).

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
The course introduces smart materials and smart structures through their physical
mechanisms, characteristic responses and engineering use. Major topics include piezoelectric ceramics
and polymers; one-way, two-way and magnetic shape-memory alloys; electro- and magnetorheological
fluids; magnetostrictive and  electrostrictive  materials; and fibre-optic and FBG sensors. Basic
modelling is embedded within the relevant material modules using physically interpretable equations
and response curves. Applications include sensing, actuation, vibration control, damping, structural-
health monitoring, energy harvesting and intelligent devices.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
This undergraduate course develops a foundational understanding of stimulus-
responsive materials and their use in smart structures. Emphasis is placed on physical mechanisms,
observable behaviour, characteristic curves and straightforward engineering comparisons rather than
advanced constitutive modelling. Guided demonstrations, basic experiments, case studies, paper
reviews, assignments and project work will connect theory with practice. These activities are intended
to develop scientific curiosity and encourage interested students to pursue further project- and research-
oriented work in smart materials and structures.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
CO1: Explain the terminology, operating principles, physical mechanisms and characteristic behaviour of
major smart-material families and smart structural systems.
CO2: Interpret basic characteristic curves, experimental observations and performance data to describe
the sensing and actuation behaviour of smart materials.
CO3: Compare major smart-material families and identify suitable materials for simple engineering
applications based on their capabilities, limitations and operating requirements.
CO4: Investigate smart-material behaviour through guided demonstrations, basic experiments, case
studies, paper reviews or project work, and communicate the resulting observations and findings.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
This course presents an exposition to the modern thoughts on quality and related practices. The principles
and techniques for quality control, based on statistical methods and the procedures for quality assurance are
covered. Tools for quality engineering and quality management are dealt in detail. Concepts of reliability and
methods to improve product and systems reliability are also covered. The course is tailored to enable students
to become successful managers in a sustained manner, thereby provide support to the business houses in their
never-ending quest for quality.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
This course is designed to provide an in-depth and holistic understanding of the technology and
principles underlying modern robotics. Over the years, the demand for human-like machines
capable of replacing or assisting humans in diverse and challenging work environments has grown
significantly due to reasons such as efficiency, precision, safety, and the need to operate in
hazardous conditions. In response to this need, the field of robotics has rapidly evolved and
established itself as one of the most critical and promising areas of engineering for the future.
The course aims to build a strong interdisciplinary foundation for students, focusing particularly on
the mechanical aspects of robotic systems while integrating relevant knowledge from electronics,
computer science, and control engineering. It will cover fundamental and advanced concepts related
to mechanisms used in robotic systems, their unique characteristics, and detailed kinematic and
dynamic analysis essential for design and development. Furthermore, students will gain insights into
the  design  methodologies,  practical  implementation  principles,  and  real-world  industrial
applications of robotics. The course will also explore current issues, trends, and innovations in
robotics, enabling students to appreciate its impact across industries and prepare them for future
technological advancements in this rapidly expanding domain.
Text Book:
(T1) Mittal R. K. & Nagrath, I. J., “Robotics and Control”, TMH, 2003 (Reprint 2010 or later).
Reference Books:
(R1) Groover, M. P., et al., “Industrial Robotics”, McGraw Hill ISE, 1986.
(R2) Fu, K. S., et al., Robotic: Control, Sensing, Vision & Intelligence, McGraw Hill ISE, 1987
(R3) Robert J., Schilling, Fundamentals of Robotics: Analysis and Control, Prentice Hall, NJ, 2002.

sections.heading: Scope & Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The scope of the course is limited to an introduction to FEA as applied to elasticity problems in
solid and structural mechanics. This course will train the students to analyze real-world structural
mechanics problems using the finite element method. Students will be introduced to the mathe-
matical basis of finite element analysis, on which nearly all structural analysis software are built.
The objectives of the course are:
CO1. Understand strong and weak formulations, methods of weighted residuals Rayleigh-Ritz
method.
CO2. Understand the finite element method procedure, which converts a given boundary value
problem into a set of algebraic linear equations that can be solved using computer.
CO3. Understand the implementation of FEM for linear analysis of 1D and 2D problems of solid
mechanics and heat transfer.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Design principles of machine tools; stiffness and rigidity of separate construction
elements and their combined behaviour under load; design of stepped and stepless drives; electrical,
mechanical and hydraulic drives; design of bearings and slideways; machine tool controls; machine tool
dynamics; recent developments in machine tool design

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The Course is intended to focus the student’s attention on the
concepts of design, analysis and features of different types of machine Tools, different machine elements to
make a machine tool and new concepts in machine tool engineering.
Course Objectives (CO):
CLO1. To advance the theoretical and fundamental understanding of machining processes
CLO2. To understand the concept of hydraulic and mechanical transmissions employed in machine tools
CLO3. Calculation of machining time of various operations
CLO4. To understand the design of gear boxes for stepped control of speed and feed in machine tools
CLO5. To understand the design solution of different machine tool elements
CLO6. To understand the functioning and operation of numerically control machine tools.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
This course provides a comprehensive foundation in industrial robotic systems and robot control. Topics
include principles of robot kinematics,  statics, dynamics, and control; rigid body motion and coordinate
transformations; rotation matrices, Denavit-Hartenberg parameters forward and inverse kinematics; Jacobian
analysis, workspace and singularity analysis; trajectory planning and motion optimization; robot statics and
dynamics using Euler–Lagrange and Newton–Euler formulations; control system for robot, independent joint
control, computed torque control, and force control; end-effector and gripper design for robotic manipulation
and  precision  assembly;  sensor-integrated  robotic  systems;  collaborative  robotics;  robotic  work-cell
implementation;  and  case  studies  and  applications  of  industrial  robots  in  intelligent  manufacturing
environments.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
This course provides fundamental, theoretical, and applied knowledge of industrial robotics and robot control
with a strong emphasis on hands-on learning and industry-oriented applications. The course develops a rigorous
foundation in robot kinematics, dynamics, motion planning, and control required for the modelling, analysis,
and operation of industrial robotic manipulators.
Students will gain practical exposure to industrial robotic systems used in modern manufacturing environments
for robotic manipulation, precision assembly, collaborative robotics, and  intelligent production systems.
Laboratory sessions and project-based learning will focus on robotic manipulator programming, trajectory
generation, end-effector design, sensor-integrated robotic systems, and robotic work-cell implementation using
industrial-grade platforms.
Course Outcome:
Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to:
CO1  Apply principles of robot kinematics, dynamics, and control to model and analyze industrial robotic
manipulators.
CO2  Design and implement motion planning and control strategies for industrial robotic tasks such as pick-and-
place, assembly, and material handling.
CO3  Design and deploy sensor-integrated robotic work cells for real-world manufacturing applications with
closed-loop control.
CO4  Demonstrate hands-on proficiency and industry readiness by solving practical robotics problems through
labs, projects, and industry-led sessions.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
This course provides students with a comprehensive understanding of molding methods used for plastic components in
the manufacturing of electronic components. It will introduce students to different molding techniques used for plastic
components, and equipment, process considerations, and applications in the electronics industry. The second module
provides an overview of the different materials, characterization and testing procedures, and environmental safety
considerations in the electronic industry. In the third and fourth modules, students will be exposed to different plastic-
moulding processes used in the fabrication of electronic components. The last module will provide basic design aspects
related to injection mould, compression mould, transfer mould, and blow mould for fabricating electronic components.
Through a strong focus on experimental exposure and industry case studies, students will develop practical insights into
advanced manufacturing systems used in the electronics industry.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
This course introduces theoretical, analytical, and practical knowledge of plastic materials used in the electronic industry,
as well as the manufacturing methods for plastic components. It provides students with basic knowledge of advanced
casting methods for fabricating plastic components for the electronics industry. It enables learners to understand the
principles of various advanced casting methods, the casting machines used, the mechanisms of these processes, the
parameters involved, and basic design aspects related to mould. Additionally, this course provides industrial/practical
exposure to industrial component development and various application areas with case studies.

sections.heading: Course Outcomes
sections.text:
CO No.                                      Course Outcome
CO1       Develop an understanding of the moulding processes and testing techniques involved in the fabrication
of plastic components in the electronics industry.
CO2        Selection of appropriate materials for the electronic industry.
CO3       Design and fabricate different plastic components using moulding processes.
CO4       Acquire basic design skills related to injection mould, compression mould, transfer mould, and blow
mould.
CO5       Demonstrate hands-on proficiency and industry readiness by solving practical electronic component
fabrication problems through labs, projects, and industry-led sessions.

sections.text:
•  To understand the injection molding process by producing a simple plastic part of quality based on dimensional
accuracy and surface finish.
•  To study compression molding techniques by creating a composite electronic housing.
•  To study the effect of applied pressure on molten metal flow and solidification behavior during pressure casting.
•   To explore transfer molding by encapsulating a small integrated circuit (IC).
•  To study the influence of pressure on porosity reduction and the mechanical properties of die-cast components.
•  To analyze the effect of injection speed and die temperature on surface finish and dimensional accuracy.
•  To study the influence of injection pressure, temperature, and cooling time on part quality and dimensional
stability.
•  To develop a component using an additive manufacturing process and testing of the part.
•  To explore additive manufacturing techniques by creating a mold pattern for sand casting.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
This course provides a comprehensive understanding of advanced computer-aided design
(CAD) and digital product development techniques used in modern engineering design and
manufacturing. It covers geometric modelling of parametric curves, surfaces, and Non-Uniform
Rational B-Splines (NURBS), along with geometric transformations, mass property evaluation,
and product data exchange standards for seamless CAD interoperability. The course intro-
duces Design of Experiments (DoE) for design optimisation and provides extensive hands-on
training in basic and advanced Geometric Dimensioning and Tolerancing (GD&T) based on
the ASME Y14.5 standard using commercial CAD software. Students will also explore the
fundamentals of generative design, topology optimisation through industrial case studies, and
the principles and applications of additive manufacturing, enabling them to design innovative,
lightweight, and manufacturable engineering products.

sections.heading: Scope & Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The course aims to develop knowledge and practical skills in advanced CAD, geometric mod-
elling, topology optimisation, and additive manufacturing techniques.  It enables students to
apply geometric modelling, GD&T (ASME Y14.5), generative design, and modern engineering
software to design, analyse, and validate innovative and manufacturable engineering products.
The course is intended to enable students to:

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
The course has wide-ranging application in Engineering structures, Machine tool
structures, metal forming, and cold working. The studies deal with the determination of stresses and
displacements in common structural forms beams, shafts, shells etc. subjected to external forces. The
course covers basic theory of elasticity, 2-D and 3-D problems of elasticity, Theories of plastic flow,
Flow of ideally plastic and strain hardening metals, and theory of metal forming processes.

sections.heading: Course Level Objectives
sections.text:
The course is for higher degree students to prepare them in applying the
theory on some problems of practical and design interest. The students will be able to appreciate
underlying meaning of material and structural behavior under complex loading conditions. Students
are also encouraged to do assignments using the ANSYS/ABAQUS package to solve problems of
elasticity and plasticity to compare the analytical solutions.
CO1:  Understand the concept of stress and strain in situations where large deformations are involved.
CO2:  Appreciate the governing differential equations that describe a general boundary value problem
in elasticity.
CO3:  Solve the general elasticity boundary value problems with various boundary conditions using
methods of complex variable techniques
CO4:  Appreciate the concept of yielding and yield  criteria. Yield surface and normality rule,
associated flow rule

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
The course has wide-ranging application in Engineering structures, Machine tool
structures, metal forming, and cold working. The studies deal with the determination of stresses and
displacements in common structural forms beams, shafts, shells etc. subjected to external forces. The
course covers basic theory of elasticity, 2-D and 3-D problems of elasticity, Theories of plastic flow,
Flow of ideally plastic and strain hardening metals, and theory of metal forming processes.

sections.heading: Course Level Objectives
sections.text:
The course is for higher degree students to prepare them in applying the
theory on some problems of practical and design interest. The students will be able to appreciate
underlying meaning of material and structural behavior under complex loading conditions. Students
are also encouraged to do assignments using the ANSYS/ABAQUS package to solve problems of
elasticity and plasticity to compare the analytical solutions.
CO1:  Understand the concept of stress and strain in situations where large deformations are involved.
CO2:  Appreciate the governing differential equations that describe a general boundary value problem
in elasticity.
CO3:  Solve the general elasticity boundary value problems with various boundary conditions using
methods of complex variable techniques
CO4:  Appreciate the concept of yielding and yield  criteria. Yield surface and normality rule,
associated flow rule

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
The course introduces smart materials and smart structures through their physical
mechanisms, characteristic responses and engineering use. Major topics include piezoelectric ceramics
and polymers; one-way, two-way and magnetic shape-memory alloys; electro- and magnetorheological
fluids; magnetostrictive and  electrostrictive  materials; and fibre-optic and FBG sensors. Basic
modelling is embedded within the relevant material modules using physically interpretable equations
and response curves. Applications include sensing, actuation, vibration control, damping, structural-
health monitoring, energy harvesting and intelligent devices.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
This undergraduate course develops a foundational understanding of stimulus-
responsive materials and their use in smart structures. Emphasis is placed on physical mechanisms,
observable behaviour, characteristic curves and straightforward engineering comparisons rather than
advanced constitutive modelling. Guided demonstrations, basic experiments, case studies, paper
reviews, assignments and project work will connect theory with practice. These activities are intended
to develop scientific curiosity and encourage interested students to pursue further project- and research-
oriented work in smart materials and structures.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
CO1: Explain the terminology, operating principles, physical mechanisms and characteristic behaviour of
major smart-material families and smart structural systems.
CO2: Interpret basic characteristic curves, experimental observations and performance data to describe
the sensing and actuation behaviour of smart materials.
CO3: Compare major smart-material families and identify suitable materials for simple engineering
applications based on their capabilities, limitations and operating requirements.
CO4: Investigate smart-material behaviour through guided demonstrations, basic experiments, case
studies, paper reviews or project work, and communicate the resulting observations and findings.

sections.text:
Basic concepts of probability and probability distribution, Standard probability distribution, Sampling and
Sampling Distributions, Confidence intervals, testing significance, Statistical tolerance, Various types of
control charts, Statistical process control techniques, Defect diagnosis and prevention, Basic concepts of
reliability, Reliability design evaluation and control, Method of applying total quality management into
production process.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
This course presents an exposition to the modern thoughts on quality and related practices. The principles
and techniques for quality control, based on statistical methods and the procedures for quality assurance are
covered. Tools for quality engineering and quality management are dealt in detail. Concepts of reliability and
methods to improve product and systems reliability are also covered. The course is tailored to enable students
to become successful managers in a sustained manner, thereby provide support to the business houses in their
never-ending quest for quality.

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
The field of Digital Very Large-Scale Integrated Circuits has gone
through dramatic evolutions and changes. This course builds on the previous course MEL G621
VLSI DESIGN. It is intended to give a detailed knowledge and experience in the design of
advanced VLSI circuits and chips in todays and future nano-scale CMOS technologies. Design
of high-performance digital systems, failure issues, and remedies of problems. Topics will
focus on current issues, including: wiring resistance and how to deal with it, power and Ground
noise and regulation, clock (or asynchronous) system design and how to minimize clocking
overhead, high-speed I/O design, energy minimization, including leakage control. Major VLSI
design challenges are followed by careful treatment of several versatile digital and mixed
analog-digital circuit building blocks frequently utilized in VLSI chips.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
The development of digital technology over the past 50 years has
revolutionized the design and performance of everything from mobile phones to cars and
entertainment systems; and engineers continue to enhance the performance of these devices.
Recent developments in nanotechnology promise further large increases in processing power
with lower power requirements, and will open up a whole new world of applications for digital
techniques. The course aims to learn new techniques to keep up-to-date with developments in
an industrial and/or research setting, and will have hands-on experience of the different stages
of the design of a modern digital system.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
Students will develop an understanding of common design and
timing issues/challenges in digital systems. They will be introduced to high-speed/low-power
circuit logic/ power minimization techniques, as well as wiring models used in digital systems.
Additionally, they will learn about the clock system design and various noise sources that can
interfere with these systems.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
This course is designed to provide in-depth knowledge and
hands-on expertise in designing advanced analog and mixed-signal integrated circuits
with a focus on modern CMOS technologies. The course aims to bridge the gap
between analog fundamentals and practical design of performance-critical blocks
such as Phase-Locked Loops (PLLs), oscillators, and Analog-to-Digital Converters
(ADCs). It equips students to analyze, architect, and implement key mixed-signal
blocks considering design trade-offs, non-idealities, and layout constraints. Emerging
trends such as energy harvesting, sensor interface circuits, and digitally assisted
analog systems are also discussed to build readiness for research and industrial
innovation.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
Upon successful completion of this course, the students will be able to:
a.  Analyse and Design high-resolution, high-speed comparators, mixers, and
signal conditioning blocks for mixed-signal interfaces.
b.  Architect and Evaluate various ADC and DAC topologies based on speed,
resolution, power, and area metrics.
c.  Design and Simulate PLLs and oscillator-based clock generation systems
with attention to phase noise, jitter, and loop stability.
d. Implement  of  Biasing  Circuits  and  Optical/Wireline  Receiver
Transmitter circuits.
Pilani Campus
AUGSD/AGSRD Division
e.  Understand and Apply analog layout methodologies, matching principles,
and noise-aware design techniques.
f.  Demonstrate Proficiency in using industry-grade tools (e.g., Cadence) to
model, simulate, and layout mixed-signal circuits.

sections.heading: Method of conduct of the course
sections.text:
This course follows a design-centric and research-driven pedagogy, aimed at
cultivating both analytical depth and practical proficiency in analog and mixed-signal
design.
  Lecture Sessions will focus on conceptual clarity, design trade-offs, and
architecture-level intuition using real-world mixed-signal systems as case
studies. Select sessions will be used for dissecting key blocks such as PLLs,
ADCs, comparators, mixers, and voltage regulators.
  Research Paper Discussions: Students will regularly read, present, and
critique seminal and recent research papers from IEEE JSSC, TCAS, and
ISSCC  to  stay  aligned  with  state-of-the-art  trends.  Discussions  will
emphasize   circuit  innovation,  design  methodologies,  and   practical
constraints.
  Hands-on Lab Sessions will be conducted using industry-standard EDA
tools (e.g., Cadence, Spectre, Virtuoso) to implement and simulate analog and
mixed-signal building blocks. Students will perform schematic-level design,
corner simulations, layout practices, and post-layout verifications.
Pilani Campus
AUGSD/AGSRD Division
  Mini Projects and Design Challenges: Learners will undertake short design
assignments focused on specific circuit blocks (e.g., comparator, VCO, LDOs
BGRs), progressively leading to a final design project.
  Collaborative Learning will be encouraged through team-based design
reviews, lab debugging, and peer feedback on presentations and reports.
This method ensures that students develop a deep understanding of design principles while also
acquiring practical experience in implementing and validating real circuits, preparing them for
research, industry, or further academic pursuits.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The objective of the course is not only to introduce the basic principles involved in IC fabrication, but
also, to discuss processing technology. Fabrication of integrated circuits is a joint venture by electrical
engineers, chemical engineers, materials scientists, and physicists. This interdisciplinary course builds bridges
across various disciplines.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Historical perspective; Processing overview; Crystallography of semiconductors; Defects in semiconductors;
Clean room; Wafer- growth; cleaning; oxidation; epitaxy; wet and dry etching; lithographic process; diffusion;
ion implantation; deposition of films using CVD, and PVD techniques; device and circuit fabrication; Process
Integration: Passive components, Bipolar Technology and MOSFET Technology, Fabrication of advanced
VLSI devices; System on chip; Future trends and Challenges:
Laboratory components: Simulation of key fabrication processes using CAD tools; Demonstration of basic
FEOL/BEOL fabrication processes; Fabrication and testing of electronic devices.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
The objective of the course is not only to introduce the basic principles involved in IC fabrication, but
also, to discuss processing technology. Fabrication of integrated circuits is a joint venture by electrical
engineers, chemical engineers, materials scientists, and physicists. This interdisciplinary course builds bridges
across various disciplines.

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
We will study the fundamental structures of VLSI Systems at the lowest levels of system abstraction,
namely those associated with the direct application of VLSI devices to particular problems of interest.
The broad topics of coverage includes Principles of operations of CMOS transistors used as a digital
switch and various other topologies used in Digital VLSI Design, Logic implementation strategies and
performance characterization of the VLSI circuits, Low Power Design, different clocking strategies,
symbolic layout systems, CMOS subsystems design and Memory modules.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
The objective of this course is to understand the need and importance of digital VLSI design in CMOS
integrated circuits. To understand different design principles used in the design of Digital VLSI
Circuits & Systems using CMOS with emphasis on low power and high performance.

title: Physics and Modeling of Microelectronic Devices

sections.heading: Course Description
sections.text:
Physics and properties of semiconductor - a review; Semiconductor transport model,
modeling of metal-semiconductor junctions, pn homojunction and heterojunctions, bipolar transistor, JFET,
MESFET, HEMT and; MOS capacitor, modeling of MOSFET, scaling issues, and recent trends in advanced
MOSFETs
Laboratory Components: Modeling and simulation of silicon-based devices with TCAD software. I-V, C-V
measurement of MS and MOS junctions.

sections.heading: Scope and Objective of the Course
sections.text:
This course is designed to provide the basic physical concepts behind microelectronic devices and imparts
information on modeling of these devices for their use as circuit elements in integrated circuits. It will provide
the ability to deal with advanced concepts of microelectronic devices along with non-ideal effects in devices
with an attempt to establish an introduction to research methodology.

title: Verification, Test, and Testability of VLSI Circuits

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
VLSI design flow, Simulation based verification, Test bench
tools and languages, System Verilog, Formal verification, Impact of scaling, wafer
sort or probe test, DC and AC parametric test, Test economics and product quality,
Fault models and types; Fault equivalence, Fault dominance, Automated test
generation for combinational logic (fault simulation, ATPG, D-algorithm, PODEM,
FAN); Test generation for sequential logic; Testability measures, Design for
testability (Full-scan and partial scan, BIST, Boundary scan), Delay fault; Analog
and mixed signal circuit testing, Memory test, IDDQ test

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
The objective of this course is to deal with the study of VLSI
design flow, Functional verification, verification flow, need of electronic testing,
fault modeling, test generation for combinational circuits, test generation for
sequential circuits, fault simulation, Built-In Self-Test (BIST), Memory testing,
Design for Testability (DFT), SoC test, fault diagnosis, Analog/RF test.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
Students will learn the VLSI design flow, understand
the importance of design verification during design flow and also understand the
importance of post fabrication testing in VLSI design flow with exposure to the
design tools.

title: Verification, Test, and Testability of VLSI Circuits

sections.heading: Course description
sections.text:
VLSI design flow, Simulation based verification, Test bench
tools and languages, System Verilog, Formal verification, Impact of scaling, wafer
sort or probe test, DC and AC parametric test, Test economics and product quality,
Fault models and types; Fault equivalence, Fault dominance, Automated test
generation for combinational logic (fault simulation, ATPG, D-algorithm, PODEM,
FAN); Test generation for sequential logic; Testability measures, Design for
testability (Full-scan and partial scan, BIST, Boundary scan), Delay fault; Analog
and mixed signal circuit testing, Memory test, IDDQ test

sections.heading: Scope and Objective
sections.text:
The objective of this course is to deal with the study of VLSI
design flow, Functional verification, verification flow, need of electronic testing,
fault modeling, test generation for combinational circuits, test generation for
sequential circuits, fault simulation, Built-In Self-Test (BIST), Memory testing,
Design for Testability (DFT), SoC test, fault diagnosis, Analog/RF test.

sections.heading: Course learning outcomes
sections.text:
Students will learn the VLSI design flow, understand
the importance of design verification during design flow and also understand the
importance of post fabrication testing in VLSI design flow with exposure to the
design tools.
